knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static directed capacitated networks with designated source and sink nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a directed graph \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\), capacities \(u_{ij}\in[0,\infty]\) for every \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\), and designated source and sink nodes \(s,t\), the maximum-flow problem is to maximize the value of a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a directed network with nonnegative, possibly infinite arc capacities and designated source and sink nodes, the maximum-flow problem seeks a feasible source-to-sink flow of greatest value.
assumptions_latex: s,t\in\mathcal N\text{ are the designated source and sink}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{\operatorname{val}(f):f\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow respecting the arc capacities}\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: s–t Flow over Time with Intermediate Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-time feasible-flow definition for a network with transit times and a fixed horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,u,s,t)$ be a network, let $l:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ assign transit times, and let $T\in\mathbb{R}_+$. An $s$–$t$ flow over time consists of Lebesgue-measurable functions $f_e:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}_+$ satisfying $f_e(\tau)\le u(e)$ for every $e\in E(G)$ and $\tau\in[0,T]$, and, for every $v\in V(G)\setminus\{s\}$ and $a\in[0,T]$, $$\operatorname{ex}_f(v,a):=\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}\int_0^{\max\{0,a-l(e)\}}f_e(\tau)\,d\tau-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}\int_0^a f_e(\tau)\,d\tau\ge0.$$ The value $f_e(\tau)$ is the rate entering $e$ at time $\tau$ and leaving it $l(e)$ time units later; the excess condition permits storage at intermediate vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An s–t flow over time assigns each edge a nonnegative measurable entry rate bounded by its capacity. At every time and every vertex other than the source, cumulative arrived flow must be at least cumulative departed flow, allowing intermediate storage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is an }s\text{–}t\text{ flow over time when it satisfies the stated measurability, capacity, and cumulative-excess conditions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse decomposition of an arbitrary source-to-sink flow, with integral weights when the flow is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,u,s,t)$ be a network and let $f$ be an $s$-$t$ flow in $G$. There exist a family $\mathcal P$ of $s$-$t$ paths, a family $\mathcal C$ of circuits, and weights $w:\mathcal P\cup\mathcal C\to\mathbb R_+$ such that, for every $e\in E(G)$, $f(e)=\sum_{Q\in\mathcal P\cup\mathcal C:\,e\in E(Q)}w(Q)$, while $\sum_{P\in\mathcal P}w(P)=\operatorname{value}(f)$ and $|\mathcal P|+|\mathcal C|\le |E(G)|$. Moreover, if $f$ is integral, then $w$ can be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every source-to-sink flow is a nonnegative weighted sum of source-to-sink paths and circuits using at most as many components as the graph has edges. The total path weight equals the flow value, and an integral flow admits integral component weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal P,\mathcal C,w:\ f(e)=\sum_{Q\ni e}w(Q)\ (\forall e),\quad \sum_{P\in\mathcal P}w(P)=\operatorname{value}(f),\quad |\mathcal P|+|\mathcal C|\le |E(G)|;\quad f\text{ integral}\Rightarrow w\text{ may be integral}

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Walk Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed walks, allowing repeated vertices and arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph with tail and head maps \(\tau,\eta:A\to V\). A directed walk of length \(k\ge 0\) is an alternating sequence \(W=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k)\) such that \(\tau(a_i)=v_{i-1}\) and \(\eta(a_i)=v_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Its initial vertex is \(v_0\), its terminal vertex is \(v_k\), and it is closed when \(v_0=v_k\). Vertices and arcs may repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed walk is a finite, direction-respecting sequence of incident vertices and arcs; repetitions are allowed, and the walk is closed when its endpoints coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k)\) is a directed walk exactly when \(\tau(a_i)=v_{i-1}\) and \(\eta(a_i)=v_i\) for all \(i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed graphs, weak connectivity, and directed traversal objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the convention that an undirected-style walk may traverse a directed arc forward or backward, whereas a directed walk uses only forward arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed graph is \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\), where every arc \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\) is an ordered pair of distinct nodes; both \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) may occur, but \((i,i)\) may not. For \(i\in\mathcal N\), \(I(i)=\{j\in\mathcal N:(j,i)\in\mathcal A\}\) and \(O(i)=\{j\in\mathcal N:(i,j)\in\mathcal A\}\). The graph is connected when the simple undirected graph obtained by forgetting arc directions and merging opposite arcs is connected. A walk consists of nodes \(i_1,\ldots,i_t\) and arcs \(a_1,\ldots,a_{t-1}\) such that each \(a_k\) equals either \((i_k,i_{k+1})\), a forward arc, or \((i_{k+1},i_k)\), a backward arc. A path has all nodes distinct. A cycle has \(i_1,\ldots,i_{t-1}\) distinct and \(i_t=i_1\), and may contain only two distinct nodes. A walk, path, or cycle is directed exactly when every traversed arc is forward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loopless directed graph has ordered arcs and may contain both orientations between two nodes. Its in- and out-neighborhoods record incoming start nodes and outgoing end nodes. Connectivity means connectivity after directions are forgotten. Under the stated convention, a walk records which arc is used and may traverse it forward or backward; paths have distinct nodes, cycles return to their start and may use two distinct nodes, and a traversal is directed only when all arcs are forward.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W\text{ is directed}\iff \text{every arc used by }W\text{ is forward}.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Path Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite simple directed paths, including the zero-length path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A directed path from \(s\) to \(t\) is a directed walk \(P=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k)\) with \(v_0=s\), \(v_k=t\), and pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_k\). Consequently its arcs are also distinct. The case \(k=0\) is permitted and gives the path consisting of the single vertex \(s=t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed path is a direction-respecting walk with no repeated vertex; a single vertex is admitted as a path of length zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a directed \(s\)-\(t\) path exactly when it is a directed walk from \(s\) to \(t\) whose vertices are pairwise distinct.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Walks, paths, cycles, reachability, and graph distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary structural properties for directed or undirected graphs, including edge-weighted variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be directed or undirected. An edge progression from \(v_1\) to \(v_{k+1}\) is a sequence \(v_1,e_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k,e_k,v_{k+1}\), with \(k\ge0\), in which each \(e_i\) joins \(v_i\) to \(v_{i+1}\) with the appropriate orientation in a digraph. It is a walk when its edges are pairwise distinct and is closed when \(v_1=v_{k+1}\). A path is such a walk with pairwise distinct vertices; its first and last vertices are its endpoints, and any two vertices \(x,y\) on it determine a unique subpath \(P_{[x,y]}\). An edge progression from \(v\) to \(w\) exists if and only if a \(v\)-\(w\) path exists; in an undirected graph this reachability relation is an equivalence relation. A circuit or cycle is a closed walk of length \(k\ge2\) whose cyclically listed vertices are pairwise distinct, and the edge set of every closed walk can be partitioned into edge sets of circuits. In a digraph, an undirected path or circuit means one in the underlying undirected graph. Path or circuit length is its number of edges; a spanning path is Hamiltonian, a spanning circuit is a Hamiltonian circuit or tour, and a graph containing one is Hamiltonian. Moreover, \[\operatorname{dist}_G(v,w)=\min\{|E(P)|:P\text{ is a }v\text{-}w\text{ path in }G\},\] with value \(\infty\) when no such path exists, and \(\operatorname{dist}_G(v,w)=\operatorname{dist}_G(w,v)\) for undirected \(G\). Given \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb R\), define \(c(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c(e)\), including \(c(\varnothing)=0\); this is modular on \(2^{E(G)}\), and \[\operatorname{dist}_{(G,c)}(v,w)=\min_{P\text{ a }v\text{-}w\text{ path}}c(E(P)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge progression follows consecutive directed arcs or undirected edges; it is called a walk here when it repeats no edge and is closed when its endpoints coincide. A path also repeats no vertex, and every two of its vertices determine a unique subpath. Progression reachability is equivalent to path reachability and, for undirected graphs, is an equivalence relation. A cycle is a vertex-simple closed walk of at least two edges, and every closed walk's edges partition into cycle edge sets. The packet also defines underlying-undirected paths and cycles in digraphs, Hamiltonian paths and tours, ordinary distance with infinity for unreachable pairs, symmetry in undirected graphs, modular edge-set cost, and minimum-cost path distance.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a directed or undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\leadsto w\iff G\text{ contains a }v\text{-}w\text{ path};\quad \operatorname{dist}_G(v,w)=\infty\text{ if }w\text{ is unreachable from }v;\quad G\text{ undirected}\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}_G(v,w)=\operatorname{dist}_G(w,v),\text{ and every closed-walk edge set partitions into circuit edge sets.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines additive path length and the origin-to-destination shortest-path problem. The mentioned network-flow formulation remains conditional because its arc-length assumption is not supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given designated nodes s,t and arc costs c_a, the length of a directed s-t path P is \ell(P)=\sum_{a\in P}c_a. A shortest path is a directed s-t path P^* satisfying P^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{P}\ell(P). The extract states only that a network-flow formulation is available under an additional, unspecified assumption on the arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed path's length is the sum of its arc costs. A shortest path from the designated origin to the designated destination minimizes that sum. The extract does not state the condition required for the mentioned network-flow formulation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{P\text{ directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path}}\sum_{a\in P}c_a

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Cycle Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple directed cycles represented with a distinguished starting position.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A directed cycle of length \(k\ge 1\) is a closed directed walk \(C=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k)\) satisfying \(v_k=v_0\) and having pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}\). Thus each arc is traversed in its prescribed direction and no vertex repeats except the common initial-terminal vertex. Cyclic rotations represent the same unrooted cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed cycle is a nonempty closed directed walk with no repeated vertex apart from its coincident first and last vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is a directed cycle exactly when it is closed and \(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}\) are pairwise distinct.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Cut Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outgoing and incoming arc boundaries of a vertex subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph and let \(S\subseteq V\). The outgoing and incoming directed boundaries of \(S\) are \[\delta^+(S)=\{a\in A:\tau(a)\in S,\ \eta(a)\in V\setminus S\},\qquad \delta^-(S)=\{a\in A:\tau(a)\in V\setminus S,\ \eta(a)\in S\}.\] If distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\) satisfy \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), then \(S\), the bipartition \((S,V\setminus S)\), or the outgoing boundary \(\delta^+(S)\) is called a directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut, according to context.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The outgoing and incoming boundaries of a vertex subset consist of the arcs crossing its induced partition in the respective directions. An s–t cut has s in the selected subset and t outside it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta^+(S)\) contains exactly the arcs leaving \(S\), while \(\delta^-(S)\) contains exactly the arcs entering \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed Source–Sink Cut and Its Orientations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed cuts determined by a node partition separating a designated source and sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ and let $X\subseteq V$ satisfy $1\in X$ and $m\notin X$, with $\bar X=V\setminus X$. The cut $[X,\bar X]$ consists of arcs having endpoints on opposite sides of the partition. Its forward arcs are $(X,\bar X)=\{(i,j)\in E:i\in X,\ j\in\bar X\}$, and its reverse arcs are $(\bar X,X)=\{(i,j)\in E:i\in\bar X,\ j\in X\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed cut separating source 1 from sink m is induced by a node set containing 1 but not m. Crossing arcs directed out of that set form the forward cut, and crossing arcs directed into it form the reverse cut.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq V,\qquad 1\in X,\qquad m\notin X,\qquad \bar X=V\setminus X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [X,\bar X]=(X,\bar X)\cup(\bar X,X),\quad (X,\bar X)=\{(i,j)\in E:i\in X,j\in\bar X\},\quad(\bar X,X)=\{(i,j)\in E:i\in\bar X,j\in X\}.

children.top_down_role: Capacity, cost, length, lower-bound, and related arc metadata.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc Attribute Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite collections of arc-indexed data used by network models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. An arc attribute system is a finite indexed family \(\mathcal A=(\alpha_j:A\to X_j)_{j\in J}\), where each codomain \(X_j\) specifies the admissible values of attribute \(j\). Equivalently, it is a map \(\alpha:A\to\prod_{j\in J}X_j\) with coordinates \(\alpha_j\). Typical coordinates include capacity, lower bound, cost, length, or label; parallel arcs remain distinct arguments and may carry different attribute vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc attribute system assigns each arc a finite tuple of values, such as capacities, costs, bounds, lengths, or labels.
assumptions_latex: \(X_j\) is the value domain for each \(j\in J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A=(\alpha_j)_{j\in J}\) assigns the attribute vector \(\alpha(a)=(\alpha_j(a))_{j\in J}\) to every \(a\in A\).

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Arc Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc multiplicity with identical ordered endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph with endpoint map \((\tau,\eta):A\to V\times V\). Distinct arcs \(a,b\in A\) are parallel when \(\tau(a)=\tau(b)\) and \(\eta(a)=\eta(b)\). For \((u,v)\in V\times V\), the parallel class is \(A_{uv}=\{a\in A:\tau(a)=u,\ \eta(a)=v\}\), and its multiplicity is \(m_{uv}=|A_{uv}|\). The digraph has parallel-arc structure when \(m_{uv}\ge 2\) for some ordered pair \((u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel arcs are distinct arcs having the same tail and the same head; their multiplicity is the size of the corresponding endpoint class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) and \(b\) are parallel exactly when \((\tau(a),\eta(a))=(\tau(b),\eta(b))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Antiparallel-Arc Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oppositely oriented arcs joining the same two distinct vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. Arcs \(a,b\in A\) are antiparallel when their endpoints are reversed: \(\tau(a)=\eta(b)\), \(\eta(a)=\tau(b)\), and \(\tau(a)\ne\eta(a)\). Equivalently, for distinct vertices \(u,v\in V\), every arc in \(A_{uv}\) is antiparallel to every arc in \(A_{vu}\). The digraph has antiparallel-arc structure when both \(A_{uv}\) and \(A_{vu}\) are nonempty for some \(u\ne v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Antiparallel arcs connect the same two distinct vertices in opposite directions; such structure exists when arcs occur in both directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) and \(b\) are antiparallel exactly when \((\tau(a),\eta(a))=(\eta(b),\tau(b))\) with distinct endpoints.

children.top_down_role: Origins for path, reachability, and flow models.

knowledge_statements.title: Source Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural sources in a directed graph, distinguished from designated flow sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A vertex \(v\in V\) is a source vertex when no arc enters it, equivalently when \(\delta^-(v)=\varnothing\) or its indegree satisfies \(d^-(v)=0\). This structural definition does not require \(v\) to have a positive outdegree. A vertex designated to supply flow may also be called a source in flow models even when incoming arcs exist; that model-specific usage is separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural source has indegree zero. A designated flow source is a separate modeling role and need not have indegree zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is a structural source exactly when \(\delta^-(v)=\varnothing\), equivalently \(d^-(v)=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sink Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural sinks in a directed graph, distinguished from designated flow sinks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A vertex \(v\in V\) is a sink vertex when no arc leaves it, equivalently when \(\delta^+(v)=\varnothing\) or its outdegree satisfies \(d^+(v)=0\). This structural definition does not require \(v\) to have a positive indegree. A vertex designated to absorb flow may also be called a sink even when outgoing arcs exist; that model-specific usage is separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural sink has outdegree zero. A designated flow sink is a separate modeling role and need not have outdegree zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is a structural sink exactly when \(\delta^+(v)=\varnothing\), equivalently \(d^+(v)=0\).

children.title: Terminal Vertices

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Designated endpoint vertices in a directed network model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A terminal system is a specified subset \(T\subseteq V\); each \(v\in T\) is a terminal vertex. Terminal status is model data rather than an intrinsic degree property. When endpoints have distinct roles, one may specify disjoint subsets \(T^+,T^-\subseteq V\) of source and sink terminals and set \(T=T^+\cup T^-\). Depending on the model, paths, demands, or nonzero flow balances are required to begin or end at terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminal is a vertex explicitly designated as an allowed endpoint; terminal status is model data and imposes no degree condition by itself.
assumptions_latex: \(T\subseteq V\) is specified as part of the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is a terminal vertex exactly when \(v\in T\).

children.title: Root Vertices
children.top_down_role: Distinguished origins for rooted network structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Root Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Out-roots defined by directed reachability from one distinguished vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A vertex \(r\in V\) is an out-root, or root under the outward convention, when every vertex \(v\in V\) is reachable from \(r\) by a directed path. Equivalently, \(D\) contains a spanning out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) when \(V\) is finite. Under the dual inward convention, a root is reachable from every vertex; the chosen convention must therefore be stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the outward convention, a root reaches every vertex by a directed path; the inward convention reverses all reachability directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\) is an out-root exactly when for every \(v\in V\) there exists a directed path from \(r\) to \(v\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outward-reachability definition and finite spanning-out-arborescence equivalence are plausible, but no citation is supplied. An authoritative locator is required, particularly because inward and outward root conventions coexist.

knowledge_statements.title: Source–Sink Flow Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite single-commodity feasible flows with one designated source and one designated sink, including arc lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed multigraph, let distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\) be designated, and let arc bounds satisfy \(0\le \ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\). A feasible source–sink flow of value \(F\ge 0\) is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) satisfying \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\) and \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=\begin{cases}F,&v=s,\\-F,&v=t,\\0,&v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible source–sink flow on a finite directed network obeys every arc bound, conserves flow at all vertices other than the designated source and sink, and has equal nonnegative source excess and sink deficit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible with value \(F\ge 0\) exactly when it satisfies the arc bounds and has divergence \(F\) at \(s\), \(-F\) at \(t\), and \(0\) at every other vertex.

notation.meaning: lower and upper flow bounds on arc a

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Splitting Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard reduction of a capacity on the throughput of a conserved zero-balance vertex to an arc capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\in V\) be a zero-balance vertex. Replace \(v\) by \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\), redirect every arc entering \(v\) to \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\), redirect every arc leaving \(v\) from \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\), and add an internal arc \((v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\) with bounds \(0\le x_{(v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})}\le q_v\). Conservation at the two split vertices forces the internal-arc flow to equal both the total flow formerly entering and the total flow formerly leaving \(v\). Consequently, restriction and extension give a bijection between original feasible flows satisfying \(x(\delta^-(v))=x(\delta^+(v))\le q_v\) and feasible flows in the split network, while preserving all original arc flows and the flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a conserved zero-balance vertex, splitting it into input and output copies converts its throughput limit into the capacity of one internal arc and preserves feasible flows bijectively.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed network with nonnegative arc flows and prescribed node balances.
The vertex \(v\in V\) has zero prescribed balance, so feasible flows satisfy \(x(\delta^-(v))=x(\delta^+(v))\).
The throughput of \(v\) is bounded by \(q_v\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restriction and extension define a bijection between original feasible flows satisfying \(x(\delta^-(v))=x(\delta^+(v))\le q_v\) and feasible split-network flows satisfying \(0\le x_{(v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})}\le q_v\).

notation.meaning: Input and output copies of the split vertex.
Arcs entering and leaving the original vertex.

children.title: Capacity Normalization
children.top_down_role: Equivalent representations based on standardized capacity data.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elimination of finite arc lower bounds by an affine change of flow variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have arc bounds \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\) and prescribed divergence \(\operatorname{div}x=b\), where divergence means outflow minus inflow. Define \(y_e=x_e-\ell_e\), \(u'_e=u_e-\ell_e\), and \(b'=b-\operatorname{div}\ell\). Then \(x\mapsto y\) is a bijection between feasible bounded flows and vectors satisfying \(0\le y_e\le u'_e\) and \(\operatorname{div}y=b'\). For a separable objective \(\sum_e c_e(x_e)\), the transformed objective is \(\sum_e c_e(y_e+\ell_e)\). Integer data and integer feasible flows are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting each lower bound converts bounded arcs to zero-lower-bound arcs while adjusting node balances and shifting the objective, without changing feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ feasible}\Longleftrightarrow y=x-\ell\text{ satisfies }0\le y\le u-\ell,\ \operatorname{div}y=b-\operatorname{div}\ell\).

notation.meaning: vector of node outflow minus inflow

knowledge_statements.title: Balance Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a balanced transshipment into a zero-divergence circulation using fixed auxiliary arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have a balance vector \(b\) with \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), using the convention \(\operatorname{div}x=b\). Add a new vertex \(r\). For every \(v\) with \(b_v>0\), add an arc \((r,v)\) whose lower and upper bounds both equal \(b_v\); for every \(v\) with \(b_v<0\), add an arc \((v,r)\) fixed at \(-b_v\). Keeping the original arc bounds, restriction to \(E\) is a bijection between circulations in the augmented network and transshipments satisfying the original balances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed arcs incident to one auxiliary vertex exactly cancel supplies and demands, turning a balanced transshipment into a circulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\operatorname{div}x=b\}\longleftrightarrow\{\widehat{x}:\operatorname{div}\widehat{x}=0\}\) under restriction and the prescribed auxiliary-arc values.

notation.meaning: supply when positive and demand when negative

children.title: Normalization Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting preservation across normalized network representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Equivalence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which capacity and balance normalizations remain bijective and objective-preserving.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The substitutions used for capacity and balance normalization define a feasible-set bijection only when every shifted capacity satisfies \(u_e-\ell_e\ge0\), all introduced fixed arcs are permitted, and the balance vector satisfies \(\sum_v b_v=0\). They preserve integrality when the original bounds and balances are integral. Objective values are preserved only after composing each objective term with the affine substitution and retaining its constant offset. If total balance is nonzero, no closed circulation can represent the instance without an additional external source or sink; if lower-bound shifts are omitted from balances or costs, feasibility or objective equivalence can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalization is equivalent only with consistent capacities, zero total balance, and correctly shifted balances and costs; integral data preserve integrality.
assumptions_latex: Normalization is required to give a bijection of feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\ge\ell\) and \(\sum_v b_v=0\) are necessary consistency conditions for the stated closed-network equivalences.

children.title: Flow-to-Circulation Reductions
children.top_down_role: Representations translating source–sink flow instances into circulation instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-to-Circulation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-value source–sink flow represented by a circulation with one return arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have source \(s\), sink \(t\), and arc capacities \(0\le x_e\le u_e\). For a prescribed \(F\ge0\), add a return arc \(a=(t,s)\) whose lower and upper bounds both equal \(F\). An \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(F\) extends uniquely to a circulation by setting \(x_a=F\), and every circulation in the augmented network restricts uniquely to such a flow. If instead the return arc has bounds \(0\le x_a\le U\), where \(U\) is an upper bound on every feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow value in the original network, then maximizing \(x_a\) is equivalent to maximizing the source–sink flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source–sink flow becomes a circulation by returning its value from the sink to the source through one auxiliary arc; a variable return arc yields the maximum-flow formulation when its capacity does not truncate any feasible flow value.
assumptions_latex: Flow is conserved at every vertex other than \(s,t\).
For the variable-value formulation, \(U\) bounds every feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\text{ is an }s\text{--}t\text{ flow of value }F\Longleftrightarrow (x,x_{(t,s)}=F)\text{ is a circulation}.\)

notation.meaning: valid upper bound on feasible source–sink flow values

children.title: Circulation-to-Transshipment Reductions
children.top_down_role: Representations translating circulation constraints into transshipment balance data.

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation-to-Transshipment Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bounded circulation reduced to a zero-lower-bound transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a circulation \(x\) with bounds \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\) and \(\operatorname{div}x=0\). Set \(y=x-\ell\). Then \(0\le y_e\le u_e-\ell_e\) and \(\operatorname{div}y=-\operatorname{div}\ell\). Thus lower-bounded circulation feasibility is equivalent to a transshipment instance with balance vector \(b=-\operatorname{div}\ell\). Conversely, every feasible transshipment \(y\) for these capacities and balances gives the unique circulation \(x=y+\ell\). The induced balances sum to zero, and integer bounds yield an integral affine correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting lower bounds converts a circulation into a transshipment whose node balances are the negative divergence of those bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\le x\le u,\ \operatorname{div}x=0\Longleftrightarrow 0\le y=x-\ell\le u-\ell,\ \operatorname{div}y=-\operatorname{div}\ell.\)

notation.meaning: lower-bound vector regarded as an arc flow

children.title: Transshipment-to-Flow Reductions
children.top_down_role: Representations translating balanced transshipment instances into source–sink flow instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment-to-Flow Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced zero-lower-bound transshipment feasibility represented by saturation of a supersource–supersink flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have capacities \(0\le x_e\le u_e\) and balance equations \(\operatorname{div}x=b\), where \(B=\sum_{v:b_v>0}b_v=-\sum_{v:b_v<0}b_v\). Add a supersource \(\sigma\), a supersink \(\tau\), an arc \((\sigma,v)\) of capacity \(b_v\) for each \(v\) with \(b_v>0\), and an arc \((v,\tau)\) of capacity \(-b_v\) for each \(v\) with \(b_v<0\). Then the original transshipment is feasible exactly when the augmented network admits a \(\sigma\)-\(\tau\) flow of value \(B\), equivalently a flow saturating every auxiliary arc. Restriction of any such flow to \(E\) is a feasible transshipment. Instances with nonzero lower bounds must first undergo lower-bound normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a balanced transshipment with zero lower bounds, connect a supersource to supply vertices and demand vertices to a supersink; feasibility is equivalent to an auxiliary flow saturating all new arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x\text{ with }0\le x\le u\text{ and }\operatorname{div}x=b\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{maxflow}_{\sigma,\tau}=B\) in the augmented network.

notation.meaning: total supply, equal to total demand

knowledge_statements.title: Source–Sink Path Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure path decomposition for an acyclic nonnegative source–sink flow of nonnegative value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\ge0\) be a flow on a finite directed graph such that \(\operatorname{div}x=0\) on \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\), \(\operatorname{div}x(s)=F\), and \(\operatorname{div}x(t)=-F\) for some \(F\ge0\), where divergence is outflow minus inflow. Suppose the positive-support subgraph of \(x\) contains no directed cycle. Then there exist simple directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\) and coefficients \(\alpha_i>0\) such that \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i\chi^{P_i}\), where \(k\le|\{e\in E:x_e>0\}|\). Moreover, \(F=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i\), and if \(x\) is integral, the coefficients may be chosen as positive integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every acyclic nonnegative source–sink flow whose net value is nonnegative is a positive sum of simple source–sink path flows, using no more components than positive-support arcs.
assumptions_latex: The positive-support subgraph of \(x\) is acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i\chi^{P_i}\), with \(k\le|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\) and \(F=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i\).

notation.meaning: arc-incidence vector of directed path P

knowledge_statements.title: Path–Cycle Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General decomposition of a nonnegative source–sink flow of nonnegative value into paths and directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\ge0\) be a flow on a finite directed graph such that \(\operatorname{div}x=0\) on \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\), \(\operatorname{div}x(s)=F\), and \(\operatorname{div}x(t)=-F\) for some \(F\ge0\), where divergence is outflow minus inflow. Then there are simple directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths \(P_i\), simple directed cycles \(C_j\), and positive coefficients \(\alpha_i,\beta_j\) such that \(x=\sum_i\alpha_i\chi^{P_i}+\sum_j\beta_j\chi^{C_j}\). The total number of path and cycle terms is at most \(|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\), and \(F=\sum_i\alpha_i\). If \(x\) is integral, all coefficients can be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative source–sink flow of nonnegative value decomposes into positive simple source–sink path flows and directed cycle flows, with path weights summing to its value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=\sum_i\alpha_i\chi^{P_i}+\sum_j\beta_j\chi^{C_j}\), with at most \(|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\) terms and \(F=\sum_i\alpha_i\).

notation.meaning: arc-incidence vectors of a directed path and directed cycle

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation Cycle Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive decomposition of a nonnegative circulation into simple directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\ge0\) be a circulation on a finite directed graph, so \(\operatorname{div}x=0\). Then there exist simple directed cycles \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) and coefficients \(\beta_i>0\) such that \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\beta_i\chi^{C_i}\), with \(k\le|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\). Each cycle uses only arcs in \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\). If \(x\) is integral, the coefficients may be chosen as positive integers; in particular, every integral circulation is an integer sum of directed cycle-incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative circulation is a positive sum of simple directed cycle flows, and integral circulations admit integral coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\beta_i\chi^{C_i}\), where \(k\le|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\).

notation.meaning: arc-incidence vector of directed cycle C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition of nonnegative circulations into simple forward-cycle circulations, including the integral refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f\ge 0$ be a nonzero circulation. Then there exist simple circulations $f^1,\ldots,f^k$ involving only forward arcs and positive scalars $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ such that $f=\sum_{i=1}^k a_i f^i$. If $f$ is integral, all $a_i$ may be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonzero nonnegative circulation is a positive combination of simple circulations using only forward arcs. If the circulation is integral, the coefficients can be chosen as positive integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists k,\ f^1,\ldots,f^k,\ a_1,\ldots,a_k>0:\quad f=\sum_{i=1}^k a_i f^i;\qquad f\in\mathbb Z^{\mathcal A}\Rightarrow a_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\ \forall i.

knowledge_statements.title: Conformal Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-compatible decomposition of a signed arc vector into elementary paths and cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix reference orientations on a finite graph and let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) have divergence \(b\). Then \(x\) can be written as \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i g_i\), where \(\alpha_i>0\), each \(g_i\in\{-1,0,1\}^{E}\) is the signed incidence vector of a simple path joining a positive-divergence vertex to a negative-divergence vertex or of a simple cycle, and every term is conformal to \(x\): \(g_{i,e}x_e\ge0\) for all arcs. One may choose \(k\le|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\), so the sum involves no sign cancellation on any coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any signed flow vector decomposes into sign-compatible elementary paths and cycles without coordinatewise cancellation.
assumptions_latex: The underlying graph is finite with fixed reference orientations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\alpha_i g_i\), with \(\alpha_i>0\), \(g_{i,e}x_e\ge0\), and \(k\le|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\).

notation.meaning: signed incidence vector of an elementary path or cycle
divergence of the signed arc vector

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Residual Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual network for a feasible flow with lower and upper arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible flow \(x\) with \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\), its capacity residual network has the same vertices. For each original arc \(e=(v,w)\), it contains a forward residual arc \((v,w)\) of residual capacity \(u_e-x_e\) when positive and a backward residual arc \((w,v)\) of residual capacity \(x_e-\ell_e\) when positive. Distinct residual arcs are retained when parallel arcs arise. Sending \(\delta\) units on a forward residual arc increases \(x_e\) by \(\delta\); sending them backward decreases \(x_e\) by \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual arcs encode exactly how much a feasible flow may be increased or decreased on each original arc.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) satisfies \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\) on every arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_x(e^+)=u_e-x_e\) and \(r_x(e^-)=x_e-\ell_e\), retaining precisely the arcs of positive residual capacity.

notation.meaning: forward and backward residual copies of original arc e

knowledge_statements.title: Costed Residual Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual network carrying marginal linear costs for feasible flow modifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each original arc \(e\) have linear unit cost \(c_e\), and let \(x\) be feasible under bounds \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\). The costed residual network is the capacity residual network in which the forward residual copy of \(e\) has cost \(c_e\) and the backward copy has cost \(-c_e\). If a residual flow \(z\) is added to \(x\) according to these forward and backward directions, then the change in total linear cost is exactly the residual cost \(\sum_a c_x(a)z_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward residual arcs retain original costs, backward arcs negate them, so residual-flow cost equals the resulting change in objective.
assumptions_latex: Arc costs are linear and finite.
\(x\) is feasible for the stated lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_x(e^+)=c_e\), \(c_x(e^-)=-c_e\), and \(c(x\oplus z)-c(x)=\sum_a c_x(a)z_a\).

notation.meaning: cost function on residual arcs at flow x
flow obtained by applying residual modification z

children.title: Residual Path Structure
children.top_down_role: Path geometry within capacity-residual or costed-residual networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Path Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible adjustment induced by a simple directed path in a capacity residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible flow and let \(P\) be a simple directed \(a\)-to-\(b\) path in its labeled residual network \(G_x\). For \(0<\delta\leq\min_{r\in P}\rho_x(r)\), increase each original-arc flow by \(\delta\) when \(P\) uses its forward residual copy and decrease it by \(\delta\) when \(P\) uses its reverse copy. The resulting flow \(x'\) respects all capacity bounds, has the same divergence as \(x\) at every internal vertex of \(P\), and satisfies \(b_{x'}(a)=b_x(a)+\delta\) and \(b_{x'}(b)=b_x(b)-\delta\), where divergence is outflow minus inflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual path permits a capacity-feasible adjustment that preserves balance internally and transfers its augmentation amount from the path's initial vertex to its terminal vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with capacities \(u_e\geq 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x'\) is capacity-feasible and \(b_{x'}-b_x=\delta(\mathbf 1_a-\mathbf 1_b)\).

notation.meaning: Residual capacity of labeled residual arc r.
Outflow minus inflow of x at vertex v.

children.title: Residual Cycle Structure
children.top_down_role: Cycle geometry within capacity-residual or costed-residual networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Cycle Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-feasible circulation adjustment induced by a simple directed residual cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible flow and let \(C\) be a simple directed cycle in its labeled residual network \(G_x\). For \(0<\delta\leq\min_{r\in C}\rho_x(r)\), augment forward residual copies and cancel reverse residual copies by \(\delta\). The resulting flow \(x'\) satisfies \(0\leq x'_e\leq u_e\) for every original arc and \(b_{x'}(v)=b_x(v)\) for every vertex \(v\). Thus a residual-cycle adjustment changes neither the prescribed divergence vector nor the value of an \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmenting around a residual cycle preserves every vertex balance and the flow value while remaining feasible up to the cycle's minimum residual capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x'\) is feasible and \(b_{x'}=b_x\).

notation.meaning: Simple directed cycle of labeled residual arcs.

children.title: Path–Cycle Residual Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Structural separation of residual supports into path-type and cycle-type components.

knowledge_statements.title: Path–Cycle Residual Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite decomposition of a nonnegative residual flow with one source and one sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z\geq 0\) be a flow on a finite residual network such that its divergence vanishes outside distinct vertices \(s,t\), with \(b_z(s)=\lambda\geq0\) and \(b_z(t)=-\lambda\). Then there exist simple directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) paths \(P_1,\ldots,P_p\), simple directed cycles \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\), and positive coefficients \(\alpha_i,\beta_j\) such that
\[z=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_i\chi^{P_i}+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\beta_j\chi^{C_j},\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{p}\alpha_i=\lambda.\]
Every path and cycle used has support contained in \(\operatorname{supp}(z)\); hence the decomposition is conformal and introduces no oppositely directed residual adjustment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative residual flow with only source–sink imbalance decomposes into supported simple source–sink paths and directed cycles with positive weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\) has the displayed conformal path–cycle decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Reachability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachable vertex set and its closure property in a capacity residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible flow \(x\), a vertex \(v\) is residually reachable from \(s\) if the residual network \(G_x\) contains a directed \(s\)-to-\(v\) path whose arcs all have positive residual capacity. Define
\[R_x(s)=\{v\in V: v\text{ is residually reachable from }s\}.\]
The set is closed under positive-residual arcs: if \(u\in R_x(s)\) and \((u,v)\) is a residual arc with \(\rho_x(u,v)>0\), then \(v\in R_x(s)\). Consequently, when \(t\notin R_x(s)\), no positive-residual arc leaves \(R_x(s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual reachability consists of vertices accessible from a start vertex through positive-capacity residual arcs; this set is closed under such outgoing arcs.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible flow on a finite directed capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_x(s)\) is closed under traversal of positive-residual arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparison of Feasible Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding the signed difference of two feasible flows as a nonnegative residual flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x,y\) be feasible flows satisfying the same arc bounds \(0\leq x_e,y_e\leq u_e\). On the labeled residual network of \(x\), define
\[z(e^+)=\max\{y_e-x_e,0\},\qquad z(e^-)=\max\{x_e-y_e,0\}.\]
Then \(0\leq z(r)\leq\rho_x(r)\), and applying \(z\) to \(x\) recovers \(y\):
\[y_e=x_e+z(e^+)-z(e^-).\]
Moreover, residual divergence satisfies \(b_z=b_y-b_x\). In particular, if \(x\) and \(y\) have the same prescribed divergence, then \(z\) is a residual circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed difference between two capacity-feasible flows is represented uniquely arcwise by nonnegative forward or reverse residual adjustments, with divergence equal to the balance difference.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) obey the same capacity bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=x+z^+-z^-\), \(0\leq z\leq\rho_x\), and \(b_z=b_y-b_x\).

notation.meaning: Labeled forward and reverse residual copies of original arc e.

children.title: Augmentation Geometry
children.top_down_role: Feasible-flow changes associated with increasing routed support.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of increasing an source–sink flow along a directed residual path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow and let \(P\) be a directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path in \(G_x\). For \(0<\delta\leq\min_{r\in P}\rho_x(r)\), the residual-path adjustment \(x'=x\oplus\delta\chi^P\) lies on the feasible segment generated by \(P\). It preserves flow conservation at \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\) and increases the flow value by exactly \(\delta\): \(\operatorname{val}(x')=\operatorname{val}(x)+\delta\). At the maximal admissible step, at least one residual arc of \(P\) becomes saturated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Moving along a residual source–sink path gives a feasible segment that increases flow value linearly until some residual arc is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(x\oplus\delta\chi^P)=\operatorname{val}(x)+\delta\).

notation.meaning: Flow obtained by augmenting or canceling according to residual path P.

children.title: Cancellation Geometry
children.top_down_role: Feasible-flow changes associated with reversing or removing routed support.

knowledge_statements.title: Cancellation Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of decreasing an source–sink flow along a reverse residual path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow and let \(P\) be a directed \(t\)-to-\(s\) path in \(G_x\). For \(0<\delta\leq\min_{r\in P}\rho_x(r)\), applying the residual adjustment along \(P\) produces a feasible flow \(x'=x\oplus\delta\chi^P\). It preserves conservation at all vertices other than \(s,t\) and cancels exactly \(\delta\) units of flow value:
\[\operatorname{val}(x')=\operatorname{val}(x)-\delta.\]
At the maximal admissible step, at least one residual arc of \(P\) has zero remaining residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual sink–source path defines a feasible cancellation direction that decreases the flow value linearly until a residual capacity becomes tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(x\oplus\delta\chi^P)=\operatorname{val}(x)-\delta\).

children.title: Mixed Residual Adjustments
children.top_down_role: Residual changes combining forward augmentation with reverse cancellation.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Residual Adjustments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous forward augmentation and reverse cancellation on labeled residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be capacity-feasible and let \(z\) be a nonnegative flow on its labeled residual network satisfying \(0\leq z(r)\leq\rho_x(r)\). Define the mixed adjustment by
\[x'_e=x_e+z(e^+)-z(e^-)\qquad(e\in E).\]
Then \(0\leq x'_e\leq u_e\) for every \(e\), and \(b_{x'}=b_x+b_z\). Thus forward residual flow represents augmentation, reverse residual flow represents cancellation, and any balanced mixture \(b_z=0\) is a feasible circulation adjustment preserving the divergence of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded residual flow combines forward augmentation and reverse cancellation; its divergence is exactly the change in the original flow's vertex balances.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) is nonnegative and bounded by residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x'\) is capacity-feasible and \(b_{x'}-b_x=b_z\).

notation.meaning: Forward augmentation on original arc e.
Reverse cancellation on original arc e.

children.title: Support-Minimal Difference Flows
children.top_down_role: Difference flows whose nonzero arc support admits no smaller structural representative.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Minimal Difference Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support characterization of elementary nonnegative flows balanced outside two distinguished vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\neq0\) be a nonnegative flow on a finite directed graph, with \(b_z(v)=0\) for every \(v\notin\{s,t\}\). Suppose no nonzero flow \(w\geq0\) satisfying the same balance restriction has \(\operatorname{supp}(w)\subsetneq\operatorname{supp}(z)\). Then the support of \(z\) is either a simple directed cycle or a simple directed path joining \(s\) and \(t\) in one orientation. In the cycle case \(z=\alpha\chi^C\); in the path case \(z=\alpha\chi^P\), for some \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero support-minimal flow balanced away from two terminals is a positive multiple of either one simple terminal path or one directed cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) is support-minimal among flows with that balance restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=\alpha\chi^P\) or \(z=\alpha\chi^C\) for some \(\alpha>0\).

notation.meaning: Arcs on which z is positive.
A simple terminal path or simple directed cycle.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x,y\) be capacity-feasible flows and let \(d=y-x\). Encode \(d\) as the nonnegative residual flow \(z\) of \(x\), choosing the forward copy of \(e\) when \(d_e>0\) and the reverse copy when \(d_e<0\). If \(b_d\) vanishes outside \(s,t\), then
\[d=\sum_i\alpha_i g^{P_i}+\sum_j\beta_j g^{C_j},\qquad \alpha_i,\beta_j>0.\]
Here each \(g^{P_i}\) or \(g^{C_j}\) is the signed original-arc incidence vector of a simple residual terminal path or cycle. Every summand is conformal to \(d\): its nonzero coordinates have the same signs as the corresponding coordinates of \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible-flow difference decomposes into sign-compatible elementary residual paths and cycles, so no component reverses the net adjustment on any original arc.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\neq0\) be a signed arc vector whose divergence vanishes outside designated vertices \(s,t\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(c_e\in\mathbb{R}\) be the cost of each arc \(e\), and let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct. Assume that at least one directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists and that no directed cycle has negative total cost. With divergence defined as outflow minus inflow, the single-pair shortest-path value equals
\[\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e: x\geq0,\ b_x(s)=1,\ b_x(t)=-1,\ b_x(v)=0\text{ for every }v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\right\}.\]
The constraint matrix is a node-arc incidence matrix, so an optimal integral solution exists. Removing directed cycles from an optimal integral solution without increasing its cost yields the incidence vector of an optimal simple directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a directed source-to-target path exists and there are no negative-cost directed cycles, the single-pair shortest-path problem is equivalent to a minimum-cost unit source-sink flow problem, and an optimal simple path can be recovered from an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Pair Shortest-Path Models

children.title: Single-Source Shortest-Path Models
children.top_down_role: Shortest-path models from one designated origin to multiple destinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Source Shortest-Path Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the directed, weighted single-source distance problem without reachable negative cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), and fix \(s\in V\). The single-source shortest-path model asks for the vector \(d_s:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) defined by
\[d_s(v)=\inf\left\{\sum_{a\in P}\ell(a):P\text{ is a directed }s\text{-}v\text{ path}\right\}.\]
The empty path gives \(d_s(s)=0\), and \(d_s(v)=+\infty\) when \(v\) is unreachable from \(s\). If no negative directed cycle is reachable from \(s\), every finite value is attained by a simple path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model computes minimum path lengths from one fixed source to every vertex, using infinity for unreachable vertices.
assumptions_latex: No negative directed cycle is reachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_s(v)\) is the minimum length of an \(s\)-to-\(v\) path, or \(+\infty\) if none exists.

notation.meaning: distance from source s to vertex v
sum of arc lengths along path P

knowledge_statements.title: All-Pairs Shortest-Path Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the distance-matrix form of the directed all-pairs problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with length function \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\). The all-pairs shortest-path model asks for the matrix \(D\in(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\})^{V\times V}\) whose entries are
\[D_{uv}=\inf\left\{\sum_{a\in P}\ell(a):P\text{ is a directed }u\text{-}v\text{ path}\right\}.\]
Set \(D_{uu}=0\) using the empty path and \(D_{uv}=+\infty\) when \(v\) is unreachable from \(u\). In the absence of negative directed cycles, every finite entry is attained by a simple path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model computes the minimum path length for every ordered vertex pair and records infinity when no connecting path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{uv}\) equals the shortest directed \(u\)-to-\(v\) path length for every \((u,v)\in V^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bellman Optimality Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the Bellman equations and optimal-prefix property for single-source distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), fix \(s\in V\), and assume that no negative directed cycle is reachable from \(s\). Let \(d(v)\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be the shortest-path distance from \(s\) to \(v\), using \(+\infty+r=+\infty\). Then \(d(s)=0\), and every reachable \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\) satisfies
\[d(v)=\min_{(u,v)\in A}\{d(u)+\ell(u,v)\}.\]
If a shortest \(s\)-to-\(v\) path ends with \((u,v)\in A\), its prefix ending at \(u\) is a shortest \(s\)-to-\(u\) path and \(d(v)=d(u)+\ell(u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every reachable non-source vertex has distance equal to the minimum predecessor distance plus the final arc length, and every prefix of a shortest path is shortest to its endpoint.
assumptions_latex: No negative directed cycle is reachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every reachable \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\), \(d(v)=\min_{(u,v)\in A}\{d(u)+\ell(u,v)\}\), and shortest-path prefixes are shortest.

notation.meaning: shortest-path distance from s to v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bellman equation and its uniqueness boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-to-one shortest-path distances with the destination value normalized to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume every node has a directed path to destination \(n\), every directed cycle has nonnegative length, and \(p_n^*=0\). For \(O(i)=\{k:(i,k)\in\mathcal A\}\), the shortest-path distances satisfy \[p_i^*=\min_{k\in O(i)}\{c_{ik}+p_k^*\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1.\] Thus, every suffix of a shortest path is itself shortest. Bellman's equations may have multiple solutions: if every directed cycle has positive length, \(p^*\) is the unique solution; if every directed cycle has nonnegative length, \(p^*\) is the componentwise largest solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance from a node to the destination is the minimum of the first arc length plus the remaining distance, so every suffix of a shortest path is shortest. Positive cycle lengths make the distance vector the unique Bellman solution; nonnegative cycle lengths guarantee only that it is the largest solution.
assumptions_latex: \forall i\in\mathcal N\setminus\{n\},\ \exists\text{ a directed path from }i\text{ to }n.
\ell(C)\ge 0\text{ for every directed cycle }C;\ \ell(C)>0\text{ for the uniqueness conclusion.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_i^*=\min_{k\in O(i)}\{c_{ik}+p_k^*\};\quad p^*\text{ is unique under positive cycle lengths and componentwise largest under nonnegative cycle lengths.}

children.title: Feasible Potential Certificates
children.top_down_role: Potential-based certificates for shortest-path feasibility and optimality contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Potential Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies lower bounds, and optimality when paired with a tight path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with length function \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), and let \(s,t\in V\). A potential \(\pi:V\to\mathbb R\) normalized by \(\pi(s)=0\) is feasible if
\[\pi(v)-\pi(u)\le \ell(u,v)\qquad\text{for every }(u,v)\in A.\]
For every directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path \(Q\), feasibility certifies \(\pi(t)\le\ell(Q)\). If a supplied directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path \(P\) satisfies \(\ell(P)=\pi(t)\), then \((P,\pi)\) certifies that \(P\) is shortest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible normalized potential certifies a lower bound on every source-target path; a supplied path attaining that bound is certified shortest.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a directed path from \(s\) to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible \(\pi\) satisfies \(\pi(t)\le d_s(t)\); if \(\ell(P)=\pi(t)\), then \(P\) is shortest and \(d_s(t)=\pi(t)\).

notation.meaning: minimum length of a directed s-to-t path

children.title: Reduced-Length Structure
children.top_down_role: Arc-length representations induced by vertex potentials.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Length Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records telescoping, nonnegativity, and tight-arc properties of reduced lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\pi:V\to\mathbb R\). Define
\[\ell_\pi(u,v)=\ell(u,v)+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\qquad((u,v)\in A).\]
For every directed path \(P\) from \(x\in V\) to \(y\in V\),
\[\ell_\pi(P)=\ell(P)+\pi(x)-\pi(y).\]
Thus reduced lengths preserve the ordering of paths with the same endpoints, and \(\pi(v)-\pi(u)\le\ell(u,v)\) for every \((u,v)\in A\) exactly when \(\ell_\pi(u,v)\ge0\) for every \((u,v)\in A\). If \(s\in V\), every vertex is reachable from \(s\), and \(\pi(v)=d_s(v)\) for all \(v\in V\), then every arc of any shortest-path arborescence rooted at \(s\) has reduced length zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced lengths telescope along paths, preserve comparisons between paths with fixed endpoints, are nonnegative exactly for feasible potentials, and vanish on shortest-path-tree arcs under distance potentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every directed \(x\)-to-\(y\) path \(P\), \(\ell_\pi(P)=\ell(P)+\pi(x)-\pi(y)\), and potential feasibility is equivalent to \(\ell_\pi(a)\ge0\) for every \(a\in A\).

notation.meaning: length function reduced by potential pi
shortest-path distance from s to v

children.title: Potential–Length Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between feasible potentials and reduced arc lengths.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential–Length Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes shortest-path length as the greatest feasible potential difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), let \(s,t\in V\), suppose that \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), and assume that \(G\) has no negative directed cycle. Then
\[d_s(t)=\max\left\{\pi(t)-\pi(s):\pi:V\to\mathbb R,\ \pi(v)-\pi(u)\le\ell(u,v)\text{ for every }(u,v)\in A\right\}.\]
The maximum is attained. For an attaining potential \(\pi\), define \(\ell_\pi(u,v)=\ell(u,v)+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\). A directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path is shortest if and only if every one of its arcs has zero reduced length under \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shortest source-target path length equals the maximum feasible potential difference, and under an attaining potential the shortest paths are exactly the paths composed of zero-reduced-length arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_s(t)=\max\{\pi(t)-\pi(s):\pi(v)-\pi(u)\le\ell(u,v)\ \text{for every }(u,v)\in A\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines potential-based arc reweighting for a real-weighted digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a digraph, \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\), and \(\pi:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}\). For each arc \((x,y)\in E(G)\), define its reduced cost by \(c_\pi(x,y):=c(x,y)+\pi(x)-\pi(y)\). The potential \(\pi\) is feasible when \(c_\pi(e)\ge 0\) for every \(e\in E(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc's reduced cost is its original cost plus the tail potential minus the head potential. A potential is feasible when all reduced arc costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_\pi(x,y)=c(x,y)+\pi(x)-\pi(y),\qquad \pi\text{ is feasible}\iff (\forall e\in E(G))\;c_\pi(e)\ge 0

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path Tree Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies all single-source distances using tight tree arcs and global arc inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), fix \(s\in V\), and assume every vertex is reachable from \(s\). Let \(T\subseteq A\) be a spanning arborescence rooted at \(s\), with parent \(p(v)\) for each \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\), and let \(d:V\to\mathbb R\). The pair \((T,d)\) is a shortest-path-tree certificate if \(d(s)=0\),
\[d(v)=d(p(v))+\ell(p(v),v)\qquad(v\in V\setminus\{s\}),\]
and
\[d(v)\le d(u)+\ell(u,v)\qquad((u,v)\in A).\]
Under these conditions, \(d(v)=d_s(v)\) for every \(v\in V\), and the unique \(s\)-to-\(v\) path in \(T\) is shortest for every \(v\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tight parent arcs together with valid inequalities on every graph arc certify all source distances and all paths in the rooted shortest-path tree.
assumptions_latex: \(s\in V\), and every vertex is reachable from \(s\).
\(T\subseteq A\) is a spanning arborescence rooted at \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)=d_s(v)\) for every \(v\in V\), and every rooted tree path in \(T\) is shortest.

notation.meaning: candidate spanning arborescence rooted at s

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cycle Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certifies that shortest-walk values are unbounded below through an explicit reachable negative cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), and fix \(s\in V\). A negative-cycle certificate consists of a directed path from \(s\) to a vertex \(v_0\) and a directed cycle \(C=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k=v_0)\) satisfying
\[\ell(C)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\ell(v_{i-1},v_i)<0.\]
For \(t\in V\), define the shortest-walk value
\[d_s^{\mathrm{walk}}(t)=\inf\{\ell(W):W\text{ is a directed walk from }s\text{ to }t\}.\]
For every vertex \(t\) reachable from \(C\), the certificate establishes \(d_s^{\mathrm{walk}}(t)=-\infty\), so no minimum-length directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) walk exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source-reachable directed cycle of negative total length certifies that every downstream shortest-walk value is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a directed cycle reachable from \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every vertex \(t\) reachable from \(C\), \(d_s^{\mathrm{walk}}(t)=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: infimum of lengths of directed s-to-t walks

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest-Path Linear-Programming Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the single-pair path-flow primal and vertex-potential dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with \(\ell:A\to\mathbb R\), and let distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\) satisfy that a directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists. Assume that \(G\) has no negative directed cycle. Define \(b_s=1\), \(b_t=-1\), and \(b_v=0\) for \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\). The shortest \(s\)-to-\(t\) path length equals
\[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}\ell(a)x_a:\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\ \text{for every }v\in V,\ x_a\ge0\ \text{for every }a\in A\right\}.\]
Its linear-programming dual is
\[\max\left\{\pi(t)-\pi(s):\pi:V\to\mathbb R,\ \pi(v)-\pi(u)\le\ell(u,v)\ \text{for every }(u,v)\in A\right\}.\]
Both optima are attained and equal, and an optimal primal solution can be chosen as the incidence vector of a shortest directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum-cost nonnegative unit-flow formulation and the maximum feasible potential-difference formulation have equal optima, equal to the shortest source-target path length.
assumptions_latex: \(s,t\in V\), \(s\ne t\), and a directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed unit-flow minimum and feasible-potential maximum are attained and equal to \(d_s(t)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Breadth-First Search for Unit Lengths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies single-source BFS for directed or undirected unit-length graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite graph \(G=(V,A)\) with \(\ell(a)=1\) for every arc and source \(s\), initialize \(d(s)=0\), \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\), and a FIFO queue containing \(s\). Repeatedly remove the queue front \(u\). For each outgoing arc \((u,v)\), if \(d(v)=+\infty\), set \(d(v)=d(u)+1\), set \(p(v)=u\), and append \(v\). Stop when the queue is empty. The labels are shortest-path lengths, and the parent arcs form a shortest-path tree on the reachable vertices. With adjacency lists, the running time is \(O(|V|+|A|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: BFS discovers vertices by increasing numbers of arcs, producing unit-length distances and a shortest-path tree in linear time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)=d_s(v)\) for every \(v\in V\), in \(O(|V|+|A|)\) time with adjacency lists.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Shortest Paths in Acyclic Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies one-pass relaxation in topological order for weighted directed acyclic graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed acyclic graph \(G=(V,A)\), arbitrary real arc lengths, and source \(s\), compute a topological ordering \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). Initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\). Process vertices in topological order; when processing \(u\), relax every outgoing arc \((u,v)\) by replacing \(d(v)\) with \(\min\{d(v),d(u)+\ell(u,v)\}\), recording \(u\) as parent after a strict improvement. After the single pass, \(d(v)\) is the shortest distance from \(s\) to \(v\). The running time is \(O(|V|+|A|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a DAG, relaxing outgoing arcs once in topological order computes shortest distances even when arc lengths are negative.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d(v)=d_s(v)\) for all \(v\in V\), with running time \(O(|V|+|A|)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computes fixed-length minimum-walk values, applies the minimum-mean-cycle min–max criterion, and recovers a circuit through predecessor pointers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a weighted digraph $G$ with $c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}$, adjoin a new vertex $s$ and zero-weight arcs $(s,x)$ to every original vertex. Set $n=|V(G)|$, $F_0(s)=0$, and $F_0(x)=\infty$ for $x\ne s$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, compute
\[
F_k(x)=\min_{(w,x)\in E(G)}\{F_{k-1}(w)+c(w,x)\}
\]
and store a minimizing predecessor $p_k(x)$. If $F_n(x)=\infty$ for every $x$, report that $G$ is acyclic. Otherwise choose $x$ minimizing
\[
\max_{\substack{0\le k\le n-1\\F_k(x)<\infty}}\frac{F_n(x)-F_k(x)}{n-k},
\]
trace the corresponding length-$n$ predecessor walk from $s$ to $x$, and output any directed circuit contained in it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a zero-cost source reaching every vertex, compute minimum weights and predecessors for walks of every length through n, report acyclicity if no length-n walk exists, otherwise select a vertex using Karp’s min–max expression and return a circuit from its predecessor walk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure outputs a minimum-mean directed circuit, or reports that }G\text{ is acyclic}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A min–max characterization using minimum weights of fixed-length directed walks from a universally reaching source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a digraph, $n=|V|$, and $c:E\to\mathbb{R}$. Suppose $s\in V$ reaches every vertex. For $x\in V$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, let $F_k(x)$ be the minimum weight of a length-$k$ directed walk from $s$ to $x$, with $F_k(x)=\infty$ if none exists. If $\mu(G,c)$ is the minimum mean weight of a directed circuit, with $\mu(G,c)=\infty$ when $G$ is acyclic, then
\[
\mu(G,c)=\min_{x\in V}\max_{\substack{0\le k\le n-1\\F_k(x)<\infty}}\frac{F_n(x)-F_k(x)}{n-k}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a weighted digraph with a source reaching every vertex, the minimum circuit mean equals the minimum over terminal vertices of the maximum normalized difference between the minimum weights of length-n and shorter source-to-vertex walks. The value is infinity for an acyclic digraph.
assumptions_latex: F_k(x)=\min\{\text{weight}(P):P\text{ is a length-}k\text{ directed walk from }s\text{ to }x\},\text{ or }\infty\text{ if none exists}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu(G,c)=\min_{x\in V}\max_{\substack{0\le k\le n-1\\F_k(x)<\infty}}\frac{F_n(x)-F_k(x)}{n-k},\qquad \mu(G,c)=\infty\text{ if }G\text{ is acyclic}

knowledge_statements.title: Generic Relaxation Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States an edge-relaxation scheme with Bellman–Ford passes and cycle detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G=(V,A)\), lengths \(\ell\), and source \(s\), initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne s\). A relaxation of \((u,v)\) replaces \(d(v)\) by \(d(u)+\ell(u,v)\) whenever this value is smaller, and records predecessor \(u\). Perform \(|V|-1\) complete passes through \(A\), permitting any fixed arc order, and stop early if a pass changes no label. If no reachable negative cycle exists, the final labels are exact shortest distances. A further successful relaxation certifies the existence of a negative directed cycle reachable from \(s\). The running time is \(O(|V||A|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated arc relaxation computes single-source distances and detects source-reachable negative cycles through an additional successful pass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(|V|-1\) passes, \(d=d_s\) if no reachable negative cycle exists; a subsequent improvement signals one.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Dijkstra Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case array-and-matrix implementation of single-source Dijkstra on nonnegative lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\). In each of at most \(n\) iterations, scan the unsettled vertices to select one with minimum tentative label, settle it, and scan its entire adjacency-matrix row to perform relaxations. The selections and row scans each take \(\Theta(n^2)\) time over the execution. Thus this dense-graph implementation runs in \(\Theta(n^2)\) time, uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) space for the matrix, and uses \(O(n)\) additional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unsorted-array selection and complete adjacency-matrix row scans, Dijkstra runs in quadratic time, uses quadratic graph-storage space, and uses linear additional space.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with \(n=|V|\), nonnegative arc lengths \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), and source \(s\in V\).
The graph is stored as an \(n\)-by-\(n\) adjacency matrix, and tentative labels are stored in an unsorted vertex array.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implementation runs in \(\Theta(n^2)\) time, uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) graph-representation space, and uses \(O(n)\) auxiliary space.

knowledge_statements.title: Array-Based Priority Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsorted-array realization of Dijkstra's minimum-label selection operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(d(s)=0\), set \(d(v)=+\infty\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\), and set \(S=\varnothing\). While an unsettled vertex has a finite label, scan the vertex array to choose \(u\in V\setminus S\) minimizing \(d(u)\), add \(u\) to \(S\), and, for every outgoing arc \((u,v)\in E\), replace \(d(v)\) by \(\min\{d(v),d(u)+w(u,v)\}\), recording a predecessor when the label decreases. Stop when no unsettled vertex has a finite label. The final labels are the shortest-path distances from \(s\), and the recorded predecessors recover shortest paths to reachable vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dijkstra may select each next vertex by scanning an unsorted label array. It returns shortest-path distances and predecessor paths in O(n squared plus m) time while using O(n) auxiliary space beyond the graph.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), source \(s\in V\), and nonnegative arc lengths \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\).
Outgoing arcs are enumerable in total \(O(m)\) time, and tentative labels and settled indicators are stored in arrays indexed by vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implementation returns shortest-path distances from \(s\) in \(O(n^2+m)\) time and uses \(O(n)\) auxiliary space beyond the graph representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Density–Representation Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic comparison including the graph representation used by each priority-selection strategy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With an adjacency matrix and unsorted-array priority selection, Dijkstra runs in \(\Theta(n^2)\) time and uses \(\Theta(n^2)\) graph-representation space. With adjacency lists and a binary heap supporting decrease-key, it runs in \(O((m+n)\log n)\) time and uses \(O(m+n)\) graph-plus-queue space. The displayed heap bound is \(o(n^2)\) when \((m+n)\log n=o(n^2)\), as in sufficiently sparse regimes. When \(m=\Theta(n^2)\), the displayed bounds are \(\Theta(n^2)\) for the array-and-matrix implementation and \(O(n^2\log n)\) for the binary-heap implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjacency lists with a binary heap have the better displayed asymptotic bound in sufficiently sparse graphs, while an adjacency matrix with array selection gives quadratic time and avoids the heap's logarithmic factor in the usual dense regime.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and nonnegative arc lengths.
The compared implementations use an adjacency matrix with unsorted-array selection or adjacency lists with a binary heap supporting decrease-key.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The respective bounds are \(T_{\mathrm{arr}}=\Theta(n^2)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{heap}}=O((m+n)\log n)\), with representation spaces \(\Theta(n^2)\) and \(O(m+n)\); their comparison therefore depends on graph density and representation.

Dijkstra performs at most \(n\) insertions, \(n\) extract-min operations, and \(m\) successful or attempted relaxations, of which at most \(m\) invoke decrease-key. Each heap operation costs \(O(\log n)\), while adjacency-list scanning costs \(O(m)\). Therefore the total running time is \(O((m+n)\log n)\), commonly written \(O(m\log n)\) when all reachable vertices are incident to scanned arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary heap implements Dijkstra in logarithmic time per priority update or extraction, yielding near-linear-logarithmic total time on sparse graphs.
