children.title: Gap Heuristic
children.top_down_role: Use of missing label levels to identify vertices separated from the sink.

knowledge_statements.title: Gap Heuristic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Label update for a push–relabel maximum-flow implementation after an empty height level is detected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) be the residual network, let \(t\) be the sink, and let \(h:V\to\{0,\ldots,2n-1\}\) be a valid height labeling with \(h(t)=0\), where \(n=|V|\). If some level \(k<n\) is empty and \(U=\{v\in V:k<h(v)<n\}\), replace \(h(v)\) by \(n+1\) for every \(v\in U\). Each vertex in \(U\) has no residual path to \(t\), so it need not be processed toward the sink at its former height. Continue ordinary admissible pushes and relabels, excluding \(s\) and \(t\) from the active-vertex queue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a height level is empty, vertices above that gap but below the source height cannot reach the sink and are moved to a permanently high level.
assumptions_latex: \(G_f\) is the residual network of a feasible preflow.
\(h(u)\le h(v)+1\) for every residual arc \((u,v)\in E_f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in U\Longrightarrow t\text{ is unreachable from }v\text{ in }G_f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gap implication is standard, but no source or inspectable locator supports the precise update rule. The plain statement should also say that affected labels remain at least n, rather than calling n+1 a permanently fixed level.

children.title: Combined Heuristic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Push–relabel implementations combining global relabeling with gap detection.

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Heuristic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic composition of global relabeling and gap relabeling within push–relabel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a residual network \(G_f\), initialize heights by a reverse breadth-first search from \(t\), assigning each vertex its residual distance to \(t\) and assigning unreachable vertices height at least \(n\). Perform admissible pushes and local relabels. After every prescribed budget \(T\ge1\) of elementary operations, or when another fixed trigger fires, recompute all heights by reverse breadth-first search. Between recomputations, whenever a level \(k<n\) becomes empty, apply the gap update to every vertex whose height lies strictly between \(k\) and \(n\). Stop when no active vertex other than \(s\) or \(t\) remains; output the resulting feasible maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime periodically rebuilds exact sink-distance labels and applies gap updates between rebuilds, while retaining the ordinary push–relabel stopping rule.
assumptions_latex: \(G_f\) is maintained from a feasible preflow.
\(T\) and every additional global-relabel trigger are fixed before execution.
Local push and relabel operations preserve valid height labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{termination with no internal active vertex implies that the induced feasible flow is maximum}\).

notation.meaning: operation budget between scheduled global relabels

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The combined regime lacks evidence, and the reverse-BFS initialization must specify the special source label h(s)=n rather than assigning the source an ordinary sink distance. The additional trigger is also too vague to identify a definite algorithmic regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Source–Sink Minimum Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed capacitated source–sink cuts and their equality in value with maximum source–sink flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with capacities \(c:A	o\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) and distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(\delta^+(S)=\{(u,v)\in A:u\in S,\ v
otin S\}\). An \(s\)-\(t\) cut is a set \(S\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t
otin S\), and its capacity is \(c(\delta^+(S))=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}c(a)\). If \(\lambda(s,t)=\min\{c(\delta^+(S)):s\in S,\ t
otin S\}\), then \(\lambda(s,t)\) equals the maximum value of a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed source–sink minimum cut minimizes the capacity of arcs leaving a set containing the source and excluding the sink, and its value equals the maximum feasible source–sink flow value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(s,t)=\max\{|f|:f\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow}\}\).

notation.meaning: arcs directed from the set to its complement

knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Global Minimum Cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum nontrivial cut in a finite undirected capacitated graph, without designated terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(|V|\ge2\) and capacities \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\). For a nonempty proper set \(S\subset V\), let \(\delta(S)=\{uv\in E:|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}\) and \(c(\delta(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e)\). An undirected global minimum cut is any bipartition \(\{S,V\setminus S\}\) attaining \(\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}c(\delta(S))\). Because \(\delta(S)=\delta(V\setminus S)\), complementary shores define the same cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global minimum cut is a nontrivial vertex bipartition whose crossing undirected edges have minimum total capacity among all bipartitions.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with \(|V|\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e)\).

notation.meaning: undirected edge boundary of a vertex set

knowledge_statements.title: Gomory–Hu Cut Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-pairs minimum-cut values represented by one weighted tree for an undirected capacitated graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite undirected capacitated graph \(G=(V,E,c)\), there exists a weighted tree \(T=(V,F,w)\) such that, for every distinct \(s,t\in V\), the minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut value in \(G\) equals \(\min\{w(e):e\text{ lies on the unique }s\text{-}t\text{ path in }T\}\). Moreover, deleting any minimum-weight edge on that tree path partitions \(V\) into two shores that form a minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut in \(G\). Thus one tree stores all pairwise minimum-cut values and supplies a corresponding cut for every terminal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gomory–Hu tree stores every pairwise minimum-cut value as the lightest edge on the corresponding tree path and recovers an attaining cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_G(s,t)=\min_{e\in P_T(s,t)}w(e)\) for all distinct \(s,t\in V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cut Cactus Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cactus encoding of every global minimum cut of a finite undirected capacitated graph with positive global minimum-cut value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,c)\) be a finite undirected capacitated graph with \(|V|\ge2\) and positive global minimum-cut value \(\lambda(G)>0\). There exist a cactus graph \(C\) and a map \(\phi:V\to V(C)\) such that every global minimum cut of \(G\) is the inverse image under \(\phi\) of a bipartition obtained either by deleting one bridge of \(C\) or by deleting two edges belonging to one cycle of \(C\). Conversely, every such bridge deletion or same-cycle edge-pair deletion induces a global minimum cut of \(G\). Every edge of \(C\) belongs to at most one simple cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the global minimum-cut value is positive, a cactus represents all global minimum cuts by bridge deletions or by deleting two edges from one cactus cycle, and every represented deletion induces a global minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{M}(G)=\{\phi^{-1}(X):X\text{ is a shore induced by a bridge deletion or a same-cycle edge-pair deletion in }C\}\).

notation.meaning: cactus representing the global minimum-cut family

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Cut Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse subgraph certificate preserving every undirected cut up to a prescribed threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected multigraph with \(n=|V|\), and let \(k\) be a positive integer. A sparse \(k\)-cut certificate is a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) satisfying \(|F|\le k(n-1)\) and, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \(\min\{k,|\delta_H(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}\). Consequently, every cut of size less than \(k\) is preserved exactly, while every cut having at least \(k\) edges retains at least \(k\) certificate edges. Such a certificate is sufficient to verify all cut queries below threshold \(k\) using only \(O(kn)\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse certificate uses at most k(n−1) edges, preserves every cut smaller than k exactly, and keeps at least k edges in every larger cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|F|\le k(n-1)\quad\text{and}\quad\min\{k,|\delta_H(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}\text{ for all }S\subseteq V\).

children.title: Integral-Capacity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Maximum-flow settings with integer-valued capacities.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality and pseudo-polynomial augmentation bound for maximum flow with integer capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have nonnegative integral capacities, let \(m=|A|\), and define \(U_s=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(s)}c(a)\). Starting from the zero flow, Ford–Fulkerson augmentation along any residual \(s\)-\(t\) path preserves integrality and increases the flow value by at least one. Hence it terminates after at most \(F^*\le U_s\) augmentations, where \(F^*\) is the maximum-flow value. If a residual path is found in \(O(m)\) time, the resulting bound is \(O(mF^*)\subseteq O(mU_s)\). The dependence on numerical capacity magnitude makes this bound pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial in binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer capacities yield an integral maximum flow and at most F* unit-or-larger augmentations, giving an O(mF*) pseudo-polynomial Ford–Fulkerson bound.
assumptions_latex: Each augmentation uses a residual source–sink path and its bottleneck capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}\le F^*\le U_s\quad\text{and}\quad T=O(mF^*)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of rational-capacity maximum flow to an integer-capacity instance by common-denominator scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every arc capacity \(c(a)\) be a nonnegative rational number. Choose a positive integer \(D\) such that \(Dc(a)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\) for all arcs, and define \(c'(a)=Dc(a)\). A flow \(f\) is feasible for \(c\) if and only if \(Df\) is feasible for \(c'\), and optimal values satisfy \(F'^*=DF^*\). Therefore integral-capacity termination arguments apply after scaling. However, \(D\) and the scaled capacities may be exponentially large relative to their binary encodings, so the augmentation bound inherited from integer scaling is not a polynomial-time bound in the original input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common-denominator scaling turns rational capacities into integers and preserves optimal flows, but the scaled magnitudes may make augmentation bounds only pseudo-polynomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is optimal for }c\Longleftrightarrow Df\text{ is optimal for }Dc\), with \(F'^*=DF^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and duality remain valid over real capacities, but arbitrary-path augmentation need not terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite network with capacities \(c:A\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), the feasible-flow polytope is compact and a maximum flow exists; its value equals the minimum directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut capacity. Nevertheless, the arbitrary-path Ford–Fulkerson rule has no discrete lower bound on positive augmentations. There exist finite networks with irrational capacities and admissible sequences of augmenting paths for which infinitely many augmentations occur and no finite iterate is a maximum flow. Thus max-flow existence and duality do not imply finite termination of an unrestricted augmenting-path selection rule over arbitrary real capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flows and minimum cuts remain well defined for real capacities, but arbitrary Ford–Fulkerson path choices can produce infinitely many augmentations with irrational data.
assumptions_latex: Ford–Fulkerson may choose any residual source–sink path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_f|f|=\min_S c(\delta^+(S))\), but finite termination is not guaranteed for arbitrary augmenting-path choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Domain Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete augmentation bounds require positive capacity granularity; max-flow duality itself does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every positive residual bottleneck encountered by an augmenting-path method is at least \(\Delta>0\). If the maximum-flow value is \(F^*\), each augmentation increases the value by at least \(\Delta\), so at most \(\lceil F^*/\Delta\rceil\) augmentations occur. Integral capacities provide \(\Delta=1\), and rational capacities provide such a \(\Delta\) after common-denominator scaling. For unrestricted real capacities, no input-independent positive granularity need exist, so this counting argument fails even though maximum-flow minimum-cut duality remains valid. Algorithms whose operation bounds do not depend on capacity magnitudes avoid this domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmentation counting works when positive bottlenecks have fixed granularity; arbitrary real capacities remove that guarantee without invalidating max-flow minimum-cut duality.
assumptions_latex: Every augmentation increases the flow by its positive residual bottleneck.
A common lower bound \(\Delta>0\) exists when the counting bound is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}\le\lceil F^*/\Delta\rceil\); without such \(\Delta\), this bound is unavailable.

notation.meaning: lower bound on positive augmentation amounts

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed unit-capacity maximum flow as arc-disjoint path packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), and let \(c(a)=1\) for every \(a\in A\). Then the maximum value of a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow equals the maximum cardinality of a family of pairwise arc-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite directed unit-capacity network, the maximum source–sink flow value equals the largest number of pairwise arc-disjoint directed source–sink paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_f|f|=\max\{|\mathcal{P}|:\mathcal{P}\text{ is a family of pairwise arc-disjoint directed }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}\}\).

children.title: Small-Capacity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Maximum-flow instances whose capacities lie in a bounded small range.

knowledge_statements.title: Small-Capacity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of capacity-dependent bounds when integral capacities are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a maximum-flow instance have integral capacities and let \(U=\max_{e\in E}u_e\). If \(U\le n^k\) for a fixed constant \(k\), then \(\log(U+1)=O(\log n)\). Consequently, any bound polynomial in \(n\), \(m\), and \(\log(U+1)\) is polynomial in the graph dimensions. Moreover, a pseudopolynomial bound of the form \(O(U\,p(n,m))\), where \(p\) is a polynomial, becomes polynomial in \(n\) and \(m\) under this small-capacity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomially bounded integral capacities turn logarithmic capacity dependence, and even linear pseudopolynomial dependence on the largest capacity, into graph-dimension polynomial bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a directed network with \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\).
\(u_e\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(U\le n^k\) for a fixed \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\log(U+1)=O(\log n)\), and \(O(U\,p(n,m))\) is polynomial in \(n,m\).

notation.meaning: an arbitrary polynomial in graph dimensions

children.title: Capacity-Range Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Performance variation governed by the permitted capacity range.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Range Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of maximum-flow running times on the numerical capacity range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral capacities, set \(U=\max_{e\in E}u_e\). Under uniform scaling \(u'_e=\lambda u_e\) by an integer \(\lambda\ge1\), the graph dimensions remain \(n,m\), while \(U'=\lambda U\). Thus a weakly polynomial factor \(\log(U+1)\) changes to \(\log(\lambda U+1)\), a pseudopolynomial factor \(U\) changes to \(\lambda U\), and a strongly polynomial operation bound depending only on \(n,m\) is unchanged. Capacity scaling therefore distinguishes logarithmic, magnitude, and magnitude-independent complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling capacities affects logarithmic dependence mildly, pseudopolynomial dependence proportionally, and strongly polynomial operation bounds not at all.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U'=\lambda U\), separating logarithmic, pseudopolynomial, and strongly polynomial sensitivity.

children.title: Dense Graph Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity behavior for maximum-flow instances whose arc count approaches the dense range.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Graph Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic density convention for simple directed maximum-flow networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((G_n)\) of simple directed networks is in the dense-graph regime when \(G_n=(V_n,E_n)\), \(|V_n|=n\), and \(|E_n|=m_n=\Theta(n^2)\). Equivalently, there exist constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \(c n^2\le m_n\le C n^2\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). In this regime, a running-time bound expressed in \(m\) is evaluated after the substitution \(m=\Theta(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple directed graph family is dense when its number of arcs grows quadratically with its number of vertices.
assumptions_latex: \((G_n)\) is a family of simple directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_n=\Theta(n^2)\).

notation.meaning: number of arcs in the graph with n vertices

children.title: Sparse Graph Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity behavior for maximum-flow instances with near-linear arc counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Graph Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-size sparsity convention for directed maximum-flow networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \((G_n)\) of directed networks is in the sparse-graph regime when \(G_n=(V_n,E_n)\), \(|V_n|=n\), and \(|E_n|=m_n=O(n)\). Equivalently, there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \(m_n\le Cn\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). For connected underlying graphs one also has \(m_n=\Omega(n)\), hence \(m_n=\Theta(n)\). Complexity bounds are evaluated by substituting this growth rate for \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed graph family is sparse when its arc count is at most linear in its vertex count; connected families then have linear size.
assumptions_latex: \((G_n)\) is a family of directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_n=O(n)\), and connected underlying graphs satisfy \(m_n=\Theta(n)\).

notation.meaning: number of arcs in the graph with n vertices

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sparse graph families conventionally have linear edge or arc growth

children.title: Density-Sensitive Complexity Crossover
children.top_down_role: Instance-density thresholds that change the preferred complexity bound or implementation family.

knowledge_statements.title: Density-Sensitive Complexity Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic crossover between edge-sensitive and vertex-sensitive maximum-flow bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose two maximum-flow algorithms have worst-case bounds \(T_A(n,m)=O(m\alpha(n))\) and \(T_B(n,m)=O(n^2\beta(n))\), where \(\alpha,\beta>0\). Their asymptotic crossover occurs at \(m=\Theta(n^2\beta(n)/\alpha(n))\). Algorithm \(A\) has the smaller displayed bound when \(m=o(n^2\beta(n)/\alpha(n))\), while algorithm \(B\) has the smaller displayed bound when \(m=\omega(n^2\beta(n)/\alpha(n))\). Thus sparsity can change which complexity guarantee is preferable even for the same problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equating an edge-sensitive bound with a vertex-sensitive bound identifies the graph density at which their asymptotic ranking reverses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The crossover density is \(m=\Theta(n^2\beta(n)/\alpha(n))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: crossover follows by equating the two stated asymptotic bounds
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

A source and a corrected formulation are required.

children.title: Weakly Polynomial Maximum Flow
children.top_down_role: Maximum-flow bounds whose complexity depends on numerical encoding length.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity definition for integral-capacity maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed maximum-flow instance with integral capacities \(0\le u_e\le U\), an algorithm is weakly polynomial if its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the binary input length. With explicit arc encoding, this permits a bound polynomial in \(n\), \(m\), and \(\log(U+1)\). Hence the bound may depend on the number of bits used to encode the capacities, but not polynomially on their magnitudes merely because they are written in binary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly polynomial maximum-flow algorithm runs polynomially in graph size and capacity encoding length, so its bound may contain logarithmic numeric dependence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The running time is \(\operatorname{poly}(n,m,\log(U+1))\).

children.title: Strongly Polynomial Maximum Flow
children.top_down_role: Maximum-flow bounds independent of capacity magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic-operation definition independent of capacity magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A maximum-flow algorithm is strongly polynomial if the number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is bounded by a polynomial in \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\), independently of the numerical values and encoding lengths of the capacities, and every intermediate number has encoding length polynomial in the input length. Under the standard arithmetic model, these two requirements imply polynomial bit complexity while excluding iteration bounds containing \(U\) or \(\log(U+1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly polynomial algorithm uses polynomially many operations based only on graph dimensions and keeps all intermediate numbers polynomially encoded.
assumptions_latex: The input is a finite directed network with rational or integral capacities.
Arithmetic operations and comparisons use the standard exact-arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operation count is \(\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\), independent of capacity magnitudes, with polynomially bounded intermediate encoding lengths.

notation.meaning: largest capacity when capacities are integral

children.title: Numeric-Dependence Boundary
children.top_down_role: The role of capacity encoding in separating weak from strong polynomial guarantees.

assumptions_latex: Capacities are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
All nonnumeric dependence in the running-time bounds is polynomial in the graph dimensions and the remaining input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Explicit \(\operatorname{poly}(U)\) dependence is generally only pseudopolynomial; \(\operatorname{poly}(\log(U+1))\) dependence is compatible with weak polynomiality; and an operation bound depending only on \(n,m\), together with polynomially bounded intermediate encodings, is strongly polynomial.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating pseudopolynomial guarantees from weakly and strongly polynomial guarantees without treating the latter nested classes as disjoint.

source_refs.locator: 4.12 Strongly polynomial-time p. 47

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral-capacity maximum flow, let \(U=\max_{e\in E}u_e\), with capacities encoded in binary. A running-time guarantee polynomial in \(U\), even when its remaining dependence is polynomial in the graph dimensions, is generally pseudopolynomial because \(U\) requires only \(\Theta(\log(U+1))\) bits to encode. A guarantee polynomial in the full binary input length, and hence possibly polynomial in \(n\), \(m\), and \(\log(U+1)\), is weakly polynomial. Strong polynomiality additionally requires an arithmetic-operation bound polynomial only in \(n\) and \(m\), independent of capacity values and encoding lengths, together with polynomially bounded intermediate encoding lengths. Strongly polynomial algorithms are also weakly polynomial, so these labels describe increasingly restrictive guarantees rather than three disjoint algorithm classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial dependence on capacity magnitude is generally pseudopolynomial; polynomial dependence on binary encoding length is weakly polynomial; and a graph-dimension-only operation bound with controlled intermediate encodings is strongly polynomial. Strong polynomiality is a stricter form of weak polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Dependence Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), arc costs \(c_e\in\mathbb R\), and bounds \(\ell_e,u_e\in\mathbb R\) with \(\ell_e\le u_e\), assume that the bounded-circulation feasible set is nonempty. A minimum-cost circulation is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) solving
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^E}\ \sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e\]
subject to \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\) and
\[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e=0\qquad(v\in V).\]
Thus every vertex has zero net imbalance, and the objective selects a least-cost feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming a bounded circulation exists, a minimum-cost circulation obeys its arc bounds and flow conservation at every vertex while minimizing total linear arc cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Circulation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and directed, with costs \(c_e\in\mathbb R\), bounds \(\ell_e,u_e\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\ell_e\le u_e\), and prescribed balances \(b_v\in\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). Assume that the prescribed balances are feasible within the arc bounds. A minimum-cost transshipment is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) solving
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^E}\ \sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e\]
subject to \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\) and
\[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e=b_v\qquad(v\in V).\]
Positive \(b_v\) denotes net demand and negative \(b_v\) denotes net supply under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assuming the prescribed balances are feasible, a minimum-cost transshipment routes supplies to demands within arc bounds while minimizing total linear cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite directed network \(G=(V,E)\) with distinct source \(s\in V\) and sink \(t\in V\), arc costs \(c_e\in\mathbb R\), capacities \(u_e\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), and a prescribed value \(q\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), assume that a feasible flow of value \(q\) exists. A minimum-cost source-sink flow is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) minimizing \(\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e\) subject to \(0\le x_e\le u_e\) for every \(e\in E\),
\[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e=0\qquad(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}),\]
and
\[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(s)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(s)}x_e=q,
\qquad
\sum_{e\in\delta^-(t)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(t)}x_e=q.\]
The value \(q\) is fixed rather than optimized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among feasible flows carrying a prescribed amount from source to sink, a minimum-cost source-sink flow has minimum total arc cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic optimization of source–sink value followed by flow cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a capacitated directed network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and arc costs \(c_e\), let \(F^*\) be the maximum feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow value. A minimum-cost maximum flow is any feasible flow \(x\) satisfying \(\operatorname{val}(x)=F^*\) and
\[\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e=
\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_e y_e: y\text{ is feasible and }\operatorname{val}(y)=F^*\right\}.\]
Thus flow value is optimized first, and cost is minimized only among maximum-value flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First maximize source–sink flow value; then, among all maximum flows, select one of minimum total cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and directed with distinct source and sink.
Each arc has a finite nonnegative capacity and a real cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) lexicographically maximizes \((\operatorname{val}(x),-\sum_e c_e x_e)\).

children.title: Lower-Bound Elimination
children.top_down_role: Demand shifts and residual feasibility effects created when positive lower bounds are removed.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine elimination of arcwise lower bounds in a finite minimum-cost transshipment problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\), let every arc \(a\) have bounds \(\ell_a\le u_a\), and impose \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\). Define \(y_a=x_a-\ell_a\). Then \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) is equivalent to \(0\le y_a\le u_a-\ell_a\), while the balance becomes \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}y_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}y_a=b'_v\), where \(b'_v=b_v-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}\ell_a+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}\ell_a\). For linear costs, \(\sum_a c_ax_a=\sum_a c_ay_a+\sum_a c_a\ell_a\), so feasible solutions correspond bijectively and minimizers are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract each arc’s lower bound, reduce its capacity accordingly, adjust node supplies, and add the resulting constant to the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto y=x-\ell\) is a feasibility-preserving bijection and preserves optimal solutions after an objective constant shift.

children.title: Capacity Normalization
children.top_down_role: Representations that place finite or infinite upper capacities into a standard form.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization of residual arc intervals after lower-bound elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc \(a\), define its normalized capacity by \(U_a=u_a-\ell_a\) and its normalized flow by \(y_a=x_a-\ell_a\). Then the original interval \([\ell_a,u_a]\) is translated bijectively onto \([0,U_a]\). If \(u_a=+\infty\), use \(U_a=+\infty\); otherwise \(U_a\ge0\) is finite. Thus every bounded minimum-cost flow instance can be written with zero lower bounds and constraints \(0\le y_a\le U_a\), without scaling costs or changing the residual amount of flow permitted on any arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translate each feasible arc interval to start at zero; its normalized capacity is the original upper bound minus the lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([\ell_a,u_a]\ni x_a\longleftrightarrow y_a=x_a-\ell_a\in[0,u_a-\ell_a]\) is a bijection.

notation.meaning: Normalized upper capacity of arc a.

children.title: Coupled Bound Transformation

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Bound Transformation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous transformation of bounds, balances, and linear cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the program minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) subject to \(Bx=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), where the node–arc incidence matrix uses \(+1\) at an arc's tail and \(-1\) at its head. With \(x=\ell+y\), the transformed program is \(\min c^{\mathsf T}y+c^{\mathsf T}\ell\) subject to \(By=b-B\ell\) and \(0\le y\le u-\ell\). Consequently, feasibility, differences between objective values, and the ordering of feasible solutions are preserved under the affine correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same affine substitution must update capacities, node balances, and the objective constant together to produce an equivalent flow problem.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the incidence matrix of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto y=x-\ell\) bijects the two feasible sets and preserves their argmin sets.

children.title: Bound-Transformation Feasibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which transformed balances or residual capacities expose infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Transformation Feasibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact cut criterion for feasibility of lower- and upper-bounded transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, require \(\ell\le x\le u\), and use balances \(Bx=b\) with tail-positive incidence matrix \(B\). A feasible flow exists if and only if \(b(V)=0\) and, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \[\ell(\delta^+(S))-u(\delta^-(S))\le b(S)\le u(\delta^+(S))-\ell(\delta^-(S)).\] Equivalently, after setting \(y=x-\ell\), the zero-lower-bound instance \(By=b-B\ell\), \(0\le y\le u-\ell\), is feasible. Violation of any displayed cut inequality certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transformed instance is feasible exactly when total supply is zero and every node cut can carry its required net supply within the arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated family of cut inequalities is necessary and sufficient for bounded-flow feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment-to-Circulation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of balanced transshipment to circulation using one auxiliary node and fixed-flow arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have balances \(Bx=b\), where \(b(V)=0\) and positive \(b_v\) denotes supply. Add a node \(r\). For every \(v\) with \(b_v>0\), add an arc \((r,v)\) having lower and upper bound \(b_v\); for every \(v\) with \(b_v<0\), add an arc \((v,r)\) having both bounds \(-b_v\). Give all new arcs zero cost. Then a flow on the original arcs satisfies \(Bx=b\) exactly when its unique extension using these fixed auxiliary flows is a circulation. Original costs and capacities are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attach fixed zero-cost arcs to a new node so that each supply or demand becomes ordinary flow conservation in an augmented circulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible transshipments correspond bijectively to feasible circulations in the augmented network, with equal costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Source–Sink Flow-to-Circulation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-value source–sink flow represented by a circulation with one return arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s,t\in V\) and let \(F\ge0\). Augment a capacitated network by the return arc \(a_0=(t,s)\) with lower and upper bound both equal to \(F\) and cost zero. A feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(F\), satisfying conservation at all other nodes, extends uniquely to a circulation by setting \(x_{a_0}=F\). Conversely, deleting \(a_0\) from any such circulation yields an \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow of value \(F\). Costs on original arcs and their feasible values are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-value source–sink flow becomes a circulation by adding a zero-cost return arc from sink to source carrying exactly that value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-value \(s\)-to-\(t\) flows and augmented circulations are in cost-preserving bijection.

knowledge_statements.title: Shortest Path as Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source–single-target shortest path as a unit minimum-cost transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct nodes with \(t\) reachable from \(s\), and let each arc \(a\in A\) have length \(c_a\ge 0\). Let \(B\) be the tail-positive node–arc incidence matrix and define \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) by \(b_s=1\), \(b_t=-1\), and \(b_v=0\) for \(v\notin\{s,t\}\). Then the minimum-cost-flow problem \[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a:Bx=b,\ x\ge0\right\}\] has optimal value equal to the length of a shortest directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sending one unit from the source to the target as a nonnegative minimum-cost flow has the same optimal value as the shortest directed source-to-target path problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ x\ge0\}\) equals the length of a shortest directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed shortest paths, walks, and shortest-path trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed graphs with real arc lengths, including negative lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\) be a directed graph with \(|\mathcal N|=n\) and arc lengths \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\). The length of a directed walk, path, or cycle is the sum of its arc lengths. A shortest path (respectively, shortest walk) minimizes length among paths (respectively, walks) with fixed endpoints. If a negative-length cycle can be inserted into a walk to the destination, walk lengths are unbounded below, whereas every path has length at least \(-nC\), where \(C=\max_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}|c_{ij}|\). If every cycle has nonnegative length, a shortest path is also a shortest walk, and deleting the necessarily zero-length cycles from any shortest walk produces a shortest path. An intree rooted at \(n\) is a directed tree containing a directed path from every \(i\ne n\) to \(n\); it is a tree of shortest paths when each such tree path is shortest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Path and walk length is the sum of arc lengths. A shortest path or walk minimizes length for fixed endpoints. A usable negative cycle makes walk lengths unbounded below, while finite-graph path lengths remain bounded below. If all cycles are nonnegative, shortest paths and shortest walks have the same optimal length, and zero-length cycles can be removed from a shortest walk. An intree rooted at the destination is a shortest-path tree when every tree path to the root is shortest.
assumptions_latex: G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is a finite directed graph with }|\mathcal N|=n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Negative usable cycles imply unbounded walk lengths; if every cycle is nonnegative, shortest walks reduce to shortest paths, and shortest-path intrees are well defined.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold partitioned shortest-path algorithm and nonnegative-cost bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-controlled specialization of the partitioned shortest-path algorithm; the complexity guarantee applies when all arc costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At the end of each outer iteration choose a threshold $t\ge\min\{w'_i:i\in\mathrm{NEXT}\}$ and transfer to $\mathrm{NOW}$ only nodes $i\in\mathrm{NEXT}$ with $w'_i\le t$. During relaxation, an updated node $q\notin\mathrm{NOW}$ is placed in $\mathrm{NEXT}$ if $w'_q>t$ and otherwise in an auxiliary list $\mathrm{NOW}'$, being removed from $\mathrm{NEXT}$ if necessary. Whenever $\mathrm{NOW}$ empties, transfer $\mathrm{NOW}'$ into it and continue; when both are empty, terminate if $\mathrm{NEXT}=\varnothing$, or revise $t$ and transfer the newly qualifying nodes. If all arc costs are nonnegative, each minimum-label node transferred from $\mathrm{NOW}'$ or $\mathrm{NEXT}$ has its final shortest-path distance, so there are at most $m-1$ such transfers; if the work between transfers is $O(|\mathcal S|)$, the total complexity is $O(m|\mathcal S|)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The threshold variant moves from NEXT into NOW only nodes whose tentative labels do not exceed a threshold that is at least the smallest NEXT label. Updates below the threshold enter an auxiliary immediate-work list, while larger updates remain in NEXT. The algorithm exhausts NOW and the auxiliary list before revising the threshold. With nonnegative arc costs, every transferred minimum-label node is permanently settled, giving at most m−1 transfers and total work O(m|S|) when each transfer phase costs O(|S|).
assumptions_latex: c_{pq}\ge0\quad\forall(p,q)\in A\text{ for the transfer and complexity guarantees}.
\text{The work performed between successive transfers into NOW is }O(|\mathcal S|).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Under nonnegative arc costs, there are at most }m-1\text{ transfers into NOW and the running time is }O(m|\mathcal S|).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shortest-path network-flow primal and dual characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All-to-one shortest paths and their associated network-flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the all-to-one shortest-path problem on a directed graph with \(n\) nodes and its associated network-flow problem. Assume that every node \(i\ne n\) has a directed path to node \(n\), and that node \(n\) has no outgoing arcs. (a) If a negative-length cycle exists, the network-flow problem has optimal value \(-\infty\). (b) If every directed cycle has nonnegative length and a feasible tree solution is optimal, its corresponding tree is a tree of shortest paths to \(n\). (c) Under the nonnegative-cycle assumption and normalization \(p_n=0\), the dual problem has a unique solution \(p^*\), where \(p_i^*\) is the shortest-path length from \(i\) to \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the network-flow formulation of all-to-one shortest paths, a negative cycle makes the objective unbounded below. With nonnegative cycle lengths, an optimal feasible tree is a shortest-path tree, and the uniquely normalized dual node potentials are the distances to the destination.
assumptions_latex: \forall i\in\mathcal N\setminus\{n\},\ \exists\text{ a directed path from }i\text{ to }n.
\text{Parts (b) and (c) assume }\ell(C)\ge 0\text{ for every directed cycle }C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A negative cycle gives value }-\infty;\ \text{under nonnegative cycles, an optimal feasible tree is a shortest-path tree and }p_i^*=d(i,n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bellman–Ford bounded-walk recurrence and negative-cycle certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous all-to-one Bellman–Ford iteration on a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) have \(n\) nodes and \(m\) arcs, let every node have a path to destination \(n\), and assume \(n\) has no outgoing arcs. Define \(p_n(t)=0\), \(p_i(0)=\infty\) for \(i\ne n\), and \[p_i(t+1)=\min_{k\in O(i)}\{c_{ik}+p_k(t)\}.\] Then \(p_i(t)\) is the minimum length of an \(i\)-to-\(n\) walk using at most \(t\) arcs. If there is no negative-length cycle, \(p(n-1)=p(n)=p^*\). If \(p(n)\ne p(n-1)\), a negative-length cycle exists; following stored successor pointers from any node with \(p_i(n)<p_i(n-1)\) yields a walk containing such a cycle. The algorithm performs at most \(n\) iterations, scans each arc once per iteration, and therefore runs in \(O(mn)\) time. Stored minimizing successors also permit recovery of shortest paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bellman–Ford repeatedly computes the best walk using one additional arc. After at most n rounds, equality of rounds n−1 and n certifies the shortest-path distances, while a strict change certifies a negative cycle. Successor pointers recover paths or a negative cycle, and the running time is O(mn).
assumptions_latex: \forall i\ne n,\ \exists\text{ a directed path from }i\text{ to }n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_i(t)=\min\{\ell(W):W:i\leadsto n,\ |W|\le t\};\quad p(n)=p(n-1)\iff\text{no negative cycle},\quad T(n,m)=O(mn).

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Price Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian node-price dual of capacitated minimum-cost transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the feasible program \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\), with finite capacities and tail-positive incidence matrix \(B\), define \(\bar c_a(p)=c_a+p_{\operatorname{head}(a)}-p_{\operatorname{tail}(a)}\). Its node-price dual is \[\max_{p\in\mathbb R^V}\left\{p^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_{a\in A}u_a\min\{0,\bar c_a(p)\}\right\}.\] Linear-programming strong duality gives equality of the primal and dual optimal values. Adding a common constant to all components of \(p\) leaves every reduced cost unchanged when \(b(V)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node prices shift arc costs into reduced costs, and maximizing the resulting concave dual expression equals the minimum feasible flow cost.
assumptions_latex: The primal feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,0\le x\le u\}=\max_p\{p^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_a u_a\min(0,\bar c_a(p))\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary-Slackness Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise complementary-slackness certificate for capacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, let \(x\) be feasible for \(Bx=b\) and \(0\le x\le u\), where \(B\) is the tail-positive node–arc incidence matrix and \(0\le u_a<+\infty\). For \(p\in\mathbb R^V\), define \(\bar c_a=c_a+p_{\operatorname{head}(a)}-p_{\operatorname{tail}(a)}\). If every arc \(a\in A\) satisfies \[x_a=0\Rightarrow\bar c_a\ge0,\qquad 0<x_a<u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a=0,\qquad x_a=u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\le0,\] then \((x,p)\) is a primal-dual optimality certificate: \(x\) is a minimum-cost flow and \(p\) is optimal for the node-price dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow and node-price vector certify optimality when each arc’s reduced-cost sign agrees with whether its flow is at zero, strictly between its bounds, or at capacity.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le u_a<+\infty\) and \(c_a\in\mathbb R\) for every arc \(a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed arcwise conditions certify that \(x\) is a minimum-cost flow and \(p\) is node-price-dual optimal.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality characterized by nonnegative reduced costs on all residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible capacitated flow and form its residual network: an original arc \(a=(i,j)\) appears forward with cost \(c_a\) when \(x_a<u_a\), and backward with cost \(-c_a\) when \(x_a>0\). For a residual arc \((i,j)\) of cost \(c^x_{ij}\), set \(\bar c^x_{ij}=c^x_{ij}+p_j-p_i\). Then \(x\) is minimum-cost if and only if there exists \(p\in\mathbb R^V\) such that \(\bar c^x_{ij}\ge0\) for every residual arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow is optimal exactly when node prices make every usable forward or backward residual move have nonnegative reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible and has finite objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is optimal if and only if some node-price vector makes every residual reduced cost nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative Residual-Cycle Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-canceling optimality theorem for finite capacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible flow in a finite directed network with real linear arc costs and finite capacities. Construct the residual network \(G_x\), assigning cost \(c_a\) to each available forward residual arc associated with arc \(a\) and cost \(-c_a\) to each available backward residual arc. Then \(x\) is a minimum-cost flow if and only if \(G_x\) contains no directed cycle of negative total residual cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow is minimum-cost exactly when its residual network has no negative-cost directed cycle.
assumptions_latex: The directed network and all capacities are finite.
Arc costs are linear and real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is optimal if and only if every directed cycle \(C\) in \(G_x\) satisfies \(c^x(C)\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate reduced-cost certificate, including an exactness threshold for integral costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, let \(x\) be a feasible flow, let \(p\in\mathbb R^V\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). The pair \((x,p)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal when every residual arc \((i,j)\) satisfies \(c^x_{ij}+p_j-p_i\ge-\varepsilon\). Every simple residual cycle then has residual cost at least \(-|V|\varepsilon\). If all original arc costs are integers and \(0\le\varepsilon<1/|V|\), this certificate implies that \(x\) is exactly minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual reduced costs bounded below by minus epsilon form an epsilon-optimality certificate; for integral costs, epsilon below one over the number of nodes certifies exact optimality.
assumptions_latex: For the exactness conclusion, \(c_a\in\mathbb Z\) for every arc and \(\varepsilon<1/|V|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual reduced costs at least \(-\varepsilon\) define an \(\varepsilon\)-certificate; integral costs and \(\varepsilon<1/|V|\) imply exact optimality.

assumptions_latex: The network is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with finite arc capacities and costs.
The current flow \(x\) is feasible for all capacity and balance constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the residual network \(G_x\) contains no directed cycle of negative total residual cost, then \(x\) is a minimum-cost feasible flow. Otherwise, select any negative-cost residual cycle \(C\), set \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)>0\), and augment \(\delta\) units around \(C\). This preserves every node balance and decreases the objective by \(\delta\sum_{a\in C}c_x(a)<0\). Repeating this operation with integral data terminates because each augmentation produces another integral feasible flow of strictly smaller cost and only finitely many such flows exist.

notation.meaning: Residual network of the current flow, with residual capacities and costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite integral minimum-cost circulation or flow with a feasible starting flow.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.3. Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm p. 220

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible flow \(x\), construct its residual network \(G_x\). While \(G_x\) contains a directed cycle \(C\) satisfying \(\sum_{a\in C}c_x(a)<0\), choose such a cycle, compute \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)\), augment \(\delta\) units on \(C\), and update \(G_x\). Stop when no negative-cost residual cycle remains and output \(x\). Each iteration preserves feasibility and strictly decreases cost; the stopping condition is equivalent to minimum-cost optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment as much as possible around any negative-cost residual cycle. Feasibility is preserved, cost decreases, and absence of such cycles certifies optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Generic Negative-Cycle Canceling

source_witnesses.locator: Section 9.3. Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm p. 220

assumptions_latex: The network and current feasible flow satisfy the hypotheses of residual-cycle optimality.
A minimum-mean residual cycle can be computed whenever a negative residual cycle exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At each iteration choose a residual directed cycle \(C\) minimizing \(\mu_x(C)=|C|^{-1}\sum_{a\in C}c_x(a)\). If \(\mu_x(C)<0\), augment \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)\) units around \(C\); otherwise stop. The algorithm returns a minimum-cost flow. For integral capacities and costs, the minimum-mean rule admits a strongly polynomial bound on the number of cancellations, independent of the numerical magnitudes of capacities and costs.

notation.meaning: Mean residual cost of a directed cycle.
Residual capacity of an arc under the current flow.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-mean residual-cycle variant; the exact strongly polynomial iteration bound is not asserted here.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.3. Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm p. 220

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every residual directed cycle \(C\), define \(\mu_x(C)=|C|^{-1}\sum_{a\in C}c_x(a)\). Compute a cycle attaining the minimum value of \(\mu_x\). If that value is nonnegative, output \(x\). Otherwise augment by \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)\), update the residual network, and repeat. The selected cycle is negative whenever any negative residual cycle exists, so termination satisfies the residual-cycle optimality criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cancel a residual cycle of minimum average cost at every iteration. A nonnegative minimum mean proves that no negative residual cycle remains.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Mean Cycle Canceling

children.title: Cycle-Canceling Phase
children.top_down_role: The negative-cycle improvement component within the method family.

assumptions_latex: The current feasible flow \(x\) is \(\epsilon\)-optimal for a potential \(p\), meaning \(c_p(a)\geq-\epsilon\) on every residual arc.
The admissible residual subgraph consists of arcs satisfying \(c_p(a)<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: While the admissible residual subgraph contains a directed cycle \(C\), augment \(\delta=\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)\) units around \(C\). Each augmentation preserves feasibility, does not increase cost, and removes at least one residual arc of \(C\) at its current orientation. The phase ends when the admissible subgraph is acyclic; throughout the phase the unchanged potential \(p\) continues to certify \(c_p(a)\geq-\epsilon\) for all residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible-cycle cancellation within an \(\epsilon\)-optimal cancel-and-tighten framework.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\epsilon>0\) and a potential \(p\) for which every residual arc satisfies \(c_p(a)\geq-\epsilon\). Form the admissible subgraph \(H=(V,\{a:c_p(a)<0\})\). While \(H\) contains a directed cycle \(C\), augment \(\min_{a\in C}u_x(a)\) units around \(C\) and update the residual arcs. Return the resulting flow when \(H\) is acyclic, leaving \(p\) and \(\epsilon\) fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed prices and tolerance, cancel admissible residual cycles until the negative reduced-cost subgraph becomes acyclic, while retaining epsilon-optimality.

children.title: Potential-Tightening Phase
children.top_down_role: The price or potential refinement component used to strengthen reduced-cost structure.

assumptions_latex: The current flow \(x\) is feasible and its admissible residual subgraph under \((p,\epsilon)\) is acyclic.
The tightening subproblem returns \(p'\) and \(0\leq\epsilon'<\epsilon\) satisfying all residual reduced-cost inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Keep \(x\) fixed and find a potential \(p'\) and smaller tolerance \(\epsilon'\) such that \(c_x(v,w)+p'(v)-p'(w)\geq-\epsilon'\) for every residual arc \((v,w)\). Output \((x,p',\epsilon')\). Because the flow is unchanged, primal feasibility is preserved; the displayed inequalities constitute the new \(\epsilon'\)-optimality certificate. If \(\epsilon'=0\), they certify exact minimum-cost optimality.

notation.meaning: Optimality tolerance before and after tightening.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract potential update after admissible-cycle elimination; no particular tightening implementation is imposed.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With the flow \(x\) fixed, solve the difference inequalities \(c_x(v,w)+p'(v)-p'(w)\geq-\epsilon'\) over all residual arcs \((v,w)\), subject to \(0\leq\epsilon'<\epsilon\). Replace \((p,\epsilon)\) by any feasible \((p',\epsilon')\). The phase changes only the dual potential and tolerance, and its output is a strictly tighter approximate-optimality certificate for the same feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After cycle cancellation, change only the node potentials to certify the same feasible flow at a strictly smaller optimality tolerance.

children.title: Cancellation–Tightening Coupling
children.top_down_role: How cycle improvements interact with subsequent potential refinement.

assumptions_latex: Each cancellation phase preserves feasibility and the current \(\epsilon\)-optimality inequalities.
Each tightening phase leaves the flow fixed and returns a strictly smaller certified tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Starting from a feasible \(\epsilon_0\)-optimal triple \((x_0,p_0,\epsilon_0)\), alternate admissible-cycle cancellation at fixed \((p_k,\epsilon_k)\) with potential tightening at fixed flow. The resulting triples \((x_k,p_k,\epsilon_k)\) remain feasible and \(\epsilon_k\)-optimal, while \(\epsilon_{k+1}<\epsilon_k\). The cancellation phase supplies the acyclicity condition needed for tightening, and tightening creates a stronger reduced-cost certificate for the next cancellation phase.

notation.meaning: Flow, potential, and tolerance after the \(k\)-th coupled phase.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant-based coupling of primal cycle cancellations with dual potential tightening.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.3. Minimum Mean Cycle-Cancelling Algorithm p. 220

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every phase index \(k\), maintain primal feasibility and \(c_{p_k}(a)\geq-\epsilon_k\) on every residual arc. First cancel directed cycles composed of arcs with \(c_{p_k}(a)<0\) until that subgraph is acyclic. Then keep the flow fixed and compute \((p_{k+1},\epsilon_{k+1})\) satisfying \(c_{p_{k+1}}(a)\geq-\epsilon_{k+1}\) for all residual arcs and \(\epsilon_{k+1}<\epsilon_k\). Repeat until the prescribed exact-optimality boundary is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate primal cycle cancellations and dual price tightening while preserving feasibility and progressively strengthening the reduced-cost optimality certificate.

assumptions_latex: All original arc costs are integers.
The current feasible flow is \(\epsilon\)-optimal for some potential, with \(0\leq\epsilon<1/|V|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual network contains no negative-cost directed cycle. Indeed, any simple residual cycle has at most \(|V|\) arcs, and summing the inequalities \(c_p(a)\geq-\epsilon\) around it gives total cost greater than \(-1\). Because the cycle cost is integral, it is therefore nonnegative. By the residual-cycle optimality criterion, the current feasible flow is minimum-cost.

notation.meaning: Number of vertices in the network.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-cost termination threshold for an \(\epsilon\)-optimal feasible flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n=|V|\), let all arc costs be integral, and suppose a feasible flow \(x\) has a potential \(p\) satisfying \(c_p(a)\geq-\epsilon\) on every residual arc for some \(\epsilon<1/n\). Every simple residual cycle \(C\) then satisfies \(\sum_{a\in C}c_x(a)=\sum_{a\in C}c_p(a)>-1\). This sum is integral, hence nonnegative. Thus no negative residual cycle exists and \(x\) is minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integer costs, epsilon-optimality below the reciprocal of the vertex count excludes every negative residual cycle and therefore certifies exact optimality.

assumptions_latex: Capacities and node balances are integral, total balance is zero, and a feasible flow exists.
Initial potentials make every relevant residual reduced cost nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Initialize the zero pseudoflow. While a node \(s\) has positive excess, choose a deficit node \(t\) reachable from \(s\), compute a shortest residual \(s\)-to-\(t\) path \(P\), and augment \(\delta=\min\{e(s),-e(t),\min_{a\in P}u_x(a)\}\). Update potentials by shortest-path distances so residual reduced costs remain nonnegative. When all excesses vanish, the resulting feasible flow satisfies the reduced-cost optimality conditions and is minimum-cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Begin with the zero pseudoflow and feasible reduced-cost potentials. Select a node \(s\) with \(e(s)>0\), compute shortest residual distances from \(s\), and select a reachable node \(t\) with \(e(t)<0\). Augment \(\delta=\min\{e(s),-e(t),\min_{a\in P}u_x(a)\}\) along a shortest path \(P\). Update the potentials using the computed distances and repeat until \(e(v)=0\) for every \(v\). Output the resulting minimum-cost feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly route flow from an excess node to a deficit node along a shortest residual path, updating potentials until all balances are satisfied.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Shortest-Path Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential shortest-path method expressed as coupled dual-price updates and tight-arc primal augmentations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a capacity-feasible pseudoflow \(x\) and a potential \(p\) satisfying \(c_p(a)\geq0\) on every residual arc. Choose a node \(s\) with \(e(s)>0\), compute shortest reduced-cost distances \(d(v)\) from \(s\), and choose a reachable node \(t\) with \(e(t)<0\). Put \(D=d(t)\), define \(q(v)=\min\{d(v),D\}\) with \(d(v)=+\infty\) for unreachable vertices, and set \(p'(v)=p(v)+q(v)\). Then augment \(\delta=\min\{e(s),-e(t),\min_{a\in P}u_x(a)\}\) along a shortest \(s\)-to-\(t\) path \(P\), replace \(p\) by \(p'\), and repeat until every balance holds. The final feasible flow and potential satisfy the reduced-cost optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shortest-path labels, capped at the chosen deficit node's distance, update all prices while preserving nonnegative residual reduced costs; flow is then augmented along the resulting tight path until feasibility and optimality hold together.
assumptions_latex: The residual network is finite, the pseudoflow has integral residual capacities and excesses, and a feasible completion exists.
The potential \(p\) satisfies \(c_p(a)=c_x(a)+p(v)-p(w)\geq0\) for every residual arc \(a=(v,w)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every residual arc \(a=(v,w)\), the capped label satisfies \(q(w)\leq q(v)+c_p(a)\), so \(c_{p'}(a)=c_p(a)+q(v)-q(w)\geq0\). Every arc of a shortest \(s\)-to-\(t\) path is tight under \(p'\). Each integral augmentation reduces an excess or deficit or saturates a path arc, and termination with all balances satisfied yields a minimum-cost feasible flow.

notation.meaning: Shortest reduced-cost distance from the selected excess node, with value positive infinity when unreachable.
Distance label capped at the selected deficit node's distance.
Residual reduced cost under potential p.
Node excess of the current pseudoflow.

assumptions_latex: Capacities and node balances are integral and bounded in absolute value by \(U\geq1\).
Shortest paths are computed with feasible reduced-cost potentials in the eligible residual network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Set \(\Delta\) to the largest power of two not exceeding \(U\). During a \(\Delta\)-phase, retain residual arcs with capacity at least \(\Delta\), and repeatedly send \(\Delta\) units along a shortest eligible path from a node with excess at least \(\Delta\) to one with deficit at least \(\Delta\), updating potentials after each search. When no such pair remains, replace \(\Delta\) by \(\Delta/2\). After the \(\Delta=1\) phase, the output is a minimum-cost feasible integral flow.

notation.meaning: Maximum absolute capacity or balance magnitude.
Residual capacity under the current pseudoflow.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-of-two capacity scaling layered on successive shortest residual paths.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\Delta=2^{\lfloor\log_2 U\rfloor}\). At scale \(\Delta\), use only residual arcs \(a\) with \(u_x(a)\geq\Delta\). While there are nodes \(s,t\) with \(e(s)\geq\Delta\) and \(e(t)\leq-\Delta\), augment \(\Delta\) units on a shortest eligible \(s\)-to-\(t\) path and update the potential. When no such augmentation exists, set \(\Delta\leftarrow\Delta/2\). Stop after completing scale \(1\) and output the minimum-cost feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process residual capacities from large to small scales, sending one scale unit along shortest eligible paths and halving the scale after each phase.

assumptions_latex: Arc costs, capacities, and balances are integral, and an initial pseudoflow is available.
At the start of each refine phase, the flow is \(\epsilon\)-optimal under a node price function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In a refine phase, first saturate residual arcs with negative reduced cost. While a node \(v\) has positive excess, push on an admissible outgoing residual arc satisfying \(c_p(v,w)<0\); if none exists, replace \(p(v)\) by \(p(v)-\epsilon\). These operations restore feasibility while preserving \(c_p(a)\geq-\epsilon\). Between phases reduce \(\epsilon\), conventionally by a constant factor. Once \(\epsilon<1/|V|\), integrality converts \(\epsilon\)-optimality into exact minimum-cost optimality.

notation.meaning: Node price and associated reduced residual cost.
Node excess of the current pseudoflow.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-scaling push–relabel framework with integral-cost exactness threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain \(c_p(a)\geq-\epsilon\) on every residual arc. At each refine step, saturate arcs with \(c_p(a)<0\). While some \(v\) has \(e(v)>0\), push \(\delta=\min\{e(v),u_x(v,w)\}\) on an outgoing arc with \(c_p(v,w)<0\); if no such arc exists, set \(p(v)\leftarrow p(v)-\epsilon\). When all excesses vanish, reduce \(\epsilon\) by the prescribed constant factor and refine again. Stop when \(\epsilon<1/|V|\), and output the resulting minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternate admissible pushes and price relabels at a shrinking reduced-cost tolerance; the final integral epsilon threshold certifies exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Epsilon-Scaling Push–Relabel

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and the relabel direction conflicts with the record's convention c_p(v,w)=c_x(v,w)+p(v)-p(w): decreasing p(v) lowers outgoing reduced costs and can violate the claimed epsilon-optimality bound. An authoritative variant-specific source and corrected sign convention are required.

assumptions_latex: A feasible flow \(x\) and residual network \(G_x\) are fixed.
The current potential certifies \(\epsilon\)-optimality, and the target tolerance is \(\epsilon'<\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A price refinement without changing \(x\) exists exactly when the difference constraints \(c_x(v,w)+p'(v)-p'(w)\geq-\epsilon'\) are feasible on all residual arcs. Equivalently, every residual directed cycle \(C\) satisfies \(\sum_{a\in C}c_x(a)+|C|\epsilon'\geq0\). Thus a shortest-path difference-constraints computation either returns a refined potential \(p'\) or returns a negative cycle for the shifted lengths \(c_x(a)+\epsilon'\), certifying that flow-changing work is necessary.

notation.meaning: Residual network of the fixed flow.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Difference-constraints characterization of refining prices while holding the primal flow fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a target \(\epsilon'<\epsilon\), assign each residual arc \(a=(v,w)\) the shifted length \(\ell(a)=c_x(a)+\epsilon'\). A refined potential exists precisely when \(p'(w)-p'(v)\leq\ell(a)\) for all residual arcs is feasible. This holds precisely when \(\sum_{a\in C}\ell(a)\geq0\) for every residual directed cycle \(C\). A feasible solution certifies \(c_{p'}(a)\geq-\epsilon'\); a negative shifted-length cycle certifies failure of price-only refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Price refinement is a difference-constraints problem: feasible potentials tighten epsilon, while a negative shifted-cost cycle proves that the flow must change.
knowledge_statements.title: Price-Refinement Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The difference-constraints equivalence is mathematically plausible, but no source supports it. Moreover, the Methods leaf calls for an algorithmic refinement procedure, whereas the record is classified only as a certificate.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite minimum-cost flow instance with integral capacities, balances, and costs.
Arithmetic operations and comparisons on input numbers have unit cost in the strongly polynomial model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Orlin minimum-cost flow algorithm family solves the instance using a number of arithmetic operations bounded by \(O\!\left(m\log n\,(m+n\log n)\right)\), where \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|A|\). The operation count and the sizes of the intermediate combinatorial structures are polynomial in \(n\) and \(m\), independent of the numerical magnitudes of capacities, balances, and costs. The algorithm therefore gives a strongly polynomial solution method for minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical strongly polynomial Orlin bound; the precise publication variant requires source certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimum-cost flow instance on a directed graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) arcs, the classical Orlin algorithm performs \(O\!\left(m\log n\,(m+n\log n)\right)\) arithmetic operations and comparisons. This bound depends polynomially only on \(n\) and \(m\), not on the magnitudes of the integral capacities, balances, or costs; consequently, it is a strongly polynomial minimum-cost flow algorithm in the arithmetic-operation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orlin's classical algorithm solves minimum-cost flow in a strongly polynomial number of operations depending only on the vertex and arc counts.
knowledge_statements.title: Orlin Minimum-Cost Flow Family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Excess-scaling and contraction procedure for an uncapacitated minimum-cost flow instance with conservative arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let n=|V(G)|. Initialize b':=b, f:=0, r(v):=v, F:=\varnothing, G':=G, and \gamma:=\max_v|b'(v)|. If b'=0, return f. Otherwise select either s with b'(s)>(n-1)\gamma/n and a reachable t with b'(t)<-\gamma/n, or t with b'(t)<-(n-1)\gamma/n and an s with b'(s)>\gamma/n from which t is reachable in G_f; if the required reachable vertex does not exist, report that no b-flow exists. Find a minimum-cost s-t path P in G'_f, augment f along P by \gamma, and replace (b'(s),b'(t)) by (b'(s)-\gamma,b'(t)+\gamma). When neither extreme case applies, set \gamma:=\min\{\gamma/2,\max_v|b'(v)|\} if f vanishes on E(G')\setminus F, and otherwise set \gamma:=\gamma/2. While some e=(x,y)\in E(G')\setminus F has f(e)>6n\gamma, add e and \overleftarrow e to F, transfer the imbalance at r(x) along the r(x)-r(y) path in F, merge that imbalance into r(y), delete remaining arcs joining the two merged components, update representatives, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the zero flow and residual imbalance, repeatedly send the current scale amount along a cheapest residual path between suitably large surplus and deficit vertices, halve the scale when necessary, and contract arcs carrying more than six times n times the scale. The procedure stops with a minimum-cost b-flow, or reports infeasibility when the required residual reachability fails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns a minimum-cost }b\text{-flow }f\text{, or correctly reports that no }b\text{-flow exists.}

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Cheapest-Flow Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong polynomiality is stated in the arithmetic-and-comparison model, without selecting a particular implementation bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed network \(G=(V,E)\) with rational arc costs and capacities and a prescribed feasible integral flow value \(m\), a strongly polynomial cheapest-flow method returns a feasible \(m\)-flow of minimum total cost. Its number of additions, subtractions, comparisons, and combinatorial operations is bounded by a polynomial in \(|V|+|E|\), independent of the magnitudes and binary encoding lengths of costs, capacities, and \(m\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cheapest feasible flow can be computed using a number of arithmetic, comparison, and combinatorial operations polynomial in \(|V|+|E|\), independent of numerical magnitudes, with intermediate encoding lengths polynomially bounded by the input encoding length.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a primal-feasible tree basis \(T\) and choose node potentials \(\pi\) so that \(\bar c_e=c_e+\pi_i-\pi_j=0\) for every tree arc. Select a nonbasic residual arc having negative reduced cost and insert it into \(T\), creating a unique fundamental cycle. Augment flow around that cycle until some cycle arc first reaches a bound; remove such a blocking arc to restore a spanning tree, update potentials, and repeat. Stop when every residual arc has nonnegative reduced cost. The current feasible flow is then minimum-cost; if the entering augmentation is zero, the pivot is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal network simplex preserves feasible flows, augments around fundamental cycles selected by reduced cost, and stops when all residual reduced costs are nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Network Simplex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-feasible network simplex for a bounded minimum-cost flow basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a tree basis \(T\), bound statuses for nonbasic arcs, and potentials \(\pi\) satisfying the corresponding reduced-cost sign conditions, although a tree flow may violate a bound. Choose an infeasible tree arc as the leaving arc and delete it, producing a fundamental cut. Among nonbasic arcs crossing that cut in a direction capable of repairing the selected violation, choose an entering arc by the dual ratio test so that the potential change preserves all reduced-cost sign conditions. Exchange the arcs, recompute the tree flow, and repeat. Stop when all tree flows satisfy their bounds; primal and dual feasibility then certify a minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual network simplex preserves reduced-cost feasibility while exchanging arcs across fundamental cuts to repair selected bound violations, and optimality is certified once primal feasibility is restored.
assumptions_latex: A spanning-tree basis satisfying the reduced-cost sign conditions is available.
The bounded minimum-cost flow problem is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each pivot preserves dual reduced-cost feasibility; when all induced tree flows satisfy their bounds, simultaneous primal and dual feasibility certifies optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-Ascent Algorithm for Uncapacitated Network Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic dual-feasible subset-update scheme; a balanced arc is used as named in the source algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from a dual-feasible \(p\), seek \(S\subseteq\mathcal N\) such that every balanced arc \((i,j)\) with \(i\in S\) has \(j\in S\), and \(\sum_{i\in S}b_i>0\). If no such \(S\) exists, declare \(p\) dual optimal and stop. Otherwise set \(\theta^*=\sup\{\theta\ge0:p+\theta d^S\text{ is dual feasible}\}\). If \(\theta^*=\infty\), stop; otherwise replace \(p\) by \(p+\theta^*d^S\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain dual feasibility. Find a node subset closed under outgoing balanced arcs and having positive total supply, then raise all its node prices by the largest feasible common amount. Absence of such a subset certifies dual optimality; an infinite maximal step also terminates the scheme.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta^*=\sup\{\theta\ge0:p+\theta d^S\text{ is dual feasible}\},\qquad p\leftarrow p+\theta^*d^S\text{ when }\theta^*<\infty

children.title: Primal–Dual Simplex Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between primal pivots, dual pivots, plus their certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Simplex Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-cut correspondence for primal and dual network-simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a spanning-tree basis \(T\), adding a nonbasic arc creates its unique fundamental cycle, whereas deleting a tree arc creates its fundamental cut. A primal network-simplex pivot selects an entering arc from a violated reduced-cost condition, moves flow on the fundamental cycle, and chooses a bound-blocking tree arc to leave. Dually, a dual network-simplex pivot selects a bound-infeasible tree arc to leave, changes potentials across its fundamental cut, and chooses an entering nonbasic arc by a reduced-cost ratio test. Thus the variants exchange the order of enforcing primal and dual feasibility; in either orientation, a basis satisfying both bound feasibility and the reduced-cost sign conditions is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal pivots use cycles to preserve flow feasibility, while dual pivots use cuts to preserve reduced-cost feasibility. In either orientation, a basis satisfying both feasibility systems is optimal.
assumptions_latex: Primal and dual variants use the same bounded minimum-cost flow linear program and complementary bound conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal pivots act on fundamental cycles and dual pivots on fundamental cuts; in either orientation, simultaneous primal bound feasibility and dual reduced-cost feasibility certifies optimality.

If neither feasibility system holds, a phase-I construction or repair is required before either pure orientation applies. In both orientations, simultaneous primal feasibility and dual reduced-cost feasibility is the stopping certificate.
