knowledge_statements.title: Pivot-Selection Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entering- and leaving-arc rules for primal network simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E^-\) be the nonbasic residual arcs with \(\bar c_e<0\). An entering-arc family chooses some \(e\in E^-\), for example the first eligible arc in a fixed order, an arc minimizing \(\bar c_e\), or an arc maximizing a prescribed improvement score. After inserting \(e\), compute the maximum feasible augmentation on its fundamental cycle. A leaving-arc rule selects an arc attaining the minimum residual capacity; if several arcs tie, it applies its specified tie rule. Each such exchange preserves primal feasibility and cannot increase cost. A finite-termination guarantee in the presence of degenerate pivots additionally requires an anticycling rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pivot families choose an improving entering arc and a blocking leaving arc. These choices define valid pivots, while finite termination under degeneracy requires an anticycling rule.
assumptions_latex: The current network-simplex basis is primal feasible.
At least one nonbasic residual arc has negative reduced cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selecting an eligible entering arc and a valid blocking leaving arc produces a primal-feasible, non-cost-increasing pivot; finite termination under degeneracy additionally requires an anticycling rule.

children.top_down_role: Construction choices for a starting network-simplex tree basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Initial Tree-Basis Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct construction of a bounded-flow tree basis, before any phase-I augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a spanning tree \(T\) of the underlying connected graph. Partition every nontree arc into \(L\) or \(U\), and set \(x_e=\ell_e\) for \(e\in L\) and \(x_e=u_e\) for \(e\in U\). Root \(T\). Processing leaves toward the root, assign the flow on each leaf's parent arc so that the leaf balance equation holds; delete the processed leaf and continue. Because the node supplies sum to zero, the final root balance is automatic. Output \((T,L,U,x)\). This is a primal-feasible initial network-simplex basis if and only if every computed tree flow satisfies \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\); otherwise phase I or basis repair is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix each nontree arc at its selected lower or upper bound, solve the tree flows from leaf balances, and accept the tree as a primal-feasible basis exactly when every computed tree flow respects its bounds.
assumptions_latex: The underlying graph of the directed network is connected, and the node supplies sum to zero.
Each arc \(e\) has finite bounds \(\ell_e\le u_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction returns a tree partition \((T,L,U)\); it is a primal-feasible start exactly when every induced tree flow satisfies \(\ell_e\le x_e\le u_e\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Introduce an artificial root \(r\) and artificial arcs \(E_a\) joining imbalanced nodes to \(r\), oriented and initialized so that the augmented flow satisfies every node balance and bound. Choose these artificial arcs as an initial tree and minimize the phase-I objective \(z_a=\sum_{e\in E_a}x_e\) by network simplex, with original-arc phase-I costs equal to zero. If the optimum has \(z_a>0\), the original instance is infeasible. If it has \(z_a=0\), pivot any zero-flow artificial basic arcs out whenever possible, delete \(r\) and \(E_a\), and use the remaining feasible basis to start optimization with the original costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Artificial root arcs create an augmented feasible tree. Minimizing their total flow either yields an original feasible basis at zero or proves infeasibility.

children.title: Warm-Start Repair
children.top_down_role: Restoration of basis validity or feasibility before resumed pivoting.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Repair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repair of a retained network-simplex basis after supplies, bounds, costs, or network data change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Retain every still-valid arc and tree edge, replace deleted tree edges by available arcs until a spanning tree \(T\) is restored, and assign each nontree arc to a valid lower- or upper-bound status. Recompute the induced tree flow \(x'\), tree potentials, and modified reduced costs \(\bar c'_e\). If \(x'\) satisfies all modified balances and bounds, the basis is a valid primal start and primal network-simplex pivots may correct reduced-cost violations. If the reduced-cost sign conditions hold for all retained nonbasic bound statuses, the basis is a valid dual start and dual network-simplex pivots may repair tree-flow bound violations. If neither invariant holds, run a valid phase-I procedure to obtain a primal- or dual-feasible basis before resuming the corresponding network-simplex method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After restoring a spanning tree and valid bound statuses, recompute primal and dual data. Reuse the basis in the orientation whose feasibility invariant still holds; if neither holds, perform phase I before resuming network simplex.
assumptions_latex: A prior tree basis is structurally available after the data changes.
The modified minimum-cost flow instance has a connected underlying graph and is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repair produces a basis satisfying a selected primal or dual feasibility invariant, after which the corresponding network-simplex pivots may resume.

notation.meaning: tree flow induced by the modified data

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a nonbasic residual arc \(e\) enter a primal-feasible tree basis, and let \(C_e\) be its fundamental cycle with the orientation induced by \(e\). For each cycle arc, take the residual capacity in the augmentation direction and define \(\theta\) as their minimum. The network-simplex pivot is degenerate when \(\theta=0\). Equivalently, at least one blocking cycle arc is already at the bound toward which the augmentation would move it. Exchanging the entering arc with such a blocking arc changes the spanning-tree basis but leaves the entire flow vector and objective value unchanged; repeated degenerate exchanges can therefore permit cycling unless tie choices are controlled.

children.title: Pivot Cycling
children.top_down_role: Repeated basis behavior arising under unsuitable pivot choices.

assumptions_latex: The minimum-cost flow instance is finite, and network-simplex bases are represented by spanning trees.
Degenerate pivots with zero augmentation are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{k+q}=T^k\) and \(x^{k+q}=x^k\) may hold for some \(q>0\), so termination is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: the spanning-tree basis after pivot k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes cycling caused by repeated degenerate network-simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pivot sequence cycles if there are integers \(k\geq 0\) and \(q>0\) such that \(T^{k+q}=T^k\), while every intervening pivot is admissible. This can occur when each pivot is degenerate: the entering arc creates a fundamental cycle, the minimum residual capacity on that cycle is zero, and the resulting augmentation leaves \(x^{k+1}=x^k\). If tie choices subsequently reproduce the same ordered sequence of bases, neither the primal objective nor the flow changes, and the network-simplex method can continue indefinitely despite the finiteness of the set of bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-augmentation pivots can revisit the same tree basis and flow; repeated tie choices may therefore make network simplex cycle indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.title: Pivot Cycling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind and local characterization are appropriate, but the nontrivial existence claim that admissible degenerate network-simplex pivots can reproduce a basis sequence and continue indefinitely has no cited evidence or inspectable example.

children.title: Anticycling Pivot Rules
children.top_down_role: Pivot-selection safeguards designed to prevent repeated basis sequences.

assumptions_latex: The arc set is equipped with a fixed total order.
Every pivot preserves primal feasibility and uses an eligible entering arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lexicographically selected basis strictly progresses, so no basis recurs and the algorithm terminates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic anticycling specialization of network-simplex pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a total order on \(A\). At each iteration choose the least eligible nonbasic arc as the entering arc. On its fundamental cycle, choose the leaving arc by the lexicographic minimum-ratio rule induced by the same order, including when the limiting augmentation is zero. Update the tree and basic flow by the resulting pivot. Stop when no eligible entering arc exists. The lexicographic perturbation implicit in this rule makes each selected basis distinct and orders successive bases strictly; hence a finite network admits only finitely many pivots before the optimality test succeeds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed lexicographic entering and leaving rule prevents repeated bases, including during degenerate pivots, and forces finite termination.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each nonterminal pivot either strictly improves the objective or changes the basis according to an anticycling ordering that forbids basis repetition. At termination, every nonbasic arc satisfies the appropriate reduced-cost sign condition: an arc at its lower bound has nonnegative reduced cost, and an arc at its upper bound has nonpositive reduced cost. Together with primal feasibility, these conditions imply optimality of the terminal flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an unassigned supply unit \(i\). Let \(j_1\) and \(j_2\) attain, respectively, the smallest and second-smallest values of \(c_{ij}+p_j\) over the feasible objects for \(i\). Assign \(i\) to \(j_1\), displacing the previous owner of \(j_1\) if necessary, and update \(p_{j_1}\) by \(p_{j_1}\leftarrow p_{j_1}+(c_{ij_2}+p_{j_2})-(c_{ij_1}+p_{j_1})+\epsilon\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute shortest-path distances \(d(v)\) from an excess node \(s\) to a deficit node \(t\) in \(G_x\), using reduced arc costs. Choose a shortest path \(P\), set \(\delta\) to the minimum of the source excess, sink deficit, and residual capacities on \(P\), and augment \(\delta\) units along \(P\). For every reached vertex update \(p_v\leftarrow p_v-d(v)\). Repeat until all imbalances vanish. The potential update keeps residual reduced costs nonnegative, and each augmentation either resolves an imbalance or saturates a path arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Send flow along a shortest residual path, update potentials by shortest-path distances, and repeat until all supply and demand imbalances vanish.

children.title: Cost-Magnitude Dependence
children.top_down_role: Runtime sensitivity to the largest absolute arc cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Cost-Magnitude Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes dependence on numerical cost magnitude from dependence on its binary encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an integer-cost minimum-cost-flow instance have costs \(c_a\) and \(C=\max_a |c_a|\). Its cost data require only \(O(m\log(C+1))\) bits. A bound of the form \(T(n,m,C)=\operatorname{poly}(n,m,C)\) is therefore magnitude-sensitive: it does not by itself imply polynomial time in the binary input length. In particular, on a family with \(C=2^k\), any term \(C^q\), where \(q>0\) is fixed, becomes \(2^{qk}\), exponential in the \(k\)-bit cost magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial dependence on the largest numerical cost can be exponential in the number of bits used to encode that cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A runtime polynomial in \(C\) need not be polynomial in the binary input length.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: binary encoding uses logarithmically many bits while numeric-value dependence may be exponential in that length

children.title: Pseudopolynomial Runtime Regime
children.top_down_role: Bounds polynomial in numeric values but not necessarily in their encoding lengths.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudopolynomial Runtime Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies numeric-value polynomial bounds for binary-encoded integral minimum-cost-flow data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimum-cost-flow instance with \(n\) nodes, \(m\) arcs, integral capacities and costs, set \(U=\max_a u_a\) and \(C=\max_a |c_a|\). An algorithm operates in the pseudopolynomial runtime regime if its operation count is bounded by \(\operatorname{poly}(n,m,U,C)\), but no bound polynomial in \(n\), \(m\), \(\log(U+1)\), and \(\log(C+1)\) follows from that analysis. Such a bound is polynomial when numerical magnitudes are treated as parameters, not necessarily when the complete binary encoding is the input measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudopolynomial flow algorithm is polynomial in capacities and costs as numbers, but may be exponential in their binary encoding lengths.
assumptions_latex: Capacities and costs are integral and encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bound \(\operatorname{poly}(n,m,U,C)\) is pseudopolynomial unless it can be replaced by a polynomial in the encoding lengths.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pseudopolynomial time is polynomial in numeric values rather than their binary lengths

children.title: Binary-Encoding Complexity Gap
children.top_down_role: The separation between magnitude-based bounds and input-length polynomiality.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Encoding Complexity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies the gap between value-based and bit-length-based minimum-cost-flow bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) denote the binary input length of an integral minimum-cost-flow instance. Since an integer \(z\) contributes \(\Theta(\log(|z|+1))\) bits, instances may satisfy \(U=2^{\Theta(L)}\) or \(C=2^{\Theta(L)}\). Consequently, a value-based bound containing \(U^p\) or \(C^q\), for fixed \(p,q>0\), can equal \(2^{\Theta(L)}\). Thus polynomial dependence on \(U\) or \(C\) cannot establish weakly or strongly polynomial complexity under binary encoding without an additional scaling or magnitude-independent argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numeric-value polynomial bounds may become exponential after capacities and costs are measured by their binary input length.
assumptions_latex: Integral numerical data are represented in binary.
At least one positive exponent \(p\) or \(q\) is fixed independently of the instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound polynomial in \(U\) or \(C\) alone does not imply a bound polynomial in \(L\).

notation.meaning: maximum capacity and absolute cost magnitudes

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exponential separation between an integer's value and its binary length

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible Balance Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut certificate for infeasibility of bounded node-balance equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\), let \(B\) have entry \(+1\) at an arc's head and \(-1\) at its tail, and consider \(Bx=b\) with \(\ell\le x\le u\). The system is feasible exactly when every \(S\subseteq V\) satisfies
\[\ell(\delta^-(S))-u(\delta^+(S))\le b(S)\le u(\delta^-(S))-\ell(\delta^+(S)).\]
Hence infeasibility is certified by a set \(S\) violating either displayed inequality. Taking \(S=V\) also certifies infeasibility whenever \(b(V)\ne0\). The certificate is checked by summing balances and the bounds of arcs crossing the cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded balance system is infeasible exactly when some vertex set has a demand total outside the attainable net inflow across its cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A violating set \(S\subseteq V\) is a verifiable infeasibility certificate.

notation.meaning: arcs entering and leaving the vertex set
sums of lower and upper bounds over an arc set

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cost Unboundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-direction characterization of unbounded minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), where bounds may take extended-real values, and suppose its feasible set is nonempty. Its value is \(-\infty\) if and only if there exists a nonzero vector \(d\) such that \(Bd=0\), \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), and \(x+td\) remains within the bounds for every feasible point \(x\) and every \(t\ge0\). Componentwise, \(d_a=0\) when both bounds on arc \(a\) are finite, \(d_a\ge0\) when \(\ell_a\) is finite and \(u_a=+\infty\), \(d_a\le0\) when \(\ell_a=-\infty\) and \(u_a\) is finite, and \(d_a\) is unrestricted when \(\ell_a=-\infty\) and \(u_a=+\infty\). A negative-cost directed cycle whose arcs permit indefinite augmentation supplies such a direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible minimum-cost flow is unbounded below exactly when its feasible recession cone contains a negative-cost circulation.
assumptions_latex: Lower and upper bounds may take the extended-real values \(-\infty\) and \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is unbounded below exactly when a feasible recession circulation \(d\) has \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Certificate Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rounded reduced-cost test can accept a truly suboptimal circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take two nodes and two oppositely directed arcs forming a cycle, each with capacity \(1\), lower bound \(0\), and exact cost \(-\varepsilon\), where \(0<\varepsilon<\tau\) and \(\tau\) is the rounding threshold. The zero circulation is feasible, but sending one unit around the cycle has cost \(-2\varepsilon<0\), so zero is not optimal. If arithmetic rounds each cost to \(0\), the potential vector \(p=0\) yields computed reduced costs \(0\), falsely satisfying the nonnegative reduced-cost certificate at the zero flow. Thus a certificate checked only against rounded data need not certify the exact instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding tiny negative costs to zero can make a suboptimal zero flow pass a computed nonnegative-reduced-cost test.

Optimality concerns the exact, unrounded costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Node–Arc Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed incidence convention for directed static flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), its node–arc incidence matrix is \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\), with
\[B_{va}=\begin{cases}-1,&v\text{ is the tail of }a,\\+1,&v\text{ is the head of }a,\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]
Every nonloop column contains one \(-1\) and one \(+1\); a loop column is zero. For an arc-flow vector \(x\), the component \((Bx)_v\) equals total inflow to \(v\) minus total outflow from \(v\). Consequently, the balance equations are represented as \(Bx=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The node–arc incidence matrix records minus one at each arc tail and plus one at its head, so matrix multiplication gives net inflow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every flow vector \(x\), \((Bx)_v\) is the net inflow at node \(v\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A) be directed, with \mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\} and m ordered arcs having distinct start and end nodes. children.title: Reduced Incidence Matrices
children.top_down_role: Incidence representations formed by selecting a reference node row for removal.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incidence representation obtained by deleting one node equation per connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be the node–arc incidence matrix of a directed graph whose underlying undirected graph has \(k\) connected components. Choose one reference node in each component and delete the corresponding \(k\) rows of \(B\). The resulting matrix \(\bar B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{(|V|-k)\times |A|}\) is a reduced incidence matrix. It has full row rank \(|V|-k\), while \(\ker \bar B=\ker B\). When the graph is connected, deleting any single row produces a matrix with \(|V|-1\) independent rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting one incidence row from each connected component removes redundant balance equations without changing the circulation space.
assumptions_latex: Reference nodes include exactly one node from each underlying connected component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(\bar B)=|V|-k\) and \(\ker\bar B=\ker B\).

children.title: Reference-Node Reduction
children.top_down_role: The structural effect of choosing a reference node to obtain a reduced matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Node Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of full and reference-node-deleted balance systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be connected, let \(B\) be its node–arc incidence matrix, and delete the row indexed by a reference node \(r\) to obtain \(\bar B\). Delete the same component from \(b\) to obtain \(\bar b\). Because \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}B=0\), the full system \(Bx=b\) implies \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}b=0\) and \(\bar Bx=\bar b\). Conversely, if \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}b=0\), then every solution of \(\bar Bx=\bar b\) automatically satisfies the omitted balance equation at \(r\), and hence satisfies \(Bx=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With total balance zero, deleting one reference-node equation yields a system equivalent to all node-balance equations.
assumptions_latex: The underlying undirected graph is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Bx=b\) if and only if \(\bar Bx=\bar b\).

notation.meaning: matrix and balance vector with the reference-node row or entry removed

children.title: Orientation Invariance
children.top_down_role: How arc-orientation conventions alter signs without changing the underlying network structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-sign invariance for signed incidence representations, not nonnegative directed-flow bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be an incidence matrix for an arbitrary orientation of an undirected graph. Reversing any selected edges multiplies their columns by \(-1\), so the new incidence matrix is \(B'=BD\), where \(D\) is diagonal with entries in \(\{-1,1\}\). Hence \(\operatorname{rank}(B')=\operatorname{rank}(B)\), \(B'\) is totally unimodular exactly when \(B\) is, and \(x\mapsto D x\) is a bijection from \(\ker B\) to \(\ker B'\). This invariance concerns signed edge coordinates; fixed inequalities such as \(x\ge0\) must also be transformed when an orientation is reversed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing arbitrary edge orientations only changes incidence-column signs, preserving rank, total unimodularity, and the signed circulation space.
assumptions_latex: Edge variables are interpreted as signed coordinates when orientations change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Orientation reversal preserves incidence-matrix rank, total unimodularity, and circulation-space structure up to \(x\mapsto Dx\).

notation.meaning: incidence matrix after selected orientation reversals

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental-Cycle Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-space basis induced by a spanning tree and reduced incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be connected, choose a spanning tree \(T\), and order the columns of a reduced incidence matrix as \(\bar B=[B_T\ B_N]\). The square matrix \(B_T\) is nonsingular. The fundamental-cycle matrix
\[Z=\begin{bmatrix}-B_T^{-1}B_N\\ I\end{bmatrix}\]
satisfies \(\bar BZ=0\). Each column is the signed incidence vector of the unique cycle created by adding one non-tree edge to \(T\); consequently its entries lie in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). The columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\ker\bar B=\ker B\), so every circulation has a unique representation \(x=Zy\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree yields one signed fundamental cycle per non-tree edge, and these vectors form a basis for all circulations.
assumptions_latex: The underlying undirected graph is connected.
\(T\) is a spanning tree and \(\bar B\) deletes one incidence row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar BZ=0\) and the columns of \(Z\) form a basis of the circulation space.

notation.meaning: reduced incidence columns for tree and non-tree edges

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: block elimination with an invertible tree-incidence basis gives the displayed kernel basis

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental-Cut Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut-space basis induced by a spanning tree and reduced incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be connected, choose a spanning tree \(T\), and write a reduced incidence matrix as \(\bar B=[B_T\ B_N]\). The fundamental-cut matrix is
\[Q=B_T^{-1}\bar B=\begin{bmatrix}I&B_T^{-1}B_N\end{bmatrix}.\]
Its row indexed by a tree edge is the signed incidence vector of the cut obtained by deleting that edge from \(T\), with signs determined by the chosen orientations. Thus \(Q\) has entries in \(\{-1,0,1\}\), and its rows form a basis for \(\operatorname{row}(\bar B)\). Moreover, the fundamental cut and cycle matrices are orthogonal: \(QZ=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting each tree edge gives a signed fundamental cut; these cut vectors form a basis for the incidence row space.
assumptions_latex: The underlying undirected graph is connected.
\(T\) is a spanning tree and \(\bar B\) is reduced at one node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rows of \(Q\) form a cut-space basis, and \(QZ=0\).

notation.meaning: reduced incidence columns for tree and non-tree edges

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: row reduction by the tree-incidence basis produces the standard fundamental-cut representation

knowledge_statements.title: Network Matrices from Tree Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-basis representation for a connected directed graph after deleting one incidence row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a connected directed graph, let \(B\) be its node-arc incidence matrix with one row deleted, and partition \(B=[B_T\ B_R]\), where \(T\subseteq A\) is a spanning tree. Then \(B_T\) is nonsingular and the associated network matrix is \[N=B_T^{-1}B_R.\] For each non-tree arc \(a\in R\), its column in \(N\) is the signed incidence vector of the unique path in \(T\) joining the endpoints of \(a\); consequently every entry of \(N\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning-tree incidence basis transforms each non-tree arc into the signed vector of its unique tree path, producing the network matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is a spanning tree of the underlying undirected graph.
One row is deleted from the node-arc incidence matrix.

notation.meaning: Reduced incidence submatrix indexed by tree arcs.
Reduced incidence submatrix indexed by non-tree arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Incidence-Matrix Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total unimodularity of directed node-arc incidence matrices and their row-deleted forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed graph \(D=(V,A)\), define its node-arc incidence matrix \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\) by placing \(-1\) at the tail, \(1\) at the head, and \(0\) elsewhere in each non-loop column; a loop column is zero. Then \(B\) is totally unimodular: every square submatrix has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). Every matrix obtained by deleting rows or columns of \(B\), including a reduced incidence matrix, is therefore totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every directed node-arc incidence matrix is totally unimodular, as are all matrices obtained by deleting its rows or columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) and every row-column submatrix of \(B\) are totally unimodular.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Matrix Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network matrices induced by spanning-tree bases of reduced directed incidence matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(N\) is a network matrix if there exist a connected directed graph with a reduced node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), a spanning-tree arc set \(T\), and the complementary arc set \(R\), such that \(B=[B_T\ B_R]\) and \[N=B_T^{-1}B_R.\] Equivalently, after orienting every tree path consistently, each column records with signs the unique tree path joining the endpoints of one non-tree arc. Every network matrix is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network matrix expresses non-tree incidence columns in a spanning-tree incidence basis; every such matrix is totally unimodular.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a reduced incidence matrix of a connected directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=B_T^{-1}B_R\) is a network matrix and is totally unimodular.

knowledge_statements.title: Unimodularity-Preserving Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary transformations that preserve total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\) is totally unimodular, then total unimodularity is preserved by transposition; permuting rows or columns; multiplying a row or column by \(-1\); deleting or duplicating a row or column; and adjoining a unit row or unit column. It is also preserved by pivoting on an entry \(a_{ij}\in\{-1,1\}\), provided the pivot operation is followed by deleting the pivot row and column when forming the associated Schur-complement matrix. Thus every matrix obtained by a finite sequence of these operations remains totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard sign, permutation, deletion, duplication, unit-extension, transposition, and unit-pivot operations preserve total unimodularity.
assumptions_latex: Every stated pivot uses an entry \(a_{ij}\in\{-1,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each matrix produced by the listed operations is totally unimodular.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied for the combined operation list, and the exact pivot/Schur-complement convention materially affects the statement. An authoritative source with a specific theorem, proposition, section, or page locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Feasible-Flow Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of capacitated circulation polyhedra with integral balances and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a directed node-arc incidence matrix, let \(b\in\mathbb Z^{V}\), and let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^{A}\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\). The feasible-flow polyhedron \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^{A}:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\] is integral: every vertex of \(P\) belongs to \(\mathbb Z^{A}\). Consequently, if \(P\) is nonempty, it contains an integral feasible flow; and any linear objective attaining a finite optimum over \(P\) has an integral optimal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral balances and arc bounds make the feasible-flow polyhedron integral, yielding integral feasible and optimal flows whenever they exist.
assumptions_latex: The relevant feasibility or finite-attainment condition holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is integral, and every attained linear optimum has an integral optimal vertex.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Maximum Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-optimum theorem for single-source single-sink maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and capacities \(u_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). If a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow exists, then there is a maximum flow \(x\) satisfying \(x_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every \(a\in A\). In particular, the maximum-flow value is an integer. The assertion concerns existence of an integral optimum; fractional maximum flows may also exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite directed network with nonnegative integral capacities has an integral maximum flow and an integer maximum-flow value.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is finite with distinguished vertices \(s\ne t\).
Every capacity \(u_a\) is a nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an integral maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow, and its value lies in \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Minimum-Cost Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-optimum theorem for linear minimum-cost flow with integral network data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be finite, with integral node balances \(b\), integral lower bounds \(\ell\), integral upper bounds \(u\), and arbitrary real arc costs \(c\). If \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\] is feasible and has a finite attained optimum, then it has an optimal solution \(x^*\in\mathbb Z^{A}\). Integrality of the costs is unnecessary: the conclusion follows from integrality of the feasible-flow polyhedron, not from the objective coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible, attained minimum-cost flow problem with integral balances and bounds has an integral optimum, even for real costs.
assumptions_latex: The linear objective has a finite attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(x^*\in\mathbb Z^{A}\) minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over the feasible-flow polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegral-Data Limitation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of integral-flow conclusions when a capacity is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the directed graph with vertices \(s,t\) and a single arc \(a=(s,t)\) having capacity \(u_a=\tfrac12\). Its feasible flow values are exactly \(x_a\in[0,\tfrac12]\), so the unique maximum flow is \(x_a=\tfrac12\). Thus the maximum-flow value and the optimal flow are nonintegral. Total unimodularity of the incidence matrix does not imply an integral feasible polyhedron when the right-hand side or variable bounds are nonintegral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single arc of capacity one-half has unique maximum flow one-half, showing that integral-data assumptions cannot simply be dropped.
assumptions_latex: The network consists only of the arc \(a=(s,t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique maximum flow satisfies \(x_a=\tfrac12\notin\mathbb Z\).

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the square assignment polytope as a unit-margin transportation polytope and a bipartite perfect-matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite sets \(I,J\) with \(|I|=|J|=n\), the assignment polytope is
\[
P_{\mathrm{assn}}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{I\times J}:\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\ (i\in I),\ \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\ (j\in J)\right\}.
\]
It is simultaneously the transportation polytope with all supplies and demands equal to one and the perfect-matching polytope of the complete bipartite graph on \(I\cup J\). Its vertices are precisely the permutation matrices; hence every linear objective over \(P_{\mathrm{assn}}\) has an optimal permutation matrix whenever the polytope is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The assignment polytope is the unit-margin transportation polytope; its vertices are permutation matrices representing perfect bipartite matchings.
assumptions_latex: All assignment variables are continuous and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{assn}}=\operatorname{conv}\{\text{permutation matrices indexed by }I\times J\}\).

children.title: Fractional-Data Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of the integral-solution consequence when supplies, demands, or capacities are fractional.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Data Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that integral transportation solutions are not guaranteed when a margin is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the transportation system with one supply node, one demand node, a single variable \(x_{11}\ge 0\), and margins \(a_1=b_1=\tfrac12\). Its feasible set is
\[
\left\{x_{11}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}:x_{11}=a_1,\ x_{11}=b_1\right\}=\left\{\tfrac12\right\}.
\]
Thus the unique feasible point and the optimum for every linear cost are fractional. The transportation constraint matrix remains totally unimodular, so matrix integrality alone does not imply integral feasible points when the right-hand-side margins are nonintegral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-cell transportation problem with supply and demand one-half has the unique fractional solution one-half, despite its totally unimodular constraint matrix.
assumptions_latex: Supply and demand margins may be nonintegral.
Feasibility requires equal total supply and demand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{11}=\tfrac12\notin\mathbb{Z}\), so the integral-solution conclusion fails for fractional margins.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegral-Data Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the data integrality needed to transfer node-arc incidence-matrix integrality to bounded feasible flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(A\) be its entering-positive node-arc incidence matrix, and let
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\},
\]
where \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\). If \(b,\ell,u\) are integral, then every vertex of \(P\) is integral. This conclusion is not guaranteed for nonintegral data. For example, on one arc directed from \(s\) to \(t\), taking \(b_s=-\tfrac12\), \(b_t=\tfrac12\), and \(0\le x\le1\) yields the unique feasible flow \(x=\tfrac12\). Thus nonintegral balances or bounds can destroy the integral-vertex conclusion even though \(A\) remains totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral balances and finite bounds give integral flow vertices, but fractional data can force a unique fractional flow even though the incidence matrix remains totally unimodular.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is the entering-positive node-arc incidence matrix of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonintegrality of \(b\), \(\ell\), or \(u\) can produce a nonintegral vertex of \(P\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the directed simple source–sink path polytope in arc-incidence space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with distinct vertices \(s,t\). For each simple directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path \(P\), let \(\chi^P\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) satisfy \(\chi^P_e=1\) exactly when \(e\in P\). The source–sink path polytope is
\[
\mathcal{P}_{s,t}(D)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^P:P\text{ is a simple directed }s\text{-to-}t\text{ path in }D\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{E}.
\]
It is empty when no directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path exists. Every nonempty vertex set consists of incidence vectors of simple paths, although a balance-only unit-flow formulation may additionally contain circulations unless its graph or objective excludes them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The source–sink path polytope is the convex hull of the arc-incidence vectors of all simple directed source–sink paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{P}_{s,t}(D)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^P:P\text{ is a simple directed }s\text{-to-}t\text{ path}\}\).

children.title: Source–Sink Flow Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral structure for flows with distinguished source and sink roles.

knowledge_statements.title: Source–Sink Flow Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bounded single-commodity source–sink flows of prescribed value using node balances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(A\) be its node-arc incidence matrix with an entering arc contributing \(+1\), and choose distinct \(s,t\in V\). Given flow value \(v\ge0\) and capacities \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{E}\), define \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) by \(b_s=-v\), \(b_t=v\), and \(b_i=0\) otherwise. The prescribed-value source–sink flow polyhedron is
\[
F_{s,t}(v,u)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}.
\]
Thus every intermediate node conserves flow, while the source exports and the sink imports exactly \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source–sink flow polyhedron contains capacity-feasible arc flows that conserve flow internally and transport a prescribed amount from source to sink.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{s,t}(v,u)=\{x:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\) with \(b_s=-v\), \(b_t=v\), and all other balances zero.

children.title: Circulation Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral structure for globally balanced network flows.

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bounded circulations as arc flows having zero divergence at every node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(A\) be its node-arc incidence matrix. For finite bound vectors \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) satisfying \(\ell\le u\), the bounded circulation polyhedron is
\[
C(D,\ell,u)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:Ax=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\}.
\]
The equality \(Ax=0\) means that total inflow equals total outflow at every vertex. If \(\ell\) and \(u\) are integral, every vertex of \(C(D,\ell,u)\) is integral because a node-arc incidence matrix is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded circulation polyhedron consists of arc flows within finite bounds and with zero net balance at every node; integral bounds give integral vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(D,\ell,u)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:Ax=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).

children.title: Transshipment Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral structure for prescribed node supplies and demands.

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines capacitated transshipment flows for an arbitrary balanced vector of node supplies and demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with entering-positive node-arc incidence matrix \(A\). Given node balances \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\) and arc bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) satisfying \(\ell\le u\), the transshipment polyhedron is
\[
T(D,b,\ell,u)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}.
\]
A positive component \(b_i\) is net demand and a negative component is net supply. Circulation and prescribed-value source–sink flow polyhedra arise by taking respectively \(b=0\) and a balance vector supported only on \(s,t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment polyhedron contains bounded arc flows realizing arbitrary balanced supplies and demands; circulations and source–sink flows are special cases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(D,b,\ell,u)=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).

children.title: Balance-Space Specialization
children.top_down_role: How node-balance restrictions connect the three network polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Balance-Space Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes which balance vectors can lie in the image of a directed incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(A\), and let \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\) be the vertex sets of its weakly connected components. Then
\[
\operatorname{im}(A)=\left\{b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}:\sum_{i\in V_r}b_i=0\text{ for every }r=1,\ldots,k\right\}.
\]
Consequently, \(Ax=b\) can be solvable only if the balance sums to zero separately on every weak component, and this condition is sufficient when arc bounds are absent. If \(D\) is weakly connected, the balance space is the codimension-one subspace \(\{b:\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}b=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence-matrix balances sum to zero on each weak component; without arc bounds, these componentwise equations exactly characterize feasible balances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\in\operatorname{im}(A)\) if and only if \(\sum_{i\in V_r}b_i=0\) for every weak component \(V_r\).

notation.meaning: linear space of realizable balance vectors
vertex set of weak component r

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the classical capacitated bipartite transportation polyhedron with prescribed supply and demand margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I,J\) be finite sets, let supplies \(a\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{I}\), demands \(b\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{J}\), and capacities \(u\in(\mathbb{R}_{+}\cup\{+\infty\})^{I\times J}\). The transportation polyhedron is
\[
T(a,b,u)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{I\times J}:\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=a_i\ (i\in I),\ \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=b_j\ (j\in J),\ x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\right\}.
\]
Its feasibility requires \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\). It is a transshipment polyhedron on a bipartite directed network whose arcs run from supply nodes to demand nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transportation polyhedron consists of nonnegative shipments meeting every supply and demand margin, optionally subject to route capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b\) are nonnegative and have equal totals.
Every capacity \(u_{ij}\) is nonnegative or infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(a,b,u)\) is the displayed bipartite balance-constrained network polyhedron.

children.title: Tree-Basis Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Adjacency relations among feasible tree bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Basis Adjacency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes adjacency of nondegenerate network-flow vertices through a single spanning-tree basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a standard-form network-flow polyhedron obtained by deleting one redundant balance equation from a weakly connected network, and suppose every feasible basic solution is nondegenerate. Each vertex then has a unique basis whose basic arcs form a spanning tree. Two distinct vertices \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent if and only if their basis trees \(T_x,T_y\) differ by one exchange:
\[
T_y=T_x\cup\{e\}\setminus\{f\},
\]
where \(e\notin T_x\) and \(f\) lies on the unique fundamental cycle created by adding \(e\) to \(T_x\). Without nondegeneracy, a vertex may have several tree bases and this basis-difference test need not characterize vertex adjacency directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nondegenerate network-flow vertices, adjacency is exactly a one-arc exchange between their unique spanning-tree bases.
assumptions_latex: The reduced incidence matrix has full row rank.
Every feasible basic solution is nondegenerate.
Basic arcs are unrestricted by active nonbasic-bound conventions after standard-form conversion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent if and only if \(|T_x\setminus T_y|=|T_y\setminus T_x|=1\).

notation.meaning: unique spanning-tree bases of vertices x and y

children.title: Network Pivot Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric interpretation of network-simplex movement between neighboring bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Pivot Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the one-dimensional feasible motion induced by a nonbasic arc leaving an active bound in a bounded network basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be feasible for \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), where \(A\) is a reduced node-arc incidence matrix and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) are finite. Let \(T\) be a spanning-tree basis, and let a nonbasic arc \(e\notin T\) leave its active bound. Set \(\sigma_e=1\) when \(e\) leaves its lower bound and \(\sigma_e=-1\) when it leaves its upper bound. Adding \(e\) to \(T\) creates a unique undirected fundamental cycle \(C(T,e)\), and there is a unique direction \(d\in\{-1,0,1\}^{E}\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d_e=\sigma_e\), and \(\operatorname{supp}(d)\subseteq C(T,e)\). The feasible motion is \(x(\theta)=x+\theta d\) for \(0\le\theta\le\theta^*\), where
\[
\theta^*=\max\{\theta\ge0:\ell\le x+\theta d\le u\}.
\]
Outside \(C(T,e)\), all flow components remain unchanged. If a tree arc first reaches a bound, it may leave the basis; if only \(e\) reaches its opposite bound, the step is a bound flip and the tree basis is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonbasic arc leaving a bound induces a signed flow change around its fundamental cycle until a tree arc blocks or the entering arc reaches its opposite bound.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
\(T\) is a spanning-tree basis of the reduced incidence system.
\(e\notin T\) leaves one of its active finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pivot direction satisfies \(Ad=0\), \(d_e=\sigma_e\), and \(\operatorname{supp}(d)\subseteq C(T,e)\); the maximal step ends in a tree-arc blocking event or a bound flip of \(e\).

notation.meaning: fundamental cycle formed by adding e to T
sign that moves the entering arc away from its active bound

children.title: Fundamental-Cycle Exchange
children.top_down_role: The cycle structure linking an entering arc to a neighboring tree basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Fundamental-Cycle Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a bounded-variable network pivot generated by inserting one nonbasic arc into a tree basis, including tree exchange and bound-flip outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a feasible flow \(x\) for \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), a spanning-tree basis \(T\), and a nonbasic arc \(e\notin T\) leaving an active finite bound. Set \(\sigma_e=1\) if \(e\) leaves its lower bound and \(\sigma_e=-1\) if it leaves its upper bound. Form the unique fundamental cycle \(C(T,e)\), and choose the unique vector \(d\in\{-1,0,1\}^{E}\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d_e=\sigma_e\), and \(\operatorname{supp}(d)\subseteq C(T,e)\). Compute
\[
\theta^*=\max\{\theta\ge0:\ell\le x+\theta d\le u\}
\]
and set \(x'=x+\theta^*d\). If at least one tree arc \(f\in C(T,e)\setminus\{e\}\) reaches a bound at \(\theta^*\), choose one such arc and set \(T'=T\cup\{e\}\setminus\{f\}\). Otherwise \(e\) has reached its opposite bound; perform a bound flip and set \(T'=T\). If \(\theta^*=0\), the tree-exchange pivot is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Move the entering arc away from its active bound around the fundamental cycle; exchange it with a blocking tree arc, or retain the tree when the entering arc instead reaches its opposite bound.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for \(Ax=b\) and finite bounds \(\ell\le x\le u\).
\(T\) is a spanning-tree basis of the reduced incidence system.
\(e\notin T\) leaves one of its active bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs feasible \(x'=x+\theta^*d\) and either \(T'=T\cup\{e\}\setminus\{f\}\) after a tree-arc blocking event or \(T'=T\) after a bound flip.

notation.meaning: fundamental cycle of entering arc e
sign moving e away from its active bound

children.top_down_role: Cases where basis exchanges fail to correspond uniquely to geometric edge movement.

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\), where \(A\) is a reduced node-arc incidence matrix.
\(B\) is a spanning-tree basis representing a basic feasible flow \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B'\ne B\) may hold while \(x'=x\); hence basis adjacency does not imply adjacency of distinct vertices when degeneracy is present.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e\notin B\) enter a tree basis. Adding \(e\) creates a fundamental cycle, and the simplex direction changes flow alternately along that cycle. Let \(\theta\ge 0\) be the largest step preserving all bounds. If a basic arc already lies at the bound that restricts this direction, then \(\theta=0\). The pivot may replace that limiting arc by \(e\), producing a different basis \(B'\), but its represented flow satisfies \(x'=x\). Thus an exchange edge in the graph of feasible tree bases can collapse to one polyhedral vertex; identifying basis exchanges with edges between distinct vertices requires a nondegeneracy hypothesis or quotienting all bases representing the same vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-length network-simplex pivot changes the tree basis without changing the flow, so adjacent bases need not represent distinct adjacent vertices.

children.title: Balanced Transportation
children.top_down_role: Transportation instances with equal aggregate supply and demand.

assumptions_latex: \(a_i\ge 0\) for \(i\in I\), \(b_j\ge 0\) for \(j\in J\), and all quantities are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transportation instance is balanced exactly when \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\).

notation.meaning: Quantity transported from i to j.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained finite transportation model with exact satisfaction of every supply and demand.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 A Transformation of Min-Cost Flow to Hitchcock p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite origin and destination sets \(I\) and \(J\), with supplies \(a_i\) and demands \(b_j\), the equality-constrained transportation model seeks \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) satisfying \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=a_i\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=b_j\) for every \(j\in J\). It is balanced when \[\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j.\] This equality is necessary for feasibility because summing either family of constraints gives the same total shipment. In the unrestricted complete bipartite model, it is also sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transportation instance is balanced when total supply equals total demand; then exact row and column shipment equations are mutually consistent.
knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Transportation

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 A Transformation of Min-Cost Flow to Hitchcock p. 148

children.title: Unbalanced Transportation
children.top_down_role: Transportation instances with unequal aggregate supply and demand.

assumptions_latex: \(a_i\ge 0\) for \(i\in I\), \(b_j\ge 0\) for \(j\in J\), and all quantities are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\sum_i a_i\ne\sum_j b_j\), no nonnegative matrix can satisfy all exact supply and demand equations simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Imbalance of aggregate supply and demand before adding dummy nodes or inequality-based shortage rules.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 A Transformation of Min-Cost Flow to Hitchcock p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\) and \(D=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\). A transportation instance is unbalanced when \(S\ne D\). Under exact constraints \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=a_i\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=b_j\), its feasible set is empty: summing the row equations yields \(\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}=S\), whereas summing the column equations yields \(\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}=D\). A usable unbalanced model must therefore relax some equalities or introduce variables, such as dummy shipments, that absorb the difference \(\lvert S-D\rvert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance is unbalanced when total supply differs from total demand; exact transportation equalities are then infeasible without augmentation or relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbalanced Transportation

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 A Transformation of Min-Cost Flow to Hitchcock p. 148

children.title: Dummy-Node Balancing
children.top_down_role: Representation choices that convert an imbalance into a balanced transportation instance.

assumptions_latex: The original transportation instance has finite nonnegative supplies and demands.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented instance has equal total supply and demand, and deleting dummy shipments recovers the original real shipments.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard dummy-origin or dummy-destination completion of an unbalanced transportation table.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 A Transformation of Min-Cost Flow to Hitchcock p. 148

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute \(S=\sum_i a_i\), \(D=\sum_j b_j\), and \(\delta=\lvert S-D\rvert\). If \(S>D\), append a dummy destination \(0\) with demand \(b_0=\delta\) and permit shipments \(x_{i0}\) from every origin. If \(D>S\), append a dummy origin \(0\) with supply \(a_0=\delta\) and permit shipments \(x_{0j}\) to every destination. If \(S=D\), add nothing. Solve the resulting balanced transportation problem and output its restriction to real origin-destination pairs; dummy shipments record unused supply in the first case and unmet demand in the second.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a dummy destination for excess supply or a dummy origin for excess demand, with quantity equal to the aggregate imbalance.
knowledge_statements.title: Dummy-Node Balancing

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 A Transformation of Min-Cost Flow to Hitchcock p. 148

children.title: Penalty-Cost Balancing
children.top_down_role: Treatment of unmet supply or demand through explicit penalty-cost structure.

assumptions_latex: The origin and destination sets \(I\) and \(J\) are finite, with supplies \(a_i\ge 0\) and demands \(b_j\ge 0\).
Unused supply at origin \(i\) has linear unit penalty \(p_i\), and unmet demand at destination \(j\) has linear unit penalty \(q_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dummy-arc costs reproduce the specified linear penalty for the applicable one-sided imbalance while balancing the augmented transportation table.

notation.meaning: Penalty per unit of unused supply at origin i.
Penalty per unit of unmet demand at destination j.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear shortage or surplus penalties represented as costs on balancing dummy arcs.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\) and \(D=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\). If \(S>D\), add a dummy destination \(0\) with demand \(S-D\), permit a dummy shipment \(x_{i0}\ge 0\) from every origin \(i\), and set its unit cost to \(c_{i0}=p_i\). The augmented balance equations identify \(x_{i0}\) with unused supply at \(i\), so the added objective term is \(\sum_{i\in I}p_i x_{i0}\). If \(D>S\), add a dummy origin \(0\) with supply \(D-S\), permit \(x_{0j}\ge 0\) to every destination \(j\), and set \(c_{0j}=q_j\). Then \(x_{0j}\) represents unmet demand at \(j\), and the added objective term is \(\sum_{j\in J}q_j x_{0j}\). Thus, after interpreting the applicable exact real-side constraints together with unused-supply or unmet-demand variables, the balanced augmentation has exactly the real transportation cost plus the prescribed linear imbalance penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalty-priced dummy shipments represent linear costs for unused supply when supply is excessive and for unmet demand when demand is excessive.
knowledge_statements.title: Penalty-Cost Balancing

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite sets; \(a_i,b_j,u_{ij}\ge 0\) and \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\) for every \((i,j)\in I\times J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible capacitated transportation plan is precisely a matrix satisfying the row sums, column sums, and route bounds simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transportation with upper bounds on individual origin-destination routes.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite origin and destination sets \(I\) and \(J\), supplies \(a_i\), demands \(b_j\), route capacities \(u_{ij}\), and unit costs \(c_{ij}\), the capacitated transportation problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\ \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=a_i\ \text{ for every }i\in I,\ \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=b_j\ \text{ for every }j\in J,\ 0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\ \text{ for every }(i,j)\in I\times J\right\}.\] A route may be forbidden by setting \(u_{ij}=0\). Aggregate balance \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\) is necessary but need not be sufficient, because route capacities can prevent realization of the required row and column sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacitated transportation minimizes shipment cost subject to exact supplies and demands and an upper bound on every origin-destination route.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given transshipment arcs \((v,w)\) with flow \(x_{vw}\), capacity \(u_{vw}\), cost \(c_{vw}\), and balance \(\sum_w x_{vw}-\sum_w x_{wv}=b_v\), choose \(M\ge\sum_{(v,w)}u_{vw}\). Subtracting each column equation from its corresponding row equation gives the original balance equation, establishing a cost-preserving correspondence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a feasible basic transportation plan whose basic cells form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph. Compute potentials satisfying \(\alpha_i+\beta_j=c_{ij}\) on every basic cell and reduced costs \(r_{ij}=c_{ij}-\alpha_i-\beta_j\) on every nonbasic cell. If every nonbasic reduced cost satisfies \(r_{ij}\ge 0\), stop and output the current plan. Otherwise, choose a nonbasic entering cell with \(r_{ij}<0\). Adding it to the tree creates a unique alternating cycle. Increase flow on the plus cells and decrease flow on the minus cells by \(\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the minimum current flow on a minus cell. Remove a limiting minus cell, apply the specified anti-cycling rule when \(\theta=0\) or a tie occurs, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transportation simplex pivots around alternating cycles of a bipartite tree basis until every nonbasic reduced cost is nonnegative.

children.title: Square Assignment
children.top_down_role: Assignment models with equal cardinalities on the two bipartite sides.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite sets with \(\lvert I\rvert=\lvert J\rvert=n\).
Every pair \((i,j)\in I\times J\) is allowed and has a finite cost \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete one-to-one assignment with equally many agents and tasks.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 9. Minimum Cost Flows p. 215

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite sets satisfying \(\lvert I\rvert=\lvert J\rvert=n\), and let \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\) be the cost of assigning \(i\in I\) to \(j\in J\). The square assignment problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\ \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\ \text{ for every }i\in I,\ \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\ \text{ for every }j\in J,\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\ \text{ for every }(i,j)\in I\times J\right\}.\] Every feasible solution is a permutation matrix: there is a bijection \(\pi:I\to J\) such that \(x_{i,\pi(i)}=1\) for every \(i\in I\). Conversely, every such bijection is feasible. Thus the model is the unit-supply, unit-demand balanced transportation problem and is equivalent to a minimum-cost perfect matching in the complete bipartite graph on vertex classes \(I\) and \(J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Square assignment matches equally many agents and tasks bijectively while minimizing total cost; its feasible solutions are permutation matrices.
knowledge_statements.title: Square Assignment

children.title: Rectangular Assignment
children.top_down_role: Assignment models with unequal bipartite-side cardinalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the regime in which every vertex of the smaller side is assigned injectively to the larger side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) and \(R\) be finite sets with \(|L|\le |R|\), and let \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) for \((i,j)\in L\times R\). A rectangular assignment is a binary vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{L\times R}\) satisfying
\[\sum_{j\in R}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in L),\qquad \sum_{i\in L}x_{ij}\le 1\quad(j\in R).\]
The minimum-cost rectangular assignment problem minimizes \(\sum_{i\in L}\sum_{j\in R}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) over these vectors. Thus every vertex of \(L\) is assigned, while vertices of \(R\) may remain unused.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rectangular assignment injectively matches every vertex on the smaller side to a distinct vertex on the larger side. The minimum-cost problem selects such an assignment of least total cost.
assumptions_latex: All costs \(c_{ij}\) are finite real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible solutions are precisely injections from \(L\) into \(R\), encoded by \(x\).

notation.meaning: Cost of assigning left vertex i to right vertex j.

children.title: Dummy-Vertex Completion
children.top_down_role: Completion of a rectangular instance to square form using dummy vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Dummy-Vertex Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pads a rectangular assignment instance to a square perfect-assignment instance without changing costs on genuine assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(|L|=m\le n=|R|\). Add a dummy set \(D\) of size \(n-m\), put \(L'=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}D\), and define \(c'_{ij}=c_{ij}\) for \(i\in L\) and \(c'_{dj}=0\) for \(d\in D\). Every perfect assignment on \(L'\times R\) restricts to a rectangular assignment on \(L\times R\); conversely, every rectangular assignment extends by matching the unused vertices of \(R\) bijectively to \(D\). Corresponding solutions have equal objective value, so restriction and extension preserve optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding enough zero-cost dummy vertices makes a rectangular instance square; perfect assignments then project to rectangular assignments with unchanged cost.
assumptions_latex: Dummy edges are permitted to every vertex of \(R\) and have zero cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rectangular optimum equals the perfect-assignment optimum on \(L'\times R\).

notation.meaning: Cost matrix extended by zero-cost dummy rows.

children.title: Partial-Assignment Regime
children.top_down_role: Rectangular settings where unmatched vertices remain part of the intended model.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Assignment Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines assignments of a prescribed cardinality without requiring either vertex class to be saturated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph, let \(c_e\in\mathbb R\), and fix an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le\min\{|L|,|R|\}\). A partial assignment of cardinality \(k\) is a vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) satisfying
\[\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le1\quad(v\in L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R),\qquad \sum_{e\in E}x_e=k.\]
Its cost is \(\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\). The regime permits unmatched vertices on both sides and may be infeasible when \(G\) contains no matching of size \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial assignment is a matching containing exactly k edges; vertices on either side may remain unmatched.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible vectors encode exactly the matchings of cardinality \(k\) in \(G\).

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment as Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a cardinality-constrained bipartite assignment as an integral minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bipartite graph \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\), construct a network with arcs \((s,i)\), \((i,j)\), and \((j,t)\) for \(i\in L\), \((i,j)\in E\), and \(j\in R\). Give every arc capacity \(1\), assign cost \(c_{ij}\) only to \((i,j)\), and require flow value \(k\). Each integral flow corresponds bijectively to a cardinality-\(k\) assignment through \(x_{ij}=f_{ij}\), and its flow cost equals \(\sum_{(i,j)\in E}c_{ij}x_{ij}\). Hence minimum-cost integral flows and minimum-cost partial assignments correspond.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Send k flow units through source–left–right–sink paths. Integral flows select k vertex-disjoint assignment edges with identical total cost.
assumptions_latex: The required flow value is an integer \(k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimum-cost integral flows of value \(k\) correspond cost-preservingly to minimum-cost assignments of cardinality \(k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hungarian Primal–Dual Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the square minimization form using feasible dual labels, equality edges, and augmenting-tree label updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a square cost matrix \(c\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Initialize \(u,v\) with \(u_i+v_j\le c_{ij}\), and maintain a matching using only equality edges \(u_i+v_j=c_{ij}\). From an unmatched left vertex, grow an alternating tree with reachable sets \(S,T\). If no augmenting equality edge exists, set
\[\Delta=\min_{i\in S,\,j\notin T}(c_{ij}-u_i-v_j),\]
replace \(u_i\) by \(u_i+\Delta\) for \(i\in S\) and \(v_j\) by \(v_j-\Delta\) for \(j\in T\), and continue. Augment when possible; output the matching when it is perfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hungarian method alternates equality-graph augmentations with dual-label updates until a perfect matching satisfying complementary slackness is obtained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output perfect matching minimizes \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i,\pi(i)}\).

notation.meaning: Feasible left and right dual labels.
Left and right vertices reached by the alternating tree.
Minimum dual slack crossing from S to the unreached right side.

knowledge_statements.title: Auction Assignment Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the forward auction algorithm for square maximum-weight assignment with additive auction increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input weights \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb R\), prices \(p_j=0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). While some bidder \(i\) is unassigned, choose \(j^*\in\arg\max_j(a_{ij}-p_j)\). Let \(V_1=a_{ij^*}-p_{j^*}\) and \(V_2=\max_{j\ne j^*}(a_{ij}-p_j)\). Raise \(p_{j^*}\) by \(V_1-V_2+\varepsilon\), assign \(i\) to \(j^*\), and unassign its previous bidder, if any. Stop when all bidders are assigned. The output satisfies \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness; for integral weights, it is optimal when \(0<\varepsilon<1/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unassigned bidders repeatedly claim their best net-valued object and raise its price beyond their second-best option; sufficiently small epsilon gives an optimal integral assignment.
assumptions_latex: There are \(n\ge2\) bidders and \(n\) objects, with finite weights \(a_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination yields an \(\varepsilon\)-complementary-slack assignment; if \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\) and \(0<\varepsilon<1/n\), the assignment is maximum-weight.

notation.meaning: Best and second-best net values for the active bidder.

children.title: Cardinality B-Matching Reduction

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality B-Matching Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduces maximum-cardinality bipartite b-matching to maximum flow using vertex-capacity arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) have integer vertex bounds \(b_v\ge0\) and integer edge capacities \(u_e\ge0\). Construct arcs \((s,i)\) of capacity \(b_i\), arcs \((i,j)\) of capacity \(u_{ij}\), and arcs \((j,t)\) of capacity \(b_j\). For every integral flow, set \(x_{ij}=f_{ij}\). Flow conservation gives \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\), and every integral capacitated b-matching extends uniquely to such an internal flow. Moreover, its cardinality \(\sum_{e\in E}x_e\) equals the flow value. Thus maximum cardinality equals maximum flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex bounds become source- and sink-side capacities, edge multiplicities become middle-arc capacities, and b-matching cardinality becomes flow value.
assumptions_latex: All bounds \(b_v\) and capacities \(u_e\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum b-matching cardinality equals the maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow value in the constructed network.

children.title: Weighted B-Matching Reduction

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted B-Matching Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translates fixed-cardinality weighted bipartite b-matching into minimum-cost flow by negating edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the bipartite network with capacities \(b_i,u_{ij},b_j\), assign cost \(-w_{ij}\) to each middle arc \((i,j)\) and zero cost to all other arcs. Require an \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(k\). Under the correspondence \(x_{ij}=f_{ij}\),
\[\operatorname{cost}(f)=-\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}x_{ij}.\]
Consequently, an integral minimum-cost flow of value \(k\) corresponds exactly to a maximum-weight capacitated b-matching of cardinality \(k\), provided such a flow exists. Integrality of capacities permits an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating edge weights turns maximum-weight b-matching of a fixed cardinality into minimum-cost flow of the same value.
assumptions_latex: The bipartite instance has integral capacities \(b_v,u_e\ge0\).
A feasible b-matching of prescribed cardinality \(k\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimum flow cost equals the negative maximum weight among b-matchings of cardinality \(k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Capacity Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes bipartite vertex-incidence bounds as capacities adjacent to the flow source and sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\), introduce a source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Give \((s,i)\) capacity \(b_i\) for every \(i\in L\), give \((j,t)\) capacity \(b_j\) for every \(j\in R\), and orient each edge \(\{i,j\}\in E\) as an arc \((i,j)\) of capacity \(u_{ij}\). Every feasible flow satisfies
\[0\le f_{ij}\le u_{ij},\qquad \sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}f_{ij}\le b_i,\qquad \sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}f_{ij}\le b_j.\]
Conversely, every vector \(x\) satisfying these nonnegativity, edge-capacity, and vertex-incidence bounds extends uniquely on the source and sink arcs by setting \(f_{si}=\sum_jx_{ij}\), \(f_{ij}=x_{ij}\), and \(f_{jt}=\sum_ix_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Left and right vertex bounds become capacities on the adjacent source and sink arcs. Vectors satisfying those bounds and the edge capacities correspond to feasible flows.
assumptions_latex: All vertex and edge capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flow feasibility on the encoded network is equivalent to the b-matching vertex-incidence inequalities together with nonnegativity and edge capacities.

notation.meaning: Capacity of the middle arc representing edge (i,j).

children.title: Objective-Translation Boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Translation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates fixed-cardinality weight translation from objectives that optimize cardinality or permit the empty matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cost substitution \(c_e=-w_e\) preserves a weighted b-matching objective only after the flow value is fixed, or after a separate construction explicitly models variable value. It does not by itself encode maximum cardinality, nor does fixed value encode the convention that an empty matching may dominate negative-weight edges. For example, in a graph consisting of one edge \(e\) with \(w_e=-1\), the unrestricted maximum-weight b-matching is empty with weight \(0\), whereas requiring flow value \(1\) selects \(e\) with weight \(-1\). Therefore cardinality, fixed-value weight, and unrestricted-weight objectives require distinct translations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating weights is correct for fixed flow value, but it does not automatically preserve maximum-cardinality or unrestricted maximum-weight conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reduction must encode the intended cardinality convention separately from the identity \(c_e=-w_e\).

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Bipartite B-Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integral bipartite b-matchings with both vertex-incidence bounds and edge-multiplicity capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph. Given integer vertex capacities \(b_v\ge0\) and integer edge capacities \(u_e\ge0\), a capacitated bipartite b-matching is a vector \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}\) satisfying
\[0\le x_e\le u_e\quad(e\in E),\qquad \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\quad(v\in L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R).\]
Its cardinality is \(\sum_{e\in E}x_e\), and, for edge weights \(w_e\), its weight is \(\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e\). The value \(x_e\) is the permitted multiplicity of edge \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated bipartite b-matching assigns a nonnegative integer multiplicity to each edge while respecting every edge capacity and each endpoint's total incidence capacity.
assumptions_latex: The data \(b_v\) and \(u_e\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities define the feasible capacitated bipartite b-matchings.

knowledge_statements.title: B-Matching Integrality Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers network-flow integrality to the capacitated bipartite b-matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph, with integer bounds \(b_v,u_e\ge0\). Define
\[P=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^{E}:0\le x_e\le u_e,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\text{ for every }v\in L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\right\}.\]
Every vertex of \(P\) is integral. Equivalently, for every linear objective \(w\in\mathbb R^{E}\), there is an optimal solution over \(P\) belonging to \(\mathbb Z^{E}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer vertex and edge capacities make the finite bipartite b-matching polytope integral, so every linear objective has an integral optimum.
assumptions_latex: All bounds \(b_v\) and \(u_e\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every extreme point of \(P\) belongs to \(\mathbb Z^{E}\).
