knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with weights \(w:V\to\mathbb R\). A set \(S\subseteq V\) is closed when \((i,j)\in A\) and \(i\in S\) imply \(j\in S\). Construct a network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), an arc \((s,i)\) of capacity \(w_i\) when \(w_i>0\), an arc \((i,t)\) of capacity \(-w_i\) when \(w_i<0\), and every dependency arc \((i,j)\) assigned capacity \(M\), where \(M>\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i\). If \((C,\bar C)\) is any minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut and \(S=C\cap V\), then \(S\) is a maximum-weight closed set and \[\max_{S'\subseteq V:\,S'\text{ closed}}\sum_{i\in S'}w_i=\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i-\operatorname{mincut}(s,t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any minimum source-sink cut, the original vertices on its source side form a maximum-weight dependency-closed selection; its weight equals total positive vertex weight minus the minimum-cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Closure Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite project set, let \(p_i\in\mathbb R\) be the net profit of project \(i\), and let \(R\subseteq P\times P\) encode prerequisites: \((i,j)\in R\) means selecting \(i\) requires selecting \(j\). With binary variables \(x_i\), the project-selection problem is \[\max\left\{\sum_{i\in P}p_i x_i:x_i\le x_j\ \text{for every }(i,j)\in R,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\] Its feasible selected sets \(S=\{i:x_i=1\}\) are exactly the closed sets of \((P,R)\). Consequently, applying the maximum-closure cut construction with vertex weights \(p_i\) yields an optimal project portfolio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projects with arbitrary net profits are selected subject to prerequisite implications. Feasible portfolios are precisely closed vertex sets, so a maximum-closure minimum-cut construction finds an optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Dependency Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed implication networks for feasible binary selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A selection-dependency network is a finite directed graph \(D=(V,A)\) together with binary selection variables \(x_i\) for \(i\in V\), where an arc \((i,j)\in A\) imposes the implication \(x_i\le x_j\). A binary vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\) is dependency-feasible precisely when all these inequalities hold. Equivalently, its support \(S(x)=\{i\in V:x_i=1\}\) is closed under outgoing arcs. Directed paths encode transitive implications: if a directed path leads from \(i\) to \(j\), then every dependency-feasible vector satisfies \(x_i\le x_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each directed arc means that selecting its tail requires selecting its head. Feasible selections are outgoing-arc-closed sets, and directed paths express transitive requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is dependency-feasible if and only if \(S(x)\) is closed in \(D\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with integral transit times \(\tau_e\ge1\), capacities \(u_e\ge0\), and integer horizon \(T\ge0\). Its discrete time expansion has vertices \((v,\theta)\) for \(v\in V\) and \(\theta\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\). For every \(e=(v,w)\in E\) and integer \(\theta\) satisfying \(\theta+\tau_e\le T\), it contains a transit arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((w,\theta+\tau_e)\) of capacity \(u_e\). For every \(v\in V\) and \(\theta<T\), it contains a holdover arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((v,\theta+1)\) of capacity \(+\infty\). With identical terminal supplies, demands, and boundary conventions in the two models, static flow conservation at time-expanded vertices is equivalent to temporal conservation with unrestricted waiting. Hence feasible discrete temporal flows through horizon \(T\) correspond to feasible static flows in the expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Copy each vertex at every integer time, shift every transit arc by its travel time, and add infinite-capacity holdover arcs for unrestricted waiting. With matching terminal and boundary conventions, static flows in this network represent discrete temporal flows.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Time Expansion

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Time Flow Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate-function formulation of deterministic flow over time with transit delays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc \(e=(v,w)\) of a finite network, let \(f_e:[0,T)\to\mathbb R_+\) be a measurable departure-rate function, with \(0\le f_e(\theta)\le u_e\) almost everywhere and constant transit time \(\tau_e\ge0\). Flow entering \(e\) at time \(\theta\) reaches \(w\) at time \(\theta+\tau_e\). At every intermediate vertex \(v\), feasibility with storage requires, for all \(t\in[0,T]\), \[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}\int_0^{(t-\tau_e)_+}f_e(\theta)\,d\theta-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}\int_0^t f_e(\theta)\,d\theta\ge0.\] Equality describes zero inventory; the nonnegative difference is inventory at \(v\) at time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous-time temporal flow uses measurable arc departure rates. Delayed cumulative inflow minus cumulative outflow is nonnegative inventory, with equality when intermediate storage is forbidden.
assumptions_latex: Arc capacities and transit times are deterministic and time-independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed delayed cumulative-balance inequalities characterize conservation with unrestricted nonnegative intermediate storage.

notation.meaning: departure rate on arc e at time theta

knowledge_statements.title: Holdover-Arc Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-expanded arcs representing one-period waiting at a vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a discrete time-expanded network with layers \(0,\ldots,T\), a holdover arc at vertex \(v\) and time \(\theta<T\) is the arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((v,\theta+1)\). A flow amount on this arc represents material retained at \(v\) throughout period \([\theta,\theta+1)\). Its capacity is the permitted inventory carried across that period: it is \(+\infty\) for unrestricted waiting, a finite value \(b_{v,\theta}\) for bounded storage, and \(0\) when waiting at \(v\) during that period is forbidden.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A holdover arc joins consecutive time copies of one vertex. Its flow is stored inventory, and its capacity specifies whether waiting is unrestricted, bounded, or forbidden.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flow on \(((v,\theta),(v,\theta+1))\) equals inventory carried at \(v\) across period \(\theta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Storage-Capacity Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inventory bounds in discrete or continuous temporal networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_v(t)\) denote inventory stored at vertex \(v\) at time \(t\), after arrivals and departures are accounted for under a fixed boundary convention. A storage-capacity function \(b_v(t)\in\mathbb R_+\cup\{+\infty\}\) imposes the feasibility condition \[0\le I_v(t)\le b_v(t)\qquad\text{for every admissible time }t.\] In a discrete time expansion, this condition is represented by assigning capacity \(b_v(\theta)\) to the holdover arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((v,\theta+1)\). Thus storage bounds are vertex-time constraints in the temporal model and ordinary arc-capacity constraints in its expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inventory at each vertex and time must lie between zero and its storage bound. In a time expansion, that bound becomes the corresponding holdover-arc capacity.
assumptions_latex: Inventory is measured using a fixed arrival-departure boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le I_v(t)\le b_v(t)\), represented discretely by a holdover-arc capacity.

notation.meaning: inventory at vertex v and time t
storage capacity at vertex v and time t

assumptions_latex: Transit times are deterministic and time-independent.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e=(v,w)\) be a physical arc with deterministic, time-independent transit time \(\tau_e\ge0\). A departure on \(e\) at time \(\theta\) arrives at \(w\) at time \(\theta+\tau_e\). In a discrete time expansion, when \(\theta\) and \(\tau_e\) are integral and both endpoint times lie in the horizon, this is represented by a transit arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((w,\theta+\tau_e)\). In continuous time, let \(f_e:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R_+\) be the departure-rate function and assume \(f_e(\theta)=0\) for \(\theta<0\). The cumulative amount delivered through \(e\) by time \(t\ge0\) is then \[A_e(t)=\int_0^{(t-\tau_e)_+}f_e(\theta)\,d\theta.\] Thus capacity constrains departures, while conservation at the head uses the transit-time-shifted arrival process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic transit arc shifts every departure forward by its transit time. The discrete expansion links the corresponding integral time states, while the continuous model obtains cumulative arrivals by shifting the departure-rate integral, assuming no flow is initially in transit.
knowledge_statements.title: Transit-Time Structure

children.title: Waiting–Transit Interaction
children.top_down_role: How waiting choices interact with traversal delays in time-expanded representations.

assumptions_latex: Time and transit times are integral.
Waiting occurs only through available holdover arcs.
Residual capacity \(r_a\) is defined relative to a fixed feasible flow in the time expansion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Waiting \(k\) periods before using \(e\) changes the arrival time from \(\theta+\tau_e\) to \(\theta+k+\tau_e\), and a path-flow amount \(q\) is admissible when each path arc has residual capacity at least \(q\).

notation.meaning: time of arrival at the tail vertex
residual capacity of expanded arc a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of waiting and transit in a discrete time-expanded network.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose flow reaches vertex \(v\) at integral time \(\theta\), waits for \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\) periods, and then enters arc \(e=(v,w)\) with integral transit time \(\tau_e\). In the time expansion this motion is represented by a path of \(k\) successive holdover arcs followed by the transit arc from \((v,\theta+k)\) to \((w,\theta+k+\tau_e)\). Its arrival time is therefore \(\theta+k+\tau_e\). Relative to a fixed feasible expanded flow, let \(r_a\) be the residual capacity of each arc \(a\) on this path. A path-flow amount \(q>0\) can be routed along the path when \(r_a\ge q\) for every path arc and \(\theta+k+\tau_e\le T\), where \(T\) is the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Waiting advances flow through holdover arcs before transit begins, so waiting time and transit time add. A specified path-flow amount can use this route when every holdover and transit arc has enough residual capacity and the resulting arrival is within the horizon.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Horizon Maximum Dynamic Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source, single-sink maximum flow delivered by a prescribed deadline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have source \(s\), sink \(t\), arc rate capacities \(u_e\ge0\), transit times \(\tau_e\ge0\), and horizon \(T>0\). A feasible dynamic flow consists of nonnegative measurable departure rates satisfying arc capacities and temporal conservation at every vertex in \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\), with waiting permitted and zero initial inventory. Its fixed-horizon value is the cumulative flow arriving at \(t\) by time \(T\), namely \[\operatorname{val}_T(f)=\sum_{e\in\delta^-(t)}\int_0^{(T-\tau_e)_+}f_e(\theta)\,d\theta-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(t)}\int_0^T f_e(\theta)\,d\theta.\] The maximum dynamic-flow problem maximizes \(\operatorname{val}_T(f)\) over all feasible dynamic flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a deadline, maximize the net amount that has reached the sink by that time, subject to rate capacities, transit delays, and temporal conservation.
assumptions_latex: Capacities and transit times are deterministic and constant.
Waiting is permitted and initial intermediate inventory is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is \(\max\{\operatorname{val}_T(f):f\text{ is a feasible dynamic flow}\}\).

notation.meaning: net flow delivered to the sink by T

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_T\) be the set of directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths \(P\) satisfying \(\tau(P)<T\), where \(\tau(P)=\sum_{e\in P}\tau_e\). Choose path rates \(x_P\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T:e\in P}x_P\le u_e\) for every arc \(e\). The associated temporally repeated flow dispatches rate \(x_P\) along path \(P\) at every departure time \(\theta\in[0,T-\tau(P))\), with each downstream arc entered after the cumulative transit time of the preceding arcs. This dynamic flow is feasible and delivers value \[\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T}(T-\tau(P))x_P.\] Consequently, the best temporally repeated flow is represented by the static path-flow problem \[\max\left\{\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T}(T-\tau(P))x_P:\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T:e\in P}x_P\le u_e\ \text{for every }e,\ x_P\ge0\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every source-sink path that can reach the sink before the horizon, a static path rate is dispatched continuously until its last deadline-feasible departure. Its delivered amount is the rate multiplied by the horizon minus the path transit time, and the best repeated flow is a weighted static path-flow optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Cut Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum cuts in a time expansion certify discrete dynamic-flow optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integral-horizon temporal network and its finite time expansion, augmented by a supersource connected to admissible source-time copies and a supersink connected from sink-time copies representing deliveries by the horizon. Let \(f\) be a feasible static flow in this expansion and let \((S,\bar S)\) be a supersource-supersink cut. If \[\operatorname{val}(f)=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(S)}\ell_a,\] where \(\ell_a\) and \(u_a\) are expanded-arc lower and upper capacities, then weak duality and static max-flow min-cut imply that \(f\) is maximum. Under the temporal-flow correspondence, the cut is a verifiable certificate that the represented dynamic flow is optimal through the prescribed horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A time-expanded cut whose capacity equals a feasible dynamic flow’s delivered value certifies optimality by static max-flow min-cut duality.
assumptions_latex: Temporal flows and expanded static flows use the same boundary convention.
Every expanded arc has capacities \(0\le\ell_a\le u_a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality between expanded-flow value and cut capacity certifies fixed-horizon dynamic-flow optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Quickest Source–Sink Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-time, single-commodity quickest-flow formulation for a prescribed source–sink demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a directed network have source \(s\), sink \(t\), arc capacities \(u_a\ge 0\), transit times \(\tau_a\ge 0\), and demand \(Q\ge 0\). A feasible flow over time with horizon \(T\) consists of measurable entrance rates \(f_a:[0,T)\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfying \(f_a(\theta)\le u_a\) almost everywhere, temporal flow conservation at every intermediate vertex, and no entrance after \(T-\tau_a\) when arrival by \(T\) is required. The quickest source–sink flow problem is
\[T^*=\inf\{T\ge0:F_t(T)\ge Q\},\]
where \(F_t(T)\) is cumulative net flow arriving at \(t\) by time \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find the least horizon by which a capacity- and transit-time-feasible dynamic flow can deliver the prescribed amount from source to sink.
assumptions_latex: Flow may be held at intermediate vertices unless explicitly forbidden.

notation.meaning: entrance rate into arc a at time theta
cumulative net arrival at the sink by T

For a horizon \(T\), a feasible dynamic transshipment consists of capacity-feasible arc entrance rates and inventories \(I_v(\theta)\ge 0\) satisfying temporal balance, with initial inventories \(I_v(0)=b_v^+:=\max\{b_v,0\}\) and terminal inventories \(I_v(T)=(-b_v)^+:=\max\{-b_v,0\}\). The quickest-transshipment value is \[T^*=\inf\{T\ge 0:\text{there exists a feasible dynamic transshipment realizing }b\text{ by }T\}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Earliest-Arrival Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source, single-sink earliest-arrival criterion over a fixed maximum horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a source \(s\), sink \(t\), and horizon \(T\). For a feasible flow over time \(f\), let \(F_t^f(\theta)\) be its cumulative net arrival at \(t\) by time \(\theta\). The flow \(f^*\) is an earliest-arrival flow through horizon \(T\) if
\[F_t^{f^*}(\theta)\ge F_t^f(\theta)\qquad\text{for every feasible }f\text{ and every }\theta\in[0,T].\]
This simultaneous dominance at every intermediate time is stronger than merely maximizing the amount delivered at \(T\) or minimizing the completion time for one prescribed demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An earliest-arrival flow maximizes cumulative sink arrivals simultaneously at every time up to the chosen horizon.
assumptions_latex: All compared flows use the same temporal network and horizon \(T\).
Cumulative arrivals are measured under the same boundary-time convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_t^{f^*}(\theta)=\max_f F_t^f(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\in[0,T]\).

notation.meaning: cumulative net sink arrival under flow f by theta

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Horizon Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-horizon search using monotonicity of dynamic-flow feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an integer demand specification and a feasibility oracle \(\mathcal F(T)\), first find bounds \(L<U\) with \(\mathcal F(L)=\mathrm{false}\) and \(\mathcal F(U)=\mathrm{true}\), doubling \(U\) if necessary. While \(U-L>1\), set \(M=\lfloor(L+U)/2\rfloor\); if \(\mathcal F(M)\) is true, replace \(U\) by \(M\), and otherwise replace \(L\) by \(M\). Return \(U\) and a feasible flow supplied by the final oracle call. Correctness uses the monotonicity implication
\[\mathcal F(T)\Longrightarrow\mathcal F(T+1),\]
which holds when a feasible solution may wait or remain idle.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed network, let \(T\in\mathbb Z_+\), and let every arc \(a\in A\) have a transit time \(\tau_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\). For \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), let \(x_{a,t}\ge 0\) be flow dispatched onto arc \(a\) at the beginning of period \(t\), subject to \(x_{a,t}\le u_{a,t}\). Given initial inventories \(I_{v,0}\), external net supplies \(b_{v,t}\), and nonnegative inventories \(I_{v,t}\), dynamic balance requires \[I_{v,t+1}=I_{v,t}+b_{v,t}+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_{a,t+1-\tau_a}-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_{a,t}\] for every \(v\in V\) and \(t=0,ldots,T-1\), where variables with indices outside \(\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\) are interpreted as zero. A feasible collection \((x,I)\) satisfying these constraints and the prescribed terminal inventory or demand requirements is a dynamic transshipment.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Flow over Time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost, discrete-time dynamic transshipment over a fixed finite horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given horizon \(T\), arc-time costs \(c_{a,t}\), holding costs \(h_{v,t}\), capacities, transit times, supplies, demands, and admissible terminal inventories, the minimum-cost flow-over-time problem chooses a feasible dynamic transshipment \((x,I)\) minimizing
\[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{a\in A}c_{a,t}x_{a,t}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{v\in V}h_{v,t}I_{v,t}.\]
Feasibility includes delayed flow balance, arc-time capacity bounds, nonnegative inventories, and the stated terminal regime. If storage is disallowed, the corresponding intermediate inventories are fixed to zero; if holding is free, the relevant \(h_{v,t}\) vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a feasible flow and inventory trajectory minimizing total time-indexed transportation and storage cost.
assumptions_latex: The horizon and all temporal data are finite.
Costs are linear and all decision variables are continuous.
Dynamic balance uses the prescribed arc transit times.

children.title: Multiperiod Transportation
children.top_down_role: Transportation decisions distributed across several planning periods.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiperiod Transportation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time transportation model with period-specific shipments and carried inventory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be supply locations, \(D\) demand locations, and \(t=1,\ldots,T\). A multiperiod transportation plan chooses shipments \(x_{ij,t}\ge0\) and inventories \(I_{i,t},J_{j,t}\ge0\) satisfying
\[I_{i,t}=I_{i,t-1}+s_{i,t}-\sum_{j\in D}x_{ij,t},\qquad J_{j,t}=J_{j,t-1}+\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij,t}-d_{j,t},\]
with any prescribed shipment capacities and boundary inventories. A standard linear model minimizes \(\sum_{i,j,t}c_{ij,t}x_{ij,t}\) plus holding and shortage costs. Positive transit times are represented by shifting shipment arrivals to later balance equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Plan shipments across several periods while balancing time-varying supplies, demands, inventories, capacities, and costs.
assumptions_latex: The planning horizon is finite and discrete.
Supplies and demands are specified by location and period.
Inventory and shipment variables are nonnegative unless backlogging is explicitly allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,I,J)\) is admissible exactly when all period balances, capacities, and boundary conditions hold.

children.title: Dynamic Inventory
children.top_down_role: Inventory carryover represented through temporal storage structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Inventory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time inventory state equation with optional loss, replenishment, and withdrawal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a location \(v\) and periods \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), let \(I_{v,t}\) be beginning inventory, \(r_{v,t}\) total replenishment arriving during period \(t\), and \(q_{v,t}\) total withdrawal. With retention factor \(\alpha_{v,t}\in[0,1]\), dynamic inventory obeys
\[I_{v,t+1}=\alpha_{v,t}I_{v,t}+r_{v,t}-q_{v,t}.\]
Feasibility additionally requires prescribed bounds \(\underline I_{v,t}\le I_{v,t}\le\overline I_{v,t}\) and initial inventory \(I_{v,0}\). The lossless case has \(\alpha_{v,t}=1\); backlog models instead permit negative inventory under explicitly stated lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inventory is a time-indexed state obtained from retained stock plus arrivals minus withdrawals, subject to bounds and initial conditions.
assumptions_latex: The horizon is finite and discrete.
Arrivals and withdrawals use a fixed within-period timing convention.
Inventory bounds and initial states are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{v,t+1}=\alpha_{v,t}I_{v,t}+r_{v,t}-q_{v,t}\) with \(\underline I_{v,t}\le I_{v,t}\le\overline I_{v,t}\).

children.title: Transport–Inventory Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interaction between shipment timing and inventory carryover.

knowledge_statements.title: Transport–Inventory Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-time balance linking dispatched transport, delayed arrivals, external supply, demand, and inventory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_{a,t}\) be dispatch on arc \(a\) at time \(t\), with transit time \(\tau_a\), and let \(I_{v,t}\) be inventory. The transport and inventory decisions are coupled at every vertex \(v\) and period \(t\) by
\[I_{v,t+1}=I_{v,t}+s_{v,t}-d_{v,t}+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_{a,t+1-\tau_a}-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_{a,t},\]
where terms with invalid time indices are zero. Together with arc capacities and inventory bounds, this equality prevents material from being dispatched before it is available and credits incoming transport only upon arrival.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each node and time, next inventory equals current inventory plus supply and delayed arrivals minus demand and dispatches.
assumptions_latex: Time and transit times are integral.
A fixed convention determines whether period events occur before or after inventory measurement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{v,t+1}=I_{v,t}+s_{v,t}-d_{v,t}+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_{a,t+1-\tau_a}-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_{a,t}\).

children.title: Terminal-Inventory Regimes
children.top_down_role: Alternative end-horizon requirements for remaining inventory.

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Inventory Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary conditions distinguishing free, fixed, bounded, cyclic, and penalized terminal stock.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For terminal inventory \(I_{v,T}\), common regimes are: free terminal stock, imposing only \(I_{v,T}\in[\underline I_{v,T},\overline I_{v,T}]\); fixed stock, imposing \(I_{v,T}=\widehat I_v\); depletion, imposing \(I_{v,T}=0\); cyclic stock, imposing \(I_{v,T}=I_{v,0}\); and penalized stock, leaving \(I_{v,T}\) variable but adding a terminal value or penalty \(\phi_v(I_{v,T})\) to the objective. Exactly one declared regime, or a compatible combination of bounds and terminal cost, must be included to determine which end-of-horizon inventories are feasible and how residual stock is valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Terminal stock may be free, fixed, depleted, cyclic, or valued by a terminal cost; the chosen regime closes the finite-horizon model.
assumptions_latex: A finite terminal time \(T\) is fixed.
Terminal bounds and any terminal-value function are specified consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{v,T}\) must satisfy the declared terminal constraint and contributes \(\phi_v(I_{v,T})\) when terminal valuation is used.

knowledge_statements.title: Project-Scheduling Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activity-on-arc acyclic network representation without resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be an acyclic activity-on-arc project network with event vertices, activity durations \(p_a\ge0\), source event \(s\), and completion event \(t\). Event times \(E_v\) are feasible precisely when
\[E_w\ge E_v+p_{(v,w)}\qquad\text{for every }(v,w)\in A,\quad E_s=0.\]
The earliest feasible event times satisfy \(E_w=\max_{(v,w)\in A}(E_v+p_{(v,w)})\), and the minimum project completion time is
\[E_t=\max_{P:s\leadsto t}\sum_{a\in P}p_a.\]
Thus precedence-constrained scheduling without resource limits is represented by a longest-path problem in a directed acyclic network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an acyclic activity network, precedence constraints become difference inequalities and the earliest project completion equals the longest source-to-finish path.
assumptions_latex: The project network is finite and acyclic.
No renewable or cumulative resource constraints are imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_t=\max_{P:s\leadsto t}\sum_{a\in P}p_a\).

notation.meaning: earliest feasible time of event v

children.title: Dynamic Evacuation Flow
children.top_down_role: Temporal network models for moving populations toward designated safe destinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Evacuation Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time deterministic evacuation with capacities, transit times, and optional storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_v\ge 0\) be the initial population at each vertex, with \(q_v=0\) outside the source set unless otherwise specified. A dynamic evacuation flow consists of values \(f_a(t)\ge 0\) for every arc \(a\in A\) and admissible departure time \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), together with inventories \(z_v(t)\ge 0\). Set \(z_v(-1)=q_v\). For every nonsafe vertex \(v\) and time \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), require \[z_v(t)=z_v(t-1)+\sum_{a=(w,v)}\sum_{s:\,s+\tau_a(s)=t}f_a(s)-\sum_{a=(v,w)}f_a(t).\] Each departure satisfies \(f_a(t)\le u_a(t)\) and \(t+\tau_a(t)\le T\). Flow arriving at a vertex in \(D\) is counted as evacuated and is removed from subsequent conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic evacuation flow moves the initial population through capacitated arcs over time, conserves people and stored inventory at nonsafe vertices, and removes people from the system when they reach safe sinks.
assumptions_latex: The directed network is \(G=(V,A)\), with source set \(S\), safe-sink set \(D\), discrete horizon \(\{0,\ldots,T\}\), capacities \(u_a(t)\), and nonnegative integer transit times \(\tau_a(t)\).
Each vertex has initial population \(q_v\ge0\), and flow may be stored at nonsafe vertices unless a separate waiting restriction is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dynamic evacuation flow is a nonnegative temporal arc flow and inventory process satisfying arc capacities, horizon-admissible travel, temporal conservation at nonsafe vertices, the specified initial population, and absorption at safe sinks.

children.title: Dynamic Routing
children.top_down_role: Time-indexed routing choices under temporal capacities or travel times.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Route-departure representation of discrete-time evacuation routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R_T\) be the set of admissible route-departure pairs \(r=(P,\theta)\), where the departure time \(\theta\) and the permitted waiting steps determine the time-stamped arc-time pairs used by route \(P\). A dynamic routing assigns \(h_r\ge0\) to every \(r\in\mathcal R_T\). Its induced temporal arc flow is \[f_a(t)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_T:\,(a,t)\in r}h_r.\] The routing is feasible when these induced values respect all arc-time capacities, every used route reaches a safe sink by \(T\), and \(\sum_{r:\,s(r)=s}h_r=q_s\) for every source \(s\in S\). When waiting is allowed, it is represented by time-stamped holdover steps in \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic routing assigns evacuees to admissible route-and-departure choices whose aggregate arc-time usage respects capacities and evacuates the required amount from each source.
assumptions_latex: The discrete-time temporal network, horizon \(T\), source set \(S\), safe-sink set \(D\), and required source amounts \(q_s\ge0\) are specified.
Every admissible route-departure pair reaches a safe sink by the horizon and respects the applicable waiting policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route assignment is feasible precisely when its induced temporal arc flow satisfies the temporal capacity constraints and its source totals equal the required evacuation amounts.

assumptions_latex: A feasible evacuation flow delivers total population \(Q\) to safe sinks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two standard deterministic objectives: last-arrival clearance and aggregate arrival time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible evacuation that delivers every unit \(q\) to a safe sink at time \(A(q)\), the clearance-time objective minimizes \(T_{\mathrm{clear}}=\max_q A(q)\), the first time by which the entire population is safe. The aggregate evacuation-time objective minimizes \(C_{\mathrm{sum}}=\sum_q A(q)\) for discrete units, or \(C_{\mathrm{sum}}=\int_0^Q A(\xi)\,d\xi\) for divisible flow indexed by cumulative mass \(\xi\). The objectives are distinct: identical clearance times need not imply identical aggregate arrival times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clearance time measures the last safe arrival, whereas aggregate evacuation time sums or integrates all safe-arrival times.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Transit Times

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A time-dependent transit-time function assigns a nonnegative integer \(\tau_a(t)\) to every arc \(a=(v,w)\) and departure time \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\). Flow entering \(a\) at time \(t\) reaches \(w\) at \(\alpha_a(t)=t+\tau_a(t)\). The departure is horizon-admissible exactly when \(\alpha_a(t)\le T\), in which case its discrete time-expanded representation is the arc from \((v,t)\) to \((w,\alpha_a(t))\). When FIFO is imposed, it requires \(t\le s\Rightarrow\alpha_a(t)\le\alpha_a(s)\) for all departure times \(t,s\) on the same arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete time-dependent transit time maps each timed arc departure to an integer arrival layer; FIFO additionally prevents a later departure on the same arc from arriving earlier.
assumptions_latex: The time domain is the discrete grid \(\{0,\ldots,T\}\).
Each arc traversal has a deterministic nonnegative integer transit time depending on its departure time, and departures arriving after \(T\) are infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A departure on \(a=(v,w)\) at time \(t\) arrives at time \(\alpha_a(t)=t+\tau_a(t)\) and, when \(\alpha_a(t)\le T\), is represented by the corresponding time-expanded arc.

notation.meaning: integer transit time of arc a for departure at t

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When capacities and transit times vary jointly, each feasible arc-time choice \((a,t)\), with \(a=(v,w)\), is represented by a time-expanded arc \[((v,t),(w,t+\tau_a(t)))\] having capacity \(u_a(t)\). Its flow satisfies \(0\le f_a(t)\le u_a(t)\), and it contributes to conservation at vertex \(w\) only at time \(t+\tau_a(t)\). Thus capacity is indexed by the departure event while conservation is coupled to the associated arrival event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint variation assigns each timed arc both a departure-specific capacity and a departure-specific arrival layer.

Time expansion is required to represent every departure and arrival exactly without rounding.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A uniform finite-grid expansion with mesh \(\Delta\) is exact only if every relevant release time, deadline, capacity breakpoint, and arrival \(t+\tau_a(t)\) lies in \(\Delta\mathbb Z\). If, for example, one arc has transit time \(1\) and another has transit time \(\sqrt2\), no positive \(\Delta\) places both transit times on the same integer grid. Any finite uniform-grid model must then round or approximate an event time, potentially changing reachability, deadline feasibility, or capacity usage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact uniform discretization fails when event or transit times are not commensurate; rounding can change temporal feasibility.

In a time-expanded network where waiting is represented by holdover flow \(h_v(t)\) on \(((v,t),(v,t+1))\), the same restriction is imposed as \(0\le h_v(t)\le K_v(t)\), under the convention that all stored inventory advances through that holdover arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A storage restriction caps the inventory that may wait at each vertex and time, equivalently bounding the corresponding holdover flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A waiting-prohibition regime requires flow arriving at every nonexempt nonsink vertex to depart immediately at that same time. In a time-expanded representation this is enforced by deleting all holdover arcs \(((v,t),(v,t+1))\), or equivalently by imposing \(h_v(t)=0\) for every prohibited vertex-time pair. Temporal conservation then equates flow arriving at \((v,t)\) with flow entering transit arcs departing from \((v,t)\); feasibility may therefore fail even when the corresponding model with unrestricted waiting is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Waiting is prohibited by removing or zeroing holdover arcs, forcing all arriving flow to continue immediately.

children.title: Bounded-Waiting Regimes
children.top_down_role: Temporal models imposing finite limits on waiting duration.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Waiting Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time temporal walks with vertex-specific or global upper bounds on waiting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have integer arc transit times \(\tau_a\ge 1\) and horizon \(T\). A temporal walk is described by arc-entry times \(t_1,\ldots,t_m\) along a directed walk \(a_i=(v_{i-1},v_i)\), with waiting duration \(w_i=t_{i+1}-(t_i+\tau_{a_i})\) at \(v_i\). Given bounds \(W_v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}\), the walk satisfies the vertex-bounded-waiting regime exactly when \(0\le w_i\le W_{v_i}\) for every intermediate visit and \(t_m+\tau_{a_m}\le T\). A global total-waiting regime instead requires \(\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}w_i\le W\). These predicates restrict temporal paths independently of arc-capacity feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A temporal walk is bounded-waiting feasible when every intermediate wait respects its vertex bound, or when its aggregate waiting respects a specified global bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with integral transit times and finite horizon \(T\).
Waiting occurs only at intermediate vertices of a temporal walk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le w_i\le W_{v_i}\) for all intermediate visits, or \(\sum_i w_i\le W\) under the global convention.

notation.meaning: waiting duration after traversing the ith arc
maximum permitted wait at vertex v

children.title: Storage–Waiting Feasibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: Feasibility effects arising from the interaction of limited storage with restricted waiting.

knowledge_statements.title: Storage–Waiting Feasibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes admissible waiting from feasible storage at intermediate vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a discrete-time dynamic flow, let \(I_v(t)\) denote flow that has reached vertex \(v\) by time \(t\) but has not yet departed. Waiting at \(v\) is storage-feasible precisely when \(0\le I_v(t)\le B_v(t)\) for every permitted storage vertex and time. If storage is prohibited, \(B_v(t)=0\), hence every feasible unit must depart upon availability; if \(B_v(t)>0\), waiting remains possible only while the inventory bound holds. Thus arc-capacity and flow-conservation constraints alone do not certify temporal feasibility when waiting creates positive intermediate inventory: omitting the storage inequalities can admit schedules that exceed physical storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Waiting is feasible exactly while intermediate inventory stays within storage capacity; ignoring this condition can make an arc-feasible temporal schedule physically infeasible.
assumptions_latex: Time is discrete and all arrivals and departures use a common event convention.
\(B_v(t)\ge0\) is the available storage capacity at vertex \(v\) and time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le I_v(t)\le B_v(t)\) for every storage vertex \(v\) and event time \(t\).

notation.meaning: inventory waiting at vertex v at time t
storage capacity at vertex v and time t

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Dependent Travel Times
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of fixed-transit-time temporal-network and time-expansion models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose entry at time \(\theta\) onto arc \(a\) incurs travel time \(\tau_a(\theta,x_a)\), where \(x_a\) is the relevant arc inflow, occupancy, or flow history. A fixed time-expanded network uses predetermined arrival arcs from \((u,\theta)\) to \((v,\theta+\bar\tau_a(\theta))\). It represents the model exactly only if the realized travel time equals the predetermined value for every feasible flow. When two feasible flow profiles give different values of \(\tau_a(\theta,x_a)\), no single such expansion represents both profiles. Arrival times and conservation indices then depend on the unknown flow, producing an endogenous, generally nonlinear or equilibrium-constrained model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed time expansion fails when feasible flow profiles induce different arc travel times, because its arrival-time arcs must be chosen before the flow is known.
assumptions_latex: Arc travel time is evaluated from a specified inflow, occupancy, or flow-history state.
The comparison concerns a single fixed time-expanded graph with predetermined temporal arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_a(\theta,x_a^{(1)})\ne\tau_a(\theta,x_a^{(2)})\) for feasible profiles implies that one predetermined arrival arc cannot encode both realizations.

notation.meaning: endogenous travel time on arc a for entry time and flow state
arc flow state on which travel time depends
travel time fixed in a time expansion

review_flags: exact boundary is mathematically unambiguous but unsupported by supplied static-network locators
source distinguishing dynamic congestion or equilibrium models from fixed time expansion is required

No cited source verifies this exact limitation or the further characterization as generally nonlinear or equilibrium-constrained.

knowledge_statements.title: Multicommodity Temporal Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates splittable temporal multicommodity flow from integral or unsplittable variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For commodities \(k\in K\), a discrete time expansion with exogenous transit times represents splittable temporal flow by variables \(x_{a,t}^k\ge0\), commodity-wise conservation, and shared capacities \(\sum_{k\in K}x_{a,t}^k\le u_a(t)\). This remains a linear multicommodity-flow formulation. The boundary is crossed when each commodity must use one temporal path or its variables must be integral: the additional conditions require path-selection or integrality constraints and are not captured by the continuous relaxation. Moreover, aggregating commodities into one flow is generally invalid when origins, destinations, release times, deadlines, or admissible waiting rules differ, because aggregate conservation does not preserve commodity identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splittable temporal commodities admit a shared-capacity linear model; unsplittability, integrality, or commodity-specific timing prevents reduction to an aggregate single-commodity flow.
assumptions_latex: Transit times and temporal capacities are exogenous on a finite discrete horizon.
Each commodity has specified terminals and temporal requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\in K}x_{a,t}^k\le u_a(t)\) yields a linear relaxation, but integral or single-path requirements and heterogeneous temporal data require commodity-indexed constraints.

notation.meaning: commodity-k flow entering temporal arc a at time t
shared temporal capacity of arc a at time t
